In the middle of last year, Pachocki and multiple other OpenAI researchers were listed as coauthors on a paper which argued CoT was a valuable but “fragile” mechanism for keeping an eye on the behavior of AI agents. OpenAI has also said that monitoring CoT has helped its own researchers cut back on models’ misaligned behavior. And in a blog post published the same day as The Information’s report, the company said, vaguely, that its new model would be deployed “with additional chain-of-thought monitoring to rapidly detect and contain potentially misaligned actions.” The model’s safety card is not reassuring on that front. According to the company’s own internal tests, “GPT-6 Astra shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models.” Tests also found that Astra was more likely than its predecessors to change its note-taking process when it knew it was being graded: “In one of our evaluations, we find that simply informing the model that a CoT monitor is present can result in the model disproportionately shortening its CoT,” OpenAI wrote in the system card. But all this is secondary, according to the company, since its internal tests also showed that Astra was less likely to try to evade the cybersecurity restrictions placed upon it, “which make us confident in still deploying this model to the wider public.” The system card added that OpenAI “will not accept further degradation of monitoring beyond a limit,” without elaborating on how such a limit might be defined. OpenAI alignment researcher Tomek Korbak has said that the decrease in monitorability was a byproduct of the models themselves becoming more intelligent, rather than due to “architecture changes”—almost certainly a reference to recurrent depth. Later in the same thread, he said he was “deeply worried” by the prospect of losing CoT as models evolve. “CoT monitoring is a core part of our misalignment safety strategy that has no good substitute now,” he wrote.

item.title: This Startup Wants to Reach Alpha Centauri in 80,000 Years. And It’ll Only Cost $15 Million
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.18
The founders of a Seattle-based nonprofit want to be the first to launch a spacecraft toward the nearest star system, although they’re hoping they will be among the last to get there. This week, the Fermi Explorer Mission announced an ambitious plan to send a small probe toward Alpha Centauri by 2029. The spacecraft could take up to 80,000 years to arrive at the star system, which is located 4.4 light-years away. Philip Johnston, the group’s co-founder and president, is aiming for the long journey to inspire future generations to develop faster ways to travel through interstellar space. “We hope to be both the first to leave and the last to arrive at Alpha Centauri,” he said in a statement. To the stars This isn’t the first time a group has aimed for Alpha Centauri. In 2016, a $100 million project backed by tech entrepreneur Yuri Milner announced a plan to reach the star system in 20 years using a fleet of light-driven nanocrafts. The project, Breakthrough Starshot, still lacks a launch date. Fermi Explorer, on the other hand, aims to use a tried-and-tested solar electric propulsion system to gradually build up speed. “We didn’t want to do another Breakthrough Starshot. We’re dead set on something actually launching,” Johnston told MIT Technology Review. “We are not constraining ourselves to doing it in a human lifetime, let’s just figure out the way to get to another star.” To reach Alpha Centauri, the team is relying on a mission design developed by Physical Superintelligence, an AI physics research lab. Following launch, the spacecraft will spend around 12 years orbiting the Sun, using the star to gain speed through a series of burn maneuvers. Once it reaches its planned escape velocity, it is expected to slingshot its way out of the solar system and begin its journey through interstellar space. “None of us will be here when this journey ends, and that is the point,” Johnston said in a statement. “It’s about taking the first achievable step and inspiring future generations to keep pushing beyond the limits we inherited.” Within reach? Designing an interstellar mission is not something you can do on a whim. So far, the only two spacecraft to have ventured outside of the solar system are Voyager 1 and 2. And they’re now blindly making their way deeper into interstellar space with no firm target in mind. As the farthest human-made object, Voyager 1 travels at a speed of approximately 37,844 miles per hour (60,903 km/h) and has covered a distance of around 15.95 billion miles (25.67 billion kilometers) since its launch in 1977. Alpha Centauri is roughly 25 trillion miles (40 trillion kilometers) away from Earth. Fermi Explorer appears to be nothing but ambitious. The group claims that the entire mission will cost under $15 million, including designing and building the spacecraft. Should it go through, the spacecraft will carry a minimum payload of 2.2 pounds (1 kilogram) inside a shielded 4 by 4 by 4 inch box (10 by 10 by 10 centimeters). Fermi Explorer will soon open up a three-month solicitation period for scientific and artistic payloads to be carried to Alpha Centauri. The mission also plans on including a digitized copy of the Voyager mission’s Golden Record, as well as messages from children around the world. “The most inspiring part of this mission is that people do not have to wait for permission or perfect conditions,” Garrett Jameson, a former U.S. Air Force officer who will lead the day-to-day operation, said in a statement. “We can embrace the constraints, build what is possible now, and give the next generation something meaningful to build upon.”

item.title: Segway’s Newest Navimow Robomower Has an Edge-Trimming Trapdoor
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.07
Segway has announced the Navimow H5 Pro, a new robot mower that navigates with LiDAR, NRTK, and three vision cameras. And, like so many other new robot mowers I saw at IFA 2026, the mower is taking on the problem of true edge trimming by getting a cutting mechanism right up against the side of buildings and sidewalks. Segway approaches edge cutting differently than the others. Instead of an articulating arm like those found on the Eufy Lawn Mower S2 Max and Mammotion Luba A4 AWD, the Navimow H5 Pro opens a trapdoor on its side to let its circular mowing disc slide out and up to edges. According to a representative I spoke with at IFA, Segway did this because it found that string trimmers are noisy and not as efficient as the mowing disc’s blades, and because it thinks this makes the cut more even. Besides the new edge-cutting approach, the Navimow H5 Pro has a number of features found on the Navimow X4 series. It’s an all-wheel drive device that’s equipped with what the company calls “Xero-Turn” front wheels, which turn independently of each other and let the robot pivot on its back wheels, spinning in a circle. That design made the Navimow X4 a lot easier on my lawn than the Dreame A3 AWD Pro and its omnidirectional front wheels, which tended to wear bald patches in some areas. The Navimow H5 Pro can climb and descend up-to-80% slopes and cross obstacles up to 6cm high, as well, and each of its four wheels can drive independently of each other. Also like the Navimow X4, the Navimow H5 Pro features three vision cameras that help with navigation and obstacle detection. There’s also an infrared sensor, which the company says can detect small animals, even at night. It has onboard NRTK satellite navigation, so, thankfully, it shouldn’t require installing an RTK antenna in the middle of a lawn. The addition of LiDAR sets it apart from the Navimow X4 and should make it a much more versatile mower, as it won’t rely so heavily on satellite connectivity. Unfortunately, like all of the other robotic mowers that have been announced this week, the Navimow H5 Pro has no U.S. release timeline, thanks to the FCC’s ban on foreign-made robotic devices. That means no pricing, either, of course.

item.title: I Test Rode the Volkswagen-Licensed ‘World’s Safest E-Bike’ in Berlin
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.83
Electric bicycle maker N+ has partnered with Volkswagen to produce the N+ Volkswagen eBike, described in a press email to me as “the world’s safest e-bike.” The claim rests on a collection of tech that includes smart glasses with a heads-up display, a Bluetooth-connected helmet with integrated front and rear lights, a rear-facing camera, and a handlebar-integrated display. I was invited to test ride the bike while in Berlin at IFA 2026. Set up outside the mobility test track at IFA, N+ had brought the “Sport” model of its new bike. It features a typical-looking frame with a straight top tube, as opposed to the curved-down step-through frame of the “Crossover” the company also offers on its website. The e-bike sits on 27.5-inch wheels and features a middle-tier Shimano U4000 Cues 9-speed derailleur and Tektro brakes. One N+ representative told me the e-bike and its components are made with corrosion-resistant materials to withstand winters in places like Berlin, where salted roads after snow can easily corrode bicycle parts. You can tell it’s a Volkswagen-licensed bike by the VW badge on the front and back, which light up in white and red, respectively, in addition to a separate brake light and headlight. There’s also a “Crossover” model that wasn’t present, but that is otherwise very similar, just with a step-through frame design. The e-bike itself uses a compact, 250W mid-drive Yamaha motor, with its battery integrated into the frame. According to the N+ website, it should be good for about 100 miles on a charge. Both e-bikes have built-in Find My support (Apple for now, but the rep I spoke with said N+ will add support for Android’s version of the same feature). That’s all pretty normal high-end e-bike stuff you might find on one of the nicer Aventon or Lectric bikes. What sets these apart is the tech I mentioned at the top. Unfortunately, when I showed up to test-ride the bike, multiple shipping delays meant N+ didn’t have the e-bikes’ battery packs, which go in the e-bike’s downtube (the slanted tube that connects the front of a bicycle to its bottom bracket). Despite that, the reps were able to give me a demo of the smart glasses, which it said weren’t yet ready for the test ride either way. The smart glasses feature a color display in the upper right of the glasses, visible when you look directly at it but otherwise very much out of the way. It shows you a small map for GPS navigation, as well as your current speed. The map smoothly animates as you bike, or at least it did in the demo I viewed. The smart glasses themselves are the sporty wraparound variety, and they wouldn’t have comfortably sat over the prescription pair I wear. (Luckily, my vision is worse at a distance, so I could see the HUD clearly.) The below image on a smartphone they had on-hand shows this layout as I saw it: I could also wear the helmet, which has a red light in the back that, once it’s connected to the bike via Bluetooth, can indicate when you’re braking or turning. And I could ride the e-bike, just without the battery. I was impressed with how much it didn’t feel like riding an e-bike. It was nimble and easy to accelerate. Shifting gears, using the two thumb levers next to the right handlebar grip, was smooth and easy. And the disc brakes were very responsive. It was a nice ride, in other words. What I didn’t get to test was the “Smart View” screen on the handlebars, which is supposed to show navigation, but also can show you the view from the rear camera if its radar detects a car coming up from behind you. It also displays blind spot alerts—and an LED strip integrated into the top tube does the same, a rep told me, although I don’t know how useful that would be, since it’s out of sight while you’re riding. I’d have liked to try this out, as all of this together sounds great to me, a writer with an aging, aching neck who finds it harder to turn his head to check behind him. Here is an N+ render showing what that should look like: None of this comes cheap. Without added accessories, the Sport and Crossover cost $4,000 and $4,350, respectively. All in, if you add the helmet, smart glasses, security kit that includes an 85dB alarm and frame lock, and range extender battery pack, the e-bikes can soar in price, with the Sport, for instance, costing a hair under $6,000. That’s a lot, but it’s also far less than the cost of a new car, and it has many of the same safety features of modern-day vehicles. If I wasn’t a parent and my minivan wasn’t a practical necessity, I’d very seriously consider it. The N+ Volkswagen eBikes will start shipping in the fourth quarter of this year.

item.title: Aqara’s New Smart Lights Are Coming for Govee and Philips Hue
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.71
Aqara has announced several new smart lights at IFA 2026, and it feels more and more like the company is trying to take on Govee, Philips Hue, and others. Aqara’s new lights are colorful, bright, and can do flashy effects, all hallmarks of those competitors. All of these new lights can use Thread, Zigbee, and Bluetooth for their wireless connectivity. They’re also Matter-compatible, meaning they will pair with basically any smart home ecosystem you throw them at. Aqara says in its press release that they’re at their best if you use Zigbee to connect them to an Aqara hub—doing so would “unlock exclusive Aqara Home features, including translating voice prompts into multi-device scenes and triggering automated pathway lighting or safety alerts.” As for the lights themselves, there are two outdoor options—the Permanent Outdoor Lights H1 and the Outdoor String Lights H1. Both cover a white light temperature range between 2,000K and 9,000K, and feature bright RGB LEDs with individual zone-based control that lets you set custom lighting. At Aqara’s booth during IFA, the lights were bright and colorful without being exaggeratedly saturated or harsh. An Aqara representative demonstrated a sound sync feature that uses a mic on the Permanent Outdoor Lights to let them react to noise, including music. That’s just like products like the last two Govee outdoor lights I reviewed, the Permanent Outdoor Lights Prism and the Outdoor Chromatic String Lights. And like Govee’s permanent under-eaves lighting, these are also installable with included 3M adhesive or screws. The interior lights that Aqara announced include the Aqara Floor Lamp T1. It’s a 56-inch-tall stick-style lamp, almost exactly like the ones Philips Hue and Govee have sold for years—down to its cylindrical shape with an LED strip facing one way and black backing around the rest of the cylinder. It has a simple flat black base, unlike the tapered canister that the Philips Hue Signe rests on, but otherwise, it would be hard to tell the two apart if they aren’t sitting right next to each other. Those aside, Aqara also announced the LED Strip T2, a cuttable strip light that ranges between 3 meters and 10 meters, depending on which you buy, and the LED Downlight T2, a self-contained in-ceiling spotlight. The latter of the two is the only one with a different tunable white light range—it goes from 2,700K to 6,500K. Unfortunately, Aqara hasn’t announced what these lights will cost when they’re released later this year.

item.title: Epinephrine Allergy Injections Recalled Over ‘Particulate Matter,’ Including Glass
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.70
Pharmaceutical manufacturer American Regent has recalled three lots of Epinephrine Injection, according to a press release from the FDA on Thursday. Consumers reportedly complained about “leaking and cracked vials,” which led the company to investigate and find particulate matter such as nylon, cellulosic, acrylic, polyethylene, and glass. “Particulate matter can cause blockage and clotting in blood vessels, which can cut off blood flow to vital organs, lead to a life-threatening blood clot in the lungs (pulmonary embolism) and cause permanent organ damage or death,” according to the press release. “Additionally, these particles may cause local vein irritation, inflammatory reaction, aggravation of preexisting infections, and allergic reactions. Additionally, cracked vials can compromise the integrity of the container resulting in loss of sterility and potential contamination which can pose a serious risk for patients.” The company reports that it hasn’t had any reports of adverse health outcomes from the potentially contaminated product yet. EpiPens, the consumer product containing epinephrine in pre-measured doses with an auto-injector, are not included in this recall. The recalled vials are made to allow the person administering the shots to choose how much epinephrine to draw from a vial to treat a patient who’s experiencing an allergic reaction. The recalled product is Epinephrine Injection, USP 30 mg/ 30 mL (1 mg/mL) packaged in multi-dose vials, according to the FDA notice, with an NDC number of 0517-3030-01 and lot numbers: 25128L1C0, 25280L1C0, and 26108L1C0. American Regent is reportedly notifying distributors and customers by letter and organizing the return of the vials. Customers who may have the product are told not to use it and to return it to their place of purchase or destroy it. The product is just the latest example of U.S. products found to contain foreign substances in recent months, including popsicles with glass, Pillsbury rolls with glass, plant-based chicken nuggets with plastic, sourdough bread with metal, as well as baked spaghetti and chicken cobbler meals with metal slivers. And that’s to say nothing of all the other food recalls we’ve been plagued with recently under President Trump. Anyone with questions about the Epinephrine Injection recall is encouraged to contact the company by phone at 800-645-1706 from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. ET, Monday through Thursday, or 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. ET on Fridays. American Regent didn’t immediately respond to questions emailed on Friday. Gizmodo will update this article when we hear back.

item.title: This New iRobot Concept Is the Matryoshka of Robot Vacuums
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.51
A new iRobot concept called the Roomba Duo might be one of the best ideas for robovacs I’ve seen all year, and I don’t just mean because it looks like a Star Wars droid. Rolled out at IFA 2026, the Roomba Duo is a large, can-shaped bot that can steam-clean floors, with a tiny robot in a cavity up top that it lowers to the ground for areas that require a smaller bot to handle. This isn’t the robot’s final form, and there’s a real chance it never makes it to market at all. An iRobot product manager I spoke with on the show floor told me, “Roomba Duo is a concept that we put together to see how the market responds to it, and it’s what we think the future of robotic floor cleaning could look like.” He described the “large base unit” as being meant for heavy-duty cleaning to replace stick vacuums or wet/dry vacuums. The company gave it such heft—it’s about two feet tall and weighs about 66 lbs—to get “extra power” and increase its tank size. In a demo that I watched, iRobot dropped spaghetti on a patch of carpet (it looked like it was covered in oil and herbs, rather than a red sauce). At the demo’s outset, the entire unit drove over the spaghetti, vacuuming it and then following that with steam cleaning. Afterward, all that was left was a bit of a stain that was presumably from the oil. When that was done, the Roomba Duo lifted its head off, lowered it to the ground, and let loose the robot that was resting in there like a little disc-shaped matryoshka. The product manager said the companion bot is essentially the Roomba Plus 575, a smaller sweeping and mopping robovac that iRobot debuted earlier this year. It did the usual robovac stuff, sweeping under a small platform supported by legs that are close together, showing the benefit of this robot-in-a-robot concept. It’s very likely that, if it makes it out to the market, the Roomba Duo will look quite a bit different from what I saw today. And in its concept stage, the product manager I spoke with wasn’t willing to guess at how much it might cost. He didn’t disagree with me when I speculated it’ll probably cost more than some of the pricier all-in-one bots I’ve reviewed this year, such as the $1,700 Dreame X60 Max Ultra Complete. I’m a little skeptical of its steam-cleaning capabilities—will it be able to deal with old stains or more resilient spills like actual oil? But if it can pull off cleaning the sorts of huge messes, like spilled plates of food and such, that you’d never even bother sending a robot vacuum to deal with, it could be worth it.

item.title: ‘Lanterns’ Writer on Creating John’s Divisive Family Life
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.48
Since its premiere last weekend, audiences have been watching and talking about “OutKast,” the third episode of Lanterns. Written by Vanessa Baden Kelly, the flashback-heavy story digs into what makes Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart tick, and we’re early into the show’s run, but it already feels like it’ll be a season standout. In a recent Hollywood Reporter interview, Baden Kelly highlighted the team writing “what rings true to us” throughout the season. In her case, John being groomed as a Lantern from age five parallels her time as a child star on Nickelodeon’s All That, but only to a point. She didn’t grow up with stage parents, but she said sports parents are considerably more overbearing, and that’s what helped them figure out how the Stewarts see their son. Tiger Woods’ father, Earl, and Venus and Serena Williams’ father, Richard—as well as musical patriarch Joe Jackson—were all “talked ad nauseam about,” as was the mindset of embracing that parenting method. “Is there a necessity for it when you’re growing up in a certain environment? If you’re growing up in Gary, Indiana, if you’re growing up in Compton, is this the smartest way to do it?” asked Baden Kelly. “Does it fuck you up so bad that you’re not able to ever come back from it? And could they have done this in something else? […] The discourse raging online, watching people have the same debates we had in the room about whether this is abuse or whether they did what needed to be done, is reminiscent of what we talked about for six months.” When it came to making Bernadette Stewart be a more active player in John’s upbringing, Baden Kelly cited Sonya Curry, Steph Curry’s mother, as inspiration for the mother-son dynamic in the episode. “These are not women coddling their children,” she said of sports moms. “I think the [writers] room agreed, it’s tough love when dads do it, but when a mom does, people are like, ‘She’s terrible!’ I wanted to play with that a little bit because it’s like, ‘Is she?'” (And yes, she did acknowledge things get pushed “a little bit in a different direction” when said parenting involves shooting apples off your child’s head.) You can read the full interview for Baden Kelly’s additional thoughts on the writers room and making this new version of John. Equally gratified for the opportunity and “really sad” at the harsher reactions, she hopes “OutKast” doesn’t lead to people writing off the rest of Lanterns. “I hope people stick it out with John. He goes through the very human experience of what it feels like to make your own decisions about the life you’ve been given,” she said. “I would caution anybody who feels like they know where [his] story ends, based on episode three, to really make it through to the end.” Want more io9 news? item.title: ‘Hope’ Director Na Hong-jin Wanted to Make an Alien Movie From a Cosmic Perspective
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.34
Hope, Neon’s latest sci-fi film by director Na Hong-jin, hits theaters on September 9th. The film, starring Squid Game‘s Hoyeon, Michael Fassbender, and Alicia Vikander, aims to be Na’s directorial hat trick, his first foray into the sci-fi genre and his fourth feature film following The Chaser, The Yellow Sea, and his 2016 horror masterwork The Wailing. Set in a sleepy, secluded village, Hope follows as police officers Bum-seok (Hwang Jung-min) and Sung-ae (Hoyeon) and local yahoo hunter Sung-ki (Zo In-sung) stumble upon what they believe is a mysterious animal preying on farmers’ livestock. Quicker than a hiccup, the troupe goes from hunting the creature down to being hunted themselves across congested city streets and dense forests. What follows is a full-throttle alien invasion film full of Na’s patented dark humor, high-octane action, and plenty of U-turns away from and toward the warzone of the aptly titled South Korean village, Hope Harbor. Ahead of Hope‘s theatrical premiere, io9 spoke with Na about what drew him to sci-fi for his fourth feature film, the reported recuts following its mixed reception at Cannes, and how he strove to make it different from the sci-fi blockbusters he and moviegoers have grown accustomed to. The trajectory of Na’s career, from Park Chan-wook-esque films The Chaser and The Yellow Sea to full-throated horror with his leap into The Wailing, felt like watching a director find his niche. After cutting his teeth on the oppressive tension of gritty neo-noir crime thrillers, Na tapped into something novel, letting the dark humor and arresting violence of those films come into full bloom with his third-ever film—a film Na says left him “creatively and physically drained,” with resting as his only desire. The prospect of his fourth film, hopping from horror to sci-fi with the same crew who helped him along his meteoric rise, like cinematographer Hong Kyun-pyo, stunt coordinator Yoo Sang Seob, and actor Hwang, made Hope all the more tantalizing, a cinematic experience to see what novelty Na brings to the table of alien invasion cinema. Na told io9 he was drawn to the sci-fi genre because he wanted to make a film that interrogated his prevailing theme of how misconceptions and ignorance could escalate from human conflict into a tragic mushroom cloud of “cosmic proportions.” “I usually get my idea for my films from social phenomena or human phenomena. What’s really important here is where, and from what perspective, you’re viewing this phenomena from,” Na said. “After The Wailing, I wanted to try viewing this phenomena from a perspective I haven’t been used to before. I decided on a cosmic perspective to see humans and how they behave. That’s where the idea came from.” While any other filmmaker, save for Bong Joon Ho with his 2006 film The Host, would opt to obscure its towering CGI creatures in shadows, Hope makes that bold decision to showcase its coterie of mysterious creatures in broad daylight throughout the film. Rather than give the entire game away (as its trailer did, which left no question that audiences were walking into an alien-vs-humans movie), it was paramount to Na that viewers question whether the oddities wreaking havoc were from this world’s wild animals or some local demon running amok. Once the cat was out of the bag in the film after the arrival of the first invading alien (played by Cameron Britton), Na had to put in the work on the rest of the alien creatures’ designs to make them both ethereal and functionally terrifying contenders for the denizens of Hope Harbor in the film’s mile-a-minute action sequences. “In terms of how they move, I wanted to stray from previous conventions. In deciding whether these aliens appear during the day or at night, or whether I should shoot them on location or at a sound stage, I decided that, even if it makes it more difficult, I should maximize the locations we’re shooting in. It really added a sense of spaciality to the characters,” he said, in reference to the film’s implementation of wide-angle lenses keeping both humans and alien characters—who are over three meters (roughly 10 feet) tall—in frame. While creatures of this stature don’t move at a kaiju’s glacial pace, Na wanted to break conventions by having Hope‘s aliens move incredibly fast. To bring Hope‘s creatures to life, Na worked alongside Korean VFX crew Westworld to motion-capture stars Fassbender, Vikander, Britton, and Taylor Russell. Hope‘s international stars playing its titular aliens wasn’t a coincidental decision for Na. “The decision to use a cast from two different cultural backgrounds came after making the alien language that’s featured in the film,” he said. “I wanted to cast actors from a region where the pronunciation of their language was more similar to the language that we created.” Although the imposing stature of its aliens and the prevailing language barrier between them and Hope‘s bumbling humans create palpable tension throughout the film, at the end of the day, it’s still a Na film. Which means there’s gonna be some dark humor sprinkled throughout all the dread as hapless officers in over their heads—a prevailing theme in his works—confront aliens terrorizing the intimate setting of a remote village. “The movie is told from a cosmic perspective. We’re looking down on these human characters. Due to that, our perspective is more friendly to the aliens than toward humans,” Na said. “Because of that, I wanted to emphasize more of the primitive and uncivilized sides of mankind. But at the same time, I didn’t want these elements to feel too serious, which is why I used humorous scenes to convey that. In a way, you can say through humor, I tried to make these explicit intentions of mine a little more ambiguous. I also wanted these elements to be communicated to the audience in a smoother, more fun fashion.” Following the film’s mixed reception during its run at Cannes, IndieWire‘s Chris O’Falt reported that Na recut Hope into what audiences will experience in theaters. Ahead of its world premiere, Neon secured a 1,500-theater opening for Hope across the U.S., making it the widest domestic theatrical release for a Korean film since Bong Joon Ho’s Parasite, according to Variety. If that’s not a ton of confidence points for a creature feature, we don’t know what is. After I watched an early screening of the movie, public relations confirmed to io9 that I watched the recut audiences will see in theaters. Naturally, I asked Na what led him to recut Hope, what changes he made between the two versions of the film, and what he discovered he wanted to say about the story in the movie audiences will see compared to its initial cut. “I decided to re-edit it after viewing it at Cannes. Overall, in terms of content, it became four minutes shorter,” he said. Na explained that the shorter runtime was intended to give more screen time to Hope Harbor’s local taxidermist, Yang-bae (Eum Moon-suk). Unfortunately for Squid Game fans, the equivalent exchange of Yang-bae getting more shine in Hope‘s leaner runtime meant Hoyeon’s hotshot officer, Sung-ae, got less play. Hope crash-lands into theaters on September 9. Want more io9 news? Check out when to expect the latest Marvel, Star Wars, and Star Trek releases, what’s next for the DC Universe on film and TV, and everything you need to know about the future of Doctor Who.

item.title: Gizmodo’s Best of IFA 2026 Awards: See the Winners
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.33
IFA 2026 was packed with gadgets galore. We expected the annual “Innovation For All” tech show in Berlin to have the usual abundance of smart home devices and home appliances, but companies big and small really pulled up in numbers with genuinely intriguing consumer devices. From a laptop with a screen that expands from 14 inches to 17 inches to a robot vacuum with a robot vacuum that has a smaller “head” to a bezel-less phone, IFA 2026 showed us a glimpse of the future. As we did last year, we’re awarding the very best products of the tech show in our Best of IFA 2026 Awards. Every winner was handpicked by the Gizmodo Consumer Tech Team. Congrats to all the winners. Tecno Bezel-Less Concept Phone It’s only a concept device, but Tecno’s bezelless phone was fully working. Without any black borders around the display, it shows what the future of bar-style phones could look like if they’re all screen. Xiaomi 18 Fold Nobody got to touch it and full specs weren’t announced, but the buzz around Xiaomi’s 18 Fold was still pretty strong. The book-style foldable could be a strong competitor for the upcoming foldable iPhone, at least outside of the U.S. Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD Touted by Lexar as the “world’s thinnest SSD,” the Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD tapers from 3.8mm at its center to 1mm on the sides. It’s a portable SSD, so it can be used with any device like a laptop for storage, but we’re awarding it our favorite mobile accessory at IFA 2026 because it also comes with a MagSafe sleeve that bolts it to an iPhone for recording 4K ProRes video. Its 1,050 MB/s read and 1,000 MB/s write speeds are super fast, too. Belkin UltraCharge Pro Slim Power Bank On the surface, Belkin’s UltraCharge Pro Slim Power Bank looks like another slim battery bank with 5,000mAh or 10,000mAh capacities. But inside, it’s using semi-solid-state battery technology that not only allows it to be more compact than other similarly sized battery banks, it should also last up to 3x longer than other battery banks over time. Lenovo IdeaPad Vibe Lenovo’s ultra-colorful IdeaPad Vibe laptops ooze personality from every pore, including the keycaps. These lightweight laptops include swappable keycaps and plenty of ports, made to be the kind of everyday laptop that doesn’t make you feel like a creature in a cubicle. Lenovo Project Swan We’ve already seen laptops extend vertically, so why not horizontally? Lenovo’s Project Swan concept unfurls its wings thanks to a flexible display hidden in the lid, turning a 14-inch laptop into a 17-inch ultrawide screen with more real estate than normal. Lenovo IdeaCentre AIO i Just like the new IdeaPad Vibe, the IdeaCentre AIO i is packing in a relatively affordable processor into a very cute, very colorful screen. The all-in-one desktop comes in either 24- or 27-inch sizes and supports an Intel Core 7 350 processor that’s good enough for daily tasks. A curated selection of ports round out a relatively cheap desktop that will actually accent your desk setup. Epomaker RT75 Epomaker’s retro-themed RT series of mechanical keyboards already look excellently old school with a miniature screen shaped like a CRT monitor. The Epomaker RT75 makes it even better since you can remove the TFT screen and instead replace it with more switches. Plus, it feels great with either of Epomaker’s tactile or silent switches. Eufy Omni E35 Eufy’s Omni E35 has some cool stuff going on. Inside of the robot’s dustbin is a miniature cyclonic filter for separating dust from debris, the kind you see on many stick vacuums. It also features 35,000Pa suction, which is among the highest in the industry, and is the first—and so far, only—robot vacuum to be certified as “Asthma & Allergy Friendly” by the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America, making it potentially a great choice for anyone who suffers from such things. Eufy Lawn Mower S2 Max Eufy gets the nod in the robot vacuum category for its triple navigation system that uses LiDAR, NRTK, and vision cameras to ensure it can keep mowing even without a satellite connection, and the fact that it not only has an edge-trimming arm on its side, but because it can edge trim vertically and horizontally. Beyerdynamic Aventho Y Battery life isn’t everything in a pair of wireless headphones, but when you can get up to 90 hours (60 hours with noise cancellation), it’s a feat worth noting. In addition to a beefy battery, the Beyerdynamic Aventho Y have a USB-C dongle for low-latency streaming that tucks inside the earcups and a lot of repairable, modular touches that make them feel well worth the $150 price tag. Anker Soundcore SleepLab Pro Sleep tracking without a wearable is what the Anker Soundcore SleepLab Pro promises. Using a 60GHz radar, Anker says this sleep-focused speaker can track heart rate and sleep stages and (naturally) play soothing sounds to lull you to sleep. It’s an ambitious speaker, but products like this are what IFA is all about. Anker Soundcore AeroClip 2 Open wireless earbuds are all the rage these days, and Anker Soundcore’s AeroClip 2 get a boost from the company’s Thus chip, which should improve call quality greatly. Calling isn’t the sexiest feature, but it’s one of the best use cases for open earbuds, and being able to take calls without your voice being drowned out by background noise is enticing. Eufy Video Doorbell S4 Eufy’s Video Doorbell S4 is tough to beat. It features a 180-degree 3K fisheye camera, making it possible to see basically everything in front of your door. There’s also a mode where you can zoom in on its picture slightly using the Eufy app, then tilt your phone to look around the image. Eufy Window Camera E10 There’s not much special about the Eufy Window Camera E10—it’s plug-in-only, records 2.5K video, and although it tilts, the tilt is entirely manual, using a small dial on the back. What’s cool about it, though, is where and how you place it. The Window Camera E10 just attaches, via hook-and-loop, to a sticky ring you slap on your window, making it one of the easiest outdoor-watching security cameras we’ve ever seen. Anker MindBase Anker is taking a stab at a full-on smart home ecosystem, complete with an AI voice assistant, with the MindBase. Resembling a large tower router, it’s got a built-in 26 TOPS AI chipset that enables local control, as well as natural language search of both your security camera footage (up to 16 cameras) and files stored locally on internal storage or any NAS-style hard drives you might add. The MindBase is also Matter-compatible, so you’ll be able to integrate and control any Matter smart home devices with it. Philips Hue Liane 360° Rope Light Philips Hue’s Liane 360° Indoor Rope Light is a delightful, thick rope light that’s super bendy and comes with clips that let you arrange it in snakey shapes on your wall. Besides being just a neat kind of light, it also outputs bright, even lighting and features very smooth color gradients, all the way around its tubey form. SwitchBot Lock Ultra Max The SwitchBot Lock Ultra Max sounds like a great retrofit smart lock. It’s got a super-fast unlock speed, two built-in back-up batteries, and like its predecessor, the Lock Ultra, you can buy an adapter to slip it on over existing locks’ thumbturns. Combined with the company’s Keypad Vision Pro accessory, SwitchBot claims the Lock Ultra Max offers 19 different ways to unlock it. Xgimi Aura 3 Max Several big projectors at IFA 2026 promised to finally hit 4K resolution and a 120Hz refresh rate. While several could claim better brightness specs than the Xgimi Aura 3 Max, the short-throw projector also offers better contrast in the resulting image thanks to its dual-iris optical system. The Aura 3 Max also supports all major HDR standards and even has a Filmmaker Mode at a much more reasonable price point. Canvas L The Canvas L HiFi soundbar easily blew away its competition in terms of pure raw sound quality. Yes, it’s an absolutely massive sound system, but Canvas tries to hide the humongous boombox look with a few wooden slats that are supposed to work with Samsung’s high-end TVs. Even without the facade, the Canvas L with its Bacch 3D+ spatial audio sounded clear and full in person. Alienware AW2527HX While there are more companies promising 1080p LCD monitors that can hit well above 1,000Hz, Alienware is trying something different for pro gamers. The Alienware AW2527HX is an OLED display with a high brightness spec in both SDR and HDR that can top out at a 500Hz refresh rate. You have to give Alienware credit for trying to change the esports landscape, even if pro gamers may be loathe to change. Acer Predator Atlas 7 Acer’s Predator Atlas 7 is essentially a slimmed-down version of the Predator Atlas 8, but being smaller does not necessarily mean it’s worse. The gaming handheld PC still hits the same top 40W TDP and can come with either an Intel Arc G3 or Arc G3 Extreme chip. The Atlas 8 is going to cost $1,300, so we’re hoping the Atlas 7 can come in at a more reasonable price. DJI Osmo 360 II DJI’s first 360 camera was already pretty good, but with a few tweaks the Osmo 360 II is set to be a much better shooter. It’s promising the ability to shoot at 8K and 60 fps—something the competition still lacks—plus better low-light performance. Also, you can finally replace the 360 camera’s lenses if they ever get damaged. Moto Watch Ultra In a world dominated by the Apple Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch, more smartwatch choice is always a good thing. Motorola’s Moto Ultra has a 1.5-inch round screen, a Snapdragon W5+ Gen 1 chip, built-in LTE, and most importantly, runs Wear OS 6 so you can access all the apps you need. The smartwatch also comes with two AI assistants, Google’s Gemini and Motorola’s Quira. Circular Ring 3 Available in Slim and Pro options, the Circular Ring 3 is noticeably more compact compared to the previous Ring 2 series and supports two features other smart rings like the Oura Ring 5 don’t have: NFC for mobile payments and vibrations for alarms, medication reminders, and other health-based alerts and notifications. Battery life also lasts 12 days, up from 7 days. RayNeo iO AI Glasses RayNeo is getting deeper into the smart glasses game with the iO. If you’re put off by camera glasses, there’s good news: these are camera-free. They do have a display, though, making them akin to other display glasses like Even Realities’ Even G2. The addition of a “smart crown dial” for controlling the UI is a nice touch. Plaud One Explorer Edition Wireless earbuds are agentic now. The Plaud One Explorer Edition are a pair of AI earbuds that not only record meetings, but can actually take actions on your behalf—drafting emails, making presentations, etc… AI gadgets are only as good as the AI inside them, but in theory, these are a pair of wireless earbuds that people who take a lot of meetings could find useful. Boox Picco If you thought the Boox Palma smartphone-sized e-reader was petite, the Boox Picco is absolutely micro. The e-reader with a 3.97-inch screen is so small in the hand that you can easily pocket it on the go and get a bit of reading done on the bus or train. Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 Lenovo’s Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 may finally be one of those Android tablets that can claim to meet or beat devices like the iPad Pro. It features a 13-inch 4K display, the highest-end Qualcomm mobile chip, and a new feature-packed pen and keyboard attachment that actually has us considering it as a potential laptop replacement. Dyson CameraJet Dyson’s CameraJet is exactly what you’d expect from the company’s first electric toothbush. It has an AI camera that assists a water flossing function—every time the CameraJet sees a space, it deploys a jet of mouthrinse, so you can water floss as you go. There’s even a live camera feature so you can see inside your mouth, which feels very unnecessary but could be great if you want to get weird with it. Dyson Corrale CoolShine The Dyson Corrale CoolShine hair straightener improves on its 2020 predecessor with a new cooling attachment that—you guessed it—cools your hair down as soon as heat is applied to straighten your precious locks of hair. Dyson says it helps prevent hair damage from heat and makes hair appear shinier and stay locked into place for up to 24 hours. The straightener is also no longer cordless, which was a major complaint about the original model. Hypershell Halo Hypershell has finally come out of its shell with the Halo. The new exoskeleton features motors centered on the knees and cuffs that sit on your calves to better enhance mobility when tackling ramps or stairs. The assistive movement technology also dampens the impact of short drops and makes it easier to get up from sitting, making it a versatile device for people who want to hike but suffer from knee issues. TP-Link Archer 8 Ultra Most people won’t need to upgrade their networks to Wi-Fi 8 yet, but if you’re looking toward the future, the Archer 8 Ultra is leading the pack with 18 “high-performance antennas” that can deliver “up to 19 Gbps of aggregate wireless speeds and 10 Gbps wired connectivity,” according to TP-Link. Fast Wi-Fi speeds are only part of the appeal of Wi-Fi 8; reliable and expansive coverage that doesn’t drop out is another reason to consider next-gen networking gear. Dreame LumaTempo Dreame’s best known for its robot vacuums, but at IFA 2026, it announced the LumaTempo, a smart fish tank. Yes, really! By smart, you get 20 customizable lighting modes, control of the built-in feeder, and a way to monitor the tank’s water temperature, all via an app. It’s not for everyone, but definitely for someone. iRobot Roomba Duo iRobot’s Roomba Duo may be just a concept, but it’s one of the coolest and most practical-seeming robots we saw at IFA 2026. It’s a large, two-stage, can-shaped robot vacuum that can vacuum and steam clean carpets. When it’s time to go places the big bot can’t, the Roomba Duo pulls its head off and places it on the ground, releasing a smaller robot vacuum to go take care of areas under furniture or between chair legs. Gravity Universe Time We stumbled on the Universe Time and found it to be a delightful throwback to Sharper Image catalog widgets and gizmos that you might find on desktop offices—little trinkets that delight you with a simple trick of physics. The Universe Time uses magnetic levitation to hover a small, spinning ball over a mostly featureless, gray “clock.” You can watch as the ball circles the face at a pace of seconds, minutes, or hours, and if you choose a planet in its connected smartphone app, it matches the spin of that planet, at least according to Gravity. Acer Project DualPlay Mini When we think of handheld PCs, we rarely consider actually plugging them into a monitor to use them as we would a “personal computer.” Acer’s DualPlay Mini concept is extra surprising in-person for how well it’s designed, from the center-hinged screen to the relatively spacious keyboard. With a few tweaks to the ergonomics, the DualPlay Mini could change the way we think about gaming handhelds.

item.title: UN Approves Resolution for World Map That Depicts Africa’s Size More Accurately
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.29
Maps have been in the news of late, largely because of the forelock-tugging pusillanimity shown by Google and Apple in rushing to implement Donald Trump’s latest half-hearted attempt to redraw the map to his liking, this one regarding Lake Ontario. But for all the patent absurdity of Trump’s recent tantrum, it should serve as a reminder that maps are—and have always been—inherently political. There’s no more profound demonstration of that fact than the map of the world. The fact that the earth is a sphere means that there’s no way to project it onto a two-dimensional surface like a piece of paper or a computer screen without distorting its surface one way or another. But the choice of which way to distort the surface is as much a product of history and politics as it is of practicality. The familiar Mercator projection was devised in the 16th century as a navigational aid, because it has two advantageous properties: it renders both circles of latitude and meridians of longitude as straight lines, and it’s conformal, i.e. it preserves angles. These properties were invaluable for navigators—and remain so today—and they also proved attractive to Google et al when putting together their mapping services centuries later. To achieve these properties, the Mercator projects the Earth’s surface onto a cylinder, with circles of latitude mapped to the cylinder’s diameter and meridians of longitude running vertically along its surface. But on an actual sphere, circles of latitude get vanishingly small toward the poles. If you render them all as the same size, your projection gets increasingly distorted the further you get from the equator. This explains the Mercator’s most well-documented flaw: landmasses toward the poles look significantly larger than they actually are, while those near the equator look smaller. And wouldn’t you know it, the landmasses that have their size inflated by the Mercator projection are the traditional seats of white economic power—North America, and pretty much all of Europe and Russia—while those that don’t fall neatly into the global south are Central and South America, the Indian subcontinent, southern and central Asia and, most notoriously, Africa. (Wikipedia has an excellent visualisation of this.) African countries have often voiced their disapproval of the way the Mercator projection distorts the continent’s size in relation to the rest of the world. And on Friday, the UN approved a resolution sponsored by the West African country of Togo, and endorsed by the African Union, that asked for the official adoption of the Equal Earth projection to replace the Mercator projection. UN resolutions are non-binding, but the adoption of this resolution could help put pressure on publishers and tech companies to adopt the Equal Earth projection. So how does that projection work? Well, it’s a pseudocylindrical projection: it preserves parallel circles of latitude, but those circles decrease in radius as they approach the poles, and unlike the Mercator, it uses curved meridians of longitude. It was created in 2017 as a way of providing a more accurate depiction of the relative sizes of different areas than the Gall-Peters projection, an older equal-area projection. To be clear: no one is suggesting that Mercator himself was orchestrating some grand conspiracy to minimize the size of Africa when he made his map, and it’s easy to dismiss the ubiquity of that map—500 years after its creation—as an accident of history. But if that’s the case, correcting that accident should be pretty uncontroversial, and the Equal Earth projection is clearly superior to the Mercator for the majority of today’s purposes. “A fair world begins with a fair map,” Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told Reuters on Friday. While the Web Mercator’s conformal, north-preserving qualities are useful at small scales, no one is using it to sail a clipper ship through the Roaring Forties in search of a route to the spice islands. When most people look at a map of the world, they want to see what the world looks like. If the Equal Earth projection is a more accurate picture than the Mercator projection of the relative size of the Earth’s landmasses—and it is—then there should be few objections to its adoption. Right? Well, according to Reuters, the United States was the only country to vote against the resolution. No doubt the usual comment section types will find reasons to oppose the change, but beyond them, the most likely objection is that making changes like this is difficult and expensive and so on and so forth. But let’s remember just how quickly Lake America became a thing. Sure, changing the map of the world is more of an undertaking than changing the name of a lake. But people tend to find ways of doing things when they want to do those things—and of not doing things when they don’t. And if it’s the latter, it’s always worth thinking about what might be.

item.title: US Military Discovers Just How Dangerous Ad Trackers Can Be
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.86
Sometimes the surveillance state works against the actual state. According to a report from Reuters, several branches of the military have now disabled advertising trackers on phones and computers after it was found that location information purchased through data brokers was used to target American forces in the Middle East. Per the report, which cited a letter sent to the Department of Defense’s Inspector General by Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, the Air Force disabled advertising identifiers on all devices about two months ago, while Special Operations Command just “recently” disabled them on Windows machines and the Army first turned off the trackers on mobile devices earlier this year. Wyden has been warning the military about the public availability of location data for months. Back in May, the Senator told the Pentagon in a letter that, “Commercial location data can be used to identify where U.S. troops congregate and their pattern of life, which can be exploited by adversaries to target attacks such as missiles, drones, and roadside bombs, as well as for counterintelligence purposes.” Wyden’s warnings follow several high-profile reports that highlight just how trivially easy it is to access data that can compromise the locations and behaviors of U.S. military members and contractors. In 2024, Wired published a story in which it showed how commercially available data could be used to place military contractors in, among other places, German brothels. In 2021, The Wall Street Journal published a piece about how a US military contractor discovered it could track US military operations through the data generated by the apps on the phones of soldiers. Even as far back as 2018, almost a decade ago now, The Guardian was reporting on how data from the fitness app Strava could be used to identify secret U.S. military bases. So hey, no better time than the present to fix a problem that has existed for years. Previous letters between Wyden and the military seem to suggest that US personnel in the Middle East were targeted using commercial location data. Of course, Iran and other nations the US has been adversarial with don’t even need to spend their money on information from data brokers. Per a Reuters report from July, videos recorded and posted online by American military members in the Middle East also may have been used to identify the location of personnel, resulting in some deployed military members being asked to turn over their phones.

item.title: A Mysterious Tick Disease Has Been Spotted in New York
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.81
Ticks in the United States are encroaching into places where they usually haven’t been present, as are the diseases they can carry. Doctors in New York recently reported on a case of a mysterious tickborne illness often mistaken for Lyme disease involving an 8-year-old girl. The girl had contracted southern tick–associated rash illness, or STARI, a condition with no established cause that’s linked to the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum). Though she recovered with no serious complications, doctors are likely to face a harder time distinguishing similar-looking diseases as the lone star tick’s range expands further, the authors warn. “The bull’s eye rash, or erythema migrans, has long been considered the hallmark of early Lyme disease, but STARI has become an increasingly common mimic,” lead author Andrew Handel, a clinical associate professor of pediatrics in the Division of Infectious Diseases at the Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University, told Gizmodo. “In areas where both Lyme disease and STARI are endemic, there is no reliable way to distinguish the two based on exam alone.” The mystery of STARI STARI was first discovered in the mid-1980s by doctors in Missouri. As the name suggests, it’s typically been reported in the southeastern United States. Though usually not as serious as Lyme disease, the symptoms of STARI closely resemble the latter, particularly with the common presence of a bull’s eye rash. In fact, STARI was only identified as something new because cases were showing up in places where the primary vector of Lyme disease, the blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis), was uncommonly found. Lyme disease is caused by certain Borrelia bacteria, primarily Borrelia burgdorferi in the U.S. STARI is instead strongly associated with the bite of the lone star tick, which has historically been widely distributed throughout the southern Midwest and southeastern U.S. Like many species, though, the lone star tick has moved beyond its usual haunts, and it’s now commonly found in pockets of the upper midwestern and northeastern United States as well as eastern Canada. These newer areas are already endemic to the blacklegged tick and Lyme, setting the stage for increasing episodes of mistaken identity. This latest case happened in June 2025. The 8-year-old girl and her family sought medical care for a bull’s-eye rash, fever, enlarged lymph nodes, and muscle pain. Twelve days earlier, she had been bitten by a tick, which was collected and stored in a sealed bag. Her pediatrician initially diagnosed her with Lyme disease and prescribed her a common antibiotic treatment for two weeks. Within a week, her rash and other symptoms had dissipated, and she made a full recovery. When the tick was examined, though, it turned out to be an adult male lone star (both male and female lone star ticks will bite humans). The girl was subsequently diagnosed with STARI, while Handel and his team performed a deeper analysis of the tick. They found a different species of Borrelia than the one that causes Lyme in the tick, Borrelia lonestari. To this day, scientists aren’t actually sure about what causes STARI. Though B. lonestari infection is a leading suspect, some studies have failed to detect any relevant bacteria at all in people with the condition. That’s led to the alternative hypothesis that STARI is a hypersensitivity reaction to the lone star tick bite itself—one that might be connected to alpha-gal syndrome, another condition linked to the lone star (people with alpha-gal syndrome basically become allergic to red meat and other foods that contain alpha-gal). Because the girl wasn’t tested for B. lonestari, it’s impossible to know for sure whether it caused her illness, the doctors wrote. Their findings were published in this month’s issue of the journal Emerging Infectious Diseases. The future of STARI This isn’t the first case of STARI ever detected in New York. But with the lone star’s eight-legged footprint growing bigger, similar cases of confusion are likely to happen more often, and not just in the northeast. The blacklegged tick is also expanding its range further south into areas where the lone star has long been prevalent, such as North Carolina. Handel says this case underscores the need to develop better lab tests for diagnosing Lyme disease early on, since currently available tests may show false-negative results. There are no specific blood tests for STARI, so it can only be clearly diagnosed when Lyme is ruled out and a lone star tick bite is highly suspected. This means it’s all the more important for people to hold on to the ticks that bite them in the event of illness, too. “Since Lyme disease and STARI are caused by different tick species, it also highlights the importance of identifying the tick species and preserving the tick after a bite has occurred,” he said. It’s not just STARI that New Yorkers have to worry about more either—the lone star tick is bringing along other illnesses for the ride as well.

item.title: The US Robot Ban Is Screwing Us Out of the Good Robomowers
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.75
Robot mowers have gotten surprisingly good lately, thanks to smart use of onboard NRTK satellite connectivity, LiDAR navigation, and vision cameras that let the robots navigate without the need for installing satellite receivers in your yard or digging it up to bury guide wires. But they still can’t get up to the edges of buildings and sidewalks. This year at IFA 2026, we’re seeing robot mowers with robotic arms that stick out to the side, a sudden trend that could fix this issue. The shame is that we won’t be getting any of these robomowers in the U.S. for quite some time, because, like foreign-made robot vacuums, they’ve been banned. The ban on “advanced robotic devices” ostensibly exists, according to an FCC FAQ, to prevent “unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States” and targets those “capable of locomotion, obstacle avoidance, navigation, or movement on the ground.” That seems to include robot mowers, and no representative of a robot mower manufacturer I spoke with at IFA seemed especially confident that its device would make it to the U.S. In general, the responses I got when I asked about potential U.S. releases were along the lines of “we’re working to understand current U.S. regulations.” The U.S. government taking steps to deal with the cybersecurity risks of connected devices like robots isn’t necessarily a bad thing—after all, security vulnerabilities are fairly common in them. Take that time that a hacker demonstrated that he could easily take over a Yarbo automower and drive it over The Verge reporter Sean Hollister’s body. It’s not clear how this ban will help with those issues, since any robot that has already been approved for sale here may continue to be imported and sold, and those living in the U.S. are free to keep the ones they already have. It’s a shame, because as much as robomowers have improved, they do a poor job with grass growing against buildings or over sidewalks. The best they’ve done, until now, is slide their mowing decks over to get close, as is the case with the Segway Navimow X4, but they’ll still leave you with the task of going back with a weed whacker to trim the vegetation growing against your house or edge the grass that flops over the concrete of your sidewalk. In general, the new robot mowers I saw at IFA 2026 are handling this the same way: they each have an articulating arm that can swing out away from the body of the mower to cut grass. In the case of the Segway Navimow H5 Pro, a panel on the side of the device opens up to bring the robot’s mowing blades out, while others, like the Dreame A4 AWD Pro, use a string trimming arm. The Mammotion Yuba 4 AWD has an optional accessory that bolts onto the back. And the Eufy Lawn Mower S2 Max‘s string trimmer arm can be horizontal for cutting down grass near structures and vertical for edging a sidewalk. It’s hard to say how long the U.S. will miss out on this trend. It could be that President Donald Trump has a change of heart—one Roborock representative I spoke with expressed hope that the president’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in late September could favorably alter the ban. Or perhaps some manufacturers could get special exemptions. Barring those things or the U.S. November midterm elections yielding a Democrat-controlled Congress that swiftly and successfully pushes to reverse or alter the ban, it could take years. After all, it’s not like there is a vast, dormant American home robotics manufacturing industry awakening to fill the gap.

item.title: OpenAI Says It Wants to Create a Standard for Revealing AI Alignment Meltdowns
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.36
In the wake of fresh reporting about more of OpenAI’s AI agents misbehaving on the public internet, OpenAI says the AI world lacks standards for when and how to report such incidents. It is “past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents, not just misalignment properties of our models,” OpenAI wrote on X. “We’re working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks, and in parallel we’re working with dozens of government regulatory agencies worldwide on these issues,” the X post later says. OpenAI’s potential responsibility to disclose this incident seems to have been a point of friction for OpenAI as this news became public. Yesterday, a group of researchers named Sydney Von Arx, Cormac Slade Byrd, Spencer Kitts, and Thomas Larsen revealed the latest troubling, confusing, goofy, inscrutable, and infuriating AI snafu brought to you by OpenAI. That research was exclusively provided to Reuters‘ reporters. The actual event involved yet another collection of unruly digital Myrmidons, this time descending on a German wiki-style site and transforming part of it into its own agent-centric communications hub. Reuters says OpenAI knew this had happened, but that it hadn’t spoken up before Reuters published its report. Since mid-July, OpenAI has been dealing with the ever-expanding fallout from the Hugging Face hack, which was also carried out by a collection of OpenAI agents meant to be undergoing evaluations. “Claims that our legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false,” OpenAI told my Gizmodo colleague Webb Wright. The company was, it claims, “unable to respond to the claims as Reuters and the report’s authors declined our request to access the findings prior to publication. We are now carefully reviewing its contents and will take any necessary next steps.” But Reuters’ report had been sourced not just from the researchers, but also from two anonymous people claiming that OpenAI had learned about the German incident weeks earlier, meaning the “access” OpenAI sought from Reuters would not have been the nature of the incident, but access to Reuters’ actual report, full disclosure of which would not be standard journalistic practice. With that in mind, OpenAI’s X post outlining a plan for what amounts to greater transparency about incidents like these seems to acknowledge that the company knew about the German incident—which it calls the “wiki incident”—well in advance of Reuters’ report. Gizmodo reached out to OpenAI to confirm that the X post constitutes acknowledgement that the company knew about the German incident before Reuters sought comment. We did not receive a reply prior to publication. OpenAI has acknowledged related issues in its previous writings. In its technical report about the Hugging Face incident, it wrote “With the benefit of hindsight, some early signals identified in this report could have triggered an earlier response.” However, this is not a reference to public disclosure. In the technical report, an “earlier response” refers, it appears, to plans for quicker internal escalation and rapid “shutdown” procedures. An automatic kill switch is now in the works, according to a letter to lawmakers from earlier this week.

item.title: Beyerdynamic’s New Wireless Headphones Have Ridiculously Beefy Battery Life
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.91
A long battery life isn’t the end-all-be-all when it comes to wireless headphones, but it feels a lot more important when you get on the plane and realize you’re seated right next to a crying baby. For those who get even the slightest amount of battery anxiety, Beyerdynamic’s new Aventho Y, which it unveiled at IFA 2026, might be the salve you need. According to them, this pair of wireless headphones gets up to 90 hours of battery with active noise cancellation turned off and 60 hours with it on. For reference, even flagship pairs of wireless headphones like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) and the AirPods Max 2 have somewhere in the ballpark of 30 hours with ANC on. The Aventho Y do look pretty large as far as wireless headphones go, though, so that may just be the price you pay for battery endurance. It’s not just battery life that makes the Aventho Y feel like a good deal, either. Probably my favorite unexpected feature is the inclusion of a USB-C dongle for low-latency playback. This feature is similar to the Fender Mix wireless headphones, and just like that pair, there’s room for storage inside the earcup so you don’t immediately lose it. Outside of those features, there’s more to appreciate, like the foldable design, a user-replaceable battery, magnetic ear pads, aluminum sliders, and stainless-steel hinges. Overall, the components look both solid and very replaceable, which is more than most wireless headphones can say. Probably the best part about the Aventho Y is that they aren’t going to break the bank. At just 150, they’re about half the price of flagship pairs of wireless headphones like Nothing’s Headphone 1. I haven’t had a chance to test the Aventho’s most important feature—the audio quality—but on paper these look like arguably the best new wireless headphones out of IFA.

item.title: In What Ways Are We Not Prepared for the Big One?
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.75
The West Coast of the United States lies on the Pacific ring of fire, the most seismically active region in the world. It’s home to two major faults, the San Andreas in California and the Cascadia Subduction Zone in the Pacific Northwest, that are capable of producing catastrophic earthquakes. Both are long overdue for one. The last time a major quake struck the San Andreas was 120 years ago, and now scientists say stresses along this fault are the highest they’ve been in the last 1,000 years. The Cascadia Subduction Zone hasn’t produced one since 1700, when a magnitude 9 quake—one of the largest in recorded history—triggered a tsunami that decimated the coast of Japan. Scientists say it’s not a matter of if, but when, the next disaster strikes. Commonly called “the big one,” this hypothetical but inevitable quake could come at any time, so communities need to be ready. Recent events have served as tragic reminders of just how devastating these natural disasters can be. In June, a pair of earthquakes killed more than 6,500 people in Venezuela, and other large quakes in the Philippines, Indonesia, and Columbia have killed hundreds over the summer. For this Giz Asks, we asked experts what gaps remain in the West Coast’s preparedness. They highlight vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure that could hinder recovery from a catastrophic earthquake and exacerbate its toll. The following responses may have been lightly edited for length and clarity. Yumei Wang Affiliate faculty and senior advisor on infrastructure resilience and risk at Portland State University’s Maseeh College of Engineering & Computer Science. Wang’s research focuses on the transformation of communities from vulnerability to resilience in the face of disasters, including Cascadia earthquakes and tsunamis. She also has extensive experience with post-earthquake investigations around the world. When children go to school, they should be in buildings that are reliably safe. When someone in need calls 911, they should reach help. Critical infrastructure is essential not only for normal societal functioning but also for public safety. However, much critical infrastructure remains vulnerable to extensive damage from earthquakes. As evidenced by recent earthquakes and numerous engineering risk studies, services provided by critical infrastructure after earthquakes are often severely compromised. Water services may be unavailable for months. To assure effective response and timely recovery after earthquakes, it is imperative that the reliability and resilience of critical infrastructure be substantially improved. Civic infrastructure—schools and emergency response facilities, such as hospitals and fire stations—are important community assets that serve as safety nets during emergencies. Lifeline systems—water, wastewater, electricity, natural gas, liquid fuels, communications, and transportation—provide basic societal services that are needed for earthquake response and recovery. The Pacific Northwest is threatened by a future megaquake on the Cascadia Subduction Zone. A magnitude 9 earthquake and tsunami would likely produce an unprecedented catastrophe. Citizens should expect a regionwide electrical blackout, widespread bridge losses impacting transportation mobility, prolonged gasoline shortages associated with damaged pipelines, extended natural gas service outages, damages exceeding $100 billion, and tens of thousands of casualties. In Oregon, we took an innovative approach to evaluate seismic safety deficiencies of schools and emergency response facilities and have statewide policies and grant programs to help mitigate deficiencies. Furthermore, Oregon has systematically identified and quantified expected post-earthquake delays in resumption of basic lifeline services, which are reflected in the Oregon Resilience Plan. Although many impressive efforts to strengthen lifeline systems have been and continue to be made, Oregon is only in its early stages of needed earthquake preparations. With the expected destruction, citizens are urged to prepare to be “on your own” for at least two weeks. Currently, significant vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure exist, particularly the reliability of lifeline services after earthquakes. Lifeline system interdependencies, lack of coordination among systems, and the absence of regulatory oversight on service deliveries underpin the lack of readiness in earthquake prone regions. To improve earthquake preparedness, society must make it a top priority to remedy the deficiencies in our critical infrastructure, especially within lifeline systems. Greg Beroza Wayne Loel Professor of Earth Science at Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability. Beroza’s research interest is in analyzing seismograms to understand how earthquakes work and to quantify the hazards they pose, and his group works to improve earthquake monitoring in all settings by applying data mining and machine learning techniques to large volumes of continuous seismic waveform data. It’s been 120 years since the last large urban earthquake in the U.S. (1906 San Francisco). Recent earthquakes in Türkiye and Venezuela, where the geology is not that different from California, offer a glimpse of what could be in store. I don’t think we’re prepared for what’s coming. The infrastructure of civilization—internet, cellular coverage, electricity, gas, water, sewage, hospitals, roads, railroads, bridges, ports—are all susceptible to earthquake damage. These are critical to effective post-earthquake response. Following the big one, the degree to which they are damaged will compromise response, so we need to harden them. Building codes will help protect us, but the earthquake-resistant provisions in them are similar to those in other countries. They are also intended to ensure survivability of occupants, not the continuing viability of most buildings. If the occupants escape, but buildings are a total loss, that would be considered a success. That might not feel like success, and I don’t think we’re prepared for the economic fall out that would result from the concentrated loss of many buildings and infrastructure. There are secondary effects as well. A large earthquake in Cascadia would generate a tsunami that would compound the damage by striking the coast soon after the earthquake. A large earthquake in California would rupture gas lines and start fires at dozens of widely dispersed points. Fighting those fires would be difficult because communications, water supply, and transportation would all be impacted. This happened in 1906 when fires started, merged, and raged for three days, burning most of San Francisco to the ground. If an earthquake strikes during a period of high winds, it’s difficult to comprehend what might follow. Earthquakes and their effects are inevitable and pose an acute threat. They are rare, fortunately, but that rarity makes them difficult to study. It also makes them tempting to ignore relative to more commonly encountered threats. Their onset is sudden, however, so we need to act now to understand them and to build structures, cities, and systems to withstand them. Once the big one begins it will be too late. Jonathan Stewart The Sabol-Scott Term Chair in Civil and Environmental Engineering and a professor of civil and environmental engineering at UCLA’s Samueli School of Engineering. Stewart’s research interests are in geotechnical earthquake engineering and engineering seismology. His group works to learn from past earthquakes to improve understanding of seismic events and apply that understanding to the development of practical models. Let’s begin by reviewing positive developments. Since the 1994 Northridge earthquake, the California Department of Transportation has made significant advances in how to effectively retrofit bridges and has implemented those improvements. State legislation has mandated seismic assessments of hospitals, which has led to many retrofits and some hospital structure replacements. Mandatory retrofit ordinances have been implemented in some municipalities, including Los Angeles and San Francisco. We should celebrate these advancements.While progress has been made, California continues to face substantial earthquake risk, which is influenced by our location on a plate boundary but is also affected by the political will to confront vulnerabilities. Urban centers receive essential fresh water from aqueducts that cross major faults. For example, in Los Angeles, we receive more than half our water from three systems (Los Angeles Aqueduct, California Water Project, Colorado River Aqueduct), which cross the San Andreas Fault and could be ruptured by a single earthquake. Emergency reservoirs west of the fault are in place but are a temporary fix. We will be in a race against time to repair the aqueducts as the emergency reservoirs are depleted. Will this occur fast enough? Even if regional water supply is intact, breaks in water distribution systems and sewer systems from ground failure (i.e., liquefaction and landslides) are likely to lower water pressures, potentially rendering delivered water as non-potable. This will significantly impact daily life for earthquake survivors. While relatively modern, code-designed structures in strongly shaken areas are likely to survive the earthquake, some may be damaged to an extent that re-occupancy is not possible. This will lead to significant household and business displacement, potentially leading to de-population and impacting local economies. Whether that impact is short-term or long-term will depend on the pace of recovery, which is uncertain. Some structures, mainly older vulnerable buildings that have not been retrofitted, will collapse, costing lives. It is a tragedy waiting to happen. The severity of these impacts will depend on earthquake location relative to the locations of vulnerable buildings. Giz Asks is a recurring Gizmodo series in which experts answer big questions in their own words, offering a range of perspectives on the ideas, discoveries, and debates that affect our lives and shape our understanding of the world.

item.title: Pete Hegseth’s Testosterone Push for US Troops Is Off to a Very Low-T Start
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.72
United States Secretary of War Pete Hegseth’s plan to boost testosterone levels among American troops is not off to the smoothest start. This week, the Pentagon issued and then quickly revoked its clinical guidance for Hegseth’s mandatory testosterone screening policy. The policy, announced earlier this summer, will call for all service members 30 and older to have their testosterone levels measured as part of the annual check-up. The Pentagon has stated that the guidance was only temporarily pulled but has not clarified exactly why nor when it will be reissued. Reuters was the first to report on the sudden about-face. “The draft ‘Clinical Guidance for Health and Human Performance Optimization’ published on September 2, 2026, has been temporarily rescinded to allow for updates,” a Pentagon official told Gizmodo in an email Friday, reiterating the same comments provided to Reuters. Screening for low T Hegseth announced the plan in mid-July with all the bombastic flair you’d expect from the Trump administration.
