In an X post titled “The High-T Department of War” with an accompanying video, Hegseth stated: “We owe our warriors the absolute best medical care in the world, and this program delivers on that obligation.” The screening is ostensibly meant to detect cases of testosterone deficiency, also known as hypogonadism. People with hypogonadism can experience disruptive symptoms like fatigue, osteoporosis, and low sex drive, and they commonly benefit from testosterone replacement therapy (TRT). More recent research has also allayed earlier worries that TRT can cause serious complications like heart attack and stroke. That said, many experts have criticized the logic behind Hegseth’s universal screening plan. Up to a third of men placed on TRT today don’t actually meet the criteria for testosterone deficiency, according to the American Urological Association, while up to 25% of men aren’t even tested for their T levels prior to treatment. And though generally safe, long-term TRT can increase the odds of lasting infertility, which is why the AUA cautions younger men who still want children to be especially careful about going on it. The link between testosterone and men’s health and aging is also more complicated than many supporters of TRT—a group that includes our current health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—might want it to be. And though low T can be a real health problem that TRT helps address, it’s certainly possible many service members screened in the program could wind up receiving medical care they don’t truly need. “Taking testosterone is not going to make you more manly, more strong, or a more robust individual. That’s just not how it works,” Jason Goldman, an internal medicine physician and past president of the American College of Physicians, told Reuters. “It’s just bad policy all around.” On Wednesday, the Pentagon posted its clinical guidance for how the plan would be implemented on its website, including the recommended next steps for people to take if they tested positive for low T, along with an accompanying statement from spokesperson Sean Parnell. But by Thursday, the guidance and statement were removed with no explanation. Right now, the links only result in a 404 error page. What happens now? The Pentagon notes that interim guidance regarding the policy remains in effect. And opening stumble aside, it appears that the screening program is still going to be fully implemented. “The Department remains committed to addressing hormone deficiencies, protecting the long-term health of its Service members, and enabling peak operational performance,” the Pentagon official told Gizmodo. Regarding the timeline for the final version of the guidance, the official stated only that it would be “issued shortly.”

item.title: Would You Buy an AI Smart Home Hub for $20,000?
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.66
At IFA 2026, I stumbled on a booth where Ugreen, a company I’ve mostly known for its charging and USB-C hubs but that also makes NAS servers, has announced a new smart hub line that supports Matter, has a built-in AI assistant, and supports standard hard drives for NAS-style storage. If that all sounds familiar to you, it’s because I could just as easily be describing the MindBase that Anker announced yesterday. The HomeAgent will come in three flavors: the $1,800 HomeAgent HA100, the $6,000 HomeAgent HA100 Pro, and the $20,000 MasterAgent MA100. Ouch. (Anker, for what it’s worth, didn’t announce pricing for the MindBase.) All three of these are Matter-compatible, although the reps at the booth insisted when asked about it that Ugreen would really prefer people use its own smart home products. (It also announced three new smart home cameras yesterday.) There’s a built-in AI assistant called “Uliya” that you can talk with to control those devices. As the representatives tried to demo the unit, it often just didn’t respond to its wake phrase, although in Ugreen’s defense, it was noisy in the area. I actually had better luck getting it to respond. I got it to open some shades, for instance, although when I asked it to turn some smart lights pink, it played music on a nearby, also-newly-announced Ugreen smart speaker instead. Similar to other generative AI-based smart home assistants, it’s slow. When you say “Hi Uliya” (which might be one of the most awkward wake phrases I’ve ever used) followed by your request, it processes for a few seconds before acknowledging and carrying it out. You can also ask the assistant to do things like play music you’ve stored locally on the device. It wasn’t clear if streaming services are supported yet. Much like Anker’s MindBase, part of the pitch is that you can invoke Uliya to ask about events that occurred within sight of your cameras or search photos you’ve backed up to the HomeAgent’s internal storage. The differences appear to come down to technical prowess. The HA100 has the lowest-performing CPU, only 16GB of LPDDR5 RAM, and 64GB of built-in flash storage, for instance, while the highest-end $20,000 MA100 is equipped with an Nvidia Jetson Thor T5000—good for “up to 2,070 TFLOPS”—128GB of RAM, and a 256GB M.2 NVMe SSD. I’m sure that makes for one of the best AI computers you can own, but sheesh, that price.

item.title: ‘Silo’ Season 3 Goes Out With a Bang
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.43
If for any reason over the past few years you ever felt like, “Man, it’s been hard to stick with Silo,” the season three finale made every second worth it. It was a shocking, brutal, excellent episode that perfectly paid off the season’s dual timeline story, while answering a bunch of questions and posing even more. To say more than that would be a massive spoiler, so let’s get into those massive spoilers for the season three finale of Silo, titled “Troy.” When we last left the characters in the previous episode, we saw the opening day of the silos and a mysterious nuclear explosion. Daniel and Helen, pregnant with their child, were separated and, we assume, forced to go into the silos they had been assigned: Number one for Daniel, number 18 for Helen. Unfortunately, the finale didn’t answer any of the questions about who set off the explosion, how everyone involved with the silos knew, or anything like that. But it did reveal the fate of most of those characters, in a way no one could have expected. The finale picks up hundreds of years in the future with Daniel waking up from some sort of cryo sleep. Only, they don’t call him Daniel. They call him “Troy.” And Troy is awakened by Victor (the doctor who helped his sister all those years ago) to help with a problem. There is an insurrection in silo 17, and Troy needs to figure out how to stop it. This is the event that Steve Zahn’s character experienced as a child, several decades before the events of the main timeline of the show. Instantly, as a viewer, we’re shook. How do all of those people we saw enter the silo hundreds of years before look exactly the same? Why is Daniel not Daniel anymore? We don’t know exactly, but apparently, Victor’s memory juice is not just working. It’s thriving. Troy goes to operations to try to fix the problem, and he runs into his sister Charlotte, though they call her “Susan.” He doesn’t recognize her. She doesn’t recognize him. And, eventually, Troy/Daniel is forced to dismiss Susan/Charlotte when she refuses to act out Troy’s plan to massacre almost 10,000 people. But he does it and is rewarded for it. Meanwhile, something is bugging Troy. Not the thousands of people he just killed to keep some silo secrets we don’t understand. He’s bothered by visions of a woman. A woman we know to be his wife, Helen. Troy asks Victor about her, and Victor says he doesn’t know what he’s talking about. However, we know Victor knew Helen, and we see that he has a file full of proof that Troy has asked him about her dozens of times. They are purposely keeping this from him. Speaking of Helen, though, we’re led to believe she ended up in silo 18, right? The same silo our show is set in? The same silo where the Pez dispenser Daniel gave her years ago shows up? The silo of Juliette Nichols, who sure seems to share that same rambunctious charm Helen had, doesn’t she? Hmmm. We wonder. Fast forward a few decades, picking up events from the end of the previous episode and finally bringing the two timelines from this season together. It’s revealed that Bernard and Camille’s suspicions from the penultimate episode are true. The all-knowing AI that gives them their orders is not a computer but a person. In this case, Victor, who is about to kill every single person in silo 18 for setting off some bombs. Camille begs him for time, which he gives, and ultimately we learn that Camille turned on her superiors and helped the rebels cap the failsafe pipe. It took all season to figure it out, but the pipe that would’ve allowed silo one to kill everyone with gas was finally located and capped, saving everyone’s lives. When Victor asks Camille why she turned her back on her superiors, she says it’s because she couldn’t answer a simple question. Why would they have the power to kill everyone? Victor doesn’t answer. Victor’s answer is to wake up Troy, which is how we learn it’s been 35 years since he killed all those people at silo 17. Apparently, silo one has a cryo process, and the people there go “on” and “off shift” every few years, which is how they age so slowly. Or, at least, that’s the implication. Senator Thurman, who runs the whole thing, looks a little older, but most everyone else is close to the age they were when it all started. Anyway, Troy is awake again and ready to figure out how to kill everyone in silo 18 when Juliette and her friends all approach the mysterious doorway down by the silo digger. This, apparently, is off limits, and Troy takes over the omniscient voice. He threatens the group, but eventually they reach a compromise—as long as they don’t try to contact any other silos, there will be no safeguard attempts. Everyone will be safe. Juliette agrees. But does she really? Of course not. This is Juliette we’re talking about, and she hatches a plan to not just save everyone in her silo, but all the silos. The one thing she feels silo one won’t be expecting is a full-on assault, and that’s what she wants to do. Meanwhile, we learn that Victor killed himself after the events earlier in the episode, and Troy gets a posthumous email from him. Victor reveals that he felt relief that the people of silo 18 stopped the failsafe, implying maybe he didn’t buy into their mission as much as he had for the past few centuries. That’s why he took his life. But before he went, he had one more piece of info for Troy—a name: Helen Drew. And, it seems, the name certainly triggered something. It would, considering she was your wife and the mother of a child you never got to meet. So the tables are set for the fourth and final season of Silo. Juliette Nichols is ready to take silo 18 out into the world and save the rest of the silos. The leaders in silo one, who have been around for centuries maintaining this mysterious balance, may have started to see some cracks. And there are certainly implications that Juliette, or someone, in silo 18 has some relation to Daniel, aka Troy, one of the top leaders. And yet, there are still so many questions that it’s almost silly. Who set off the explosion in the past? How did everyone know about it? Why did they do it? Why did they set up a system that they’d rather people die than communicate with each other? Can they repopulate the world at some point? Is there even a world left out there? What is the ultimate plan? Why isn’t this cryo sleep technology being used for better things? Again, so many questions. But this is Silo. And we’d have it no other way. The season three finale proved that even though Silo is always gonna have us asking questions, when we get the answers, it will be worth it. We just have to be patient. Here are a few other things we wondered: - The Senator says that Charlotte/Susan can’t be punished for her insubordination because her skills as a pilot will be crucial at the end of the mission. What does that mean? What is the ending? - The silos were the brainchild of Per Stensen (Colin Hanks) and Senator Rosalind Thurman, right? Well, the senator is still alive, kicking, and running the whole thing. But where is Stensen? And, yes, we know Silo is based on a series of books, and the answers are out there and accessible. But we’re talking about the show and prefer to experience the story that way. Want more io9 news? Check out when to expect the latest Marvel, Star Wars, and Star Trek releases, what’s next for the DC Universe on film and TV, and everything you need to know about the future of Doctor Who.

item.title: This Hiking Exoskeleton May Actually Help Your Bad Knees, Finally
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.21
I was ready to write off the surge of exoskeletons as yet another example of cool tech without an audience to use it. Then Hypershell strapped me into its Hypershell Halo, yet another mechanical armature with servos that are supposed to “assist” your legs for every step. Finally, these exoskeletons are taking our knees into account. Hypershell Halo is much like its past hiking exoskeletons, but with a lot more on offer. The carbon fiber wearable suit sits on your hips and attaches to your thighs, then uses onboard sensors to detect your movement and kick in motors to assist your legs. The new version adds another set of motors that are meant to sit exactly at knee level with another set of straps hogtied to your calves. The entire exoskeleton operates as one, but as you step, it pulls both your thigh and lower leg, making movement feel easier, especially when climbing inclines or stairs. IFA 2026 was swarmed with exoskeletons, mostly from China-based brands, and many were promising the same thing. However, I have more experience with Hypershell than most. I’ve done multiple hikes with both the original Hypershell Pro X and several more recent jaunts with the Hypershell X Ultra S. Even with minor improvements to the exoskeleton’s ability to sense your movement, they both suffer from the same problems. The big issue is how they were not built for the right audience. An experienced hiker wouldn’t necessarily want to dress up in a steel cage that only takes away the pleasurable burn and triumph of making it to the top of a mountain. Hypershell marketed its exoskeleton only to physically fit people, not the people with bad knees who could actually use assistive technology. The Halo isn’t just helping you lift your legs. It provides a cushioning sensation if you jump off a small ledge. There’s a sit-up feature that lets you take little effort from sitting to standing. Toby Knisely, Hypercshell’s director of communications, told me that the team considers Halo as a device “for everyone,” including those who are healthy and those who actually need help with mobility. “A lot of people were about asking the knees, asking for more support—especially that cushioning on the way down,” he said. There are other upgrades as well, including a new, more compact battery that sits to the side rather than behind. It’s also a more involved device, requiring several minutes of fitting to make sure your exoskeleton is positioned correctly and snug to the body. It’s more invasive, as well, and you’ll naturally look like a cyborg dressed up for Halloween in a human suit. There’s even an optional over-arm strap that can help support its weight more for when you’re going the distance. It is not a subtle device. There are several other companies at IFA trying to promote the same type of device. Dnsys rolled out its Z1, a more low-key, knee-specific ekoskeleton with only one motor that surrounds one or both legs at the joint. Then there’s Ascentiz with its “K” model exoskeleton that includes a separate attachable below-the-knee motor. I asked Ascentiz to use their K model, but the company told me only the above-the-knee “H” model was available to try on. Beyond those devices, the Hypershell Halo seems to be the most feature-rich and fully realized of its kind. That means it will cost extra. The Halo is up for preorder now, and it will cost you $2,300. Unless you can try it for yourself, there’s no way to tell if it will assist your needs or not. At least, now there’s a chance it will help.

item.title: This ‘Super’ El Niño Has Whipped Up a Never-Before-Seen Cyclone Trio in the Pacific
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.13
The Pacific Ocean is only midway through peak hurricane season, but it’s already been super-charged by this year’s historic El Niño. So far, 15 named storms and six hurricanes have formed in the northeastern Pacific—which is well above average—and even more have taken shape in the northwestern Pacific. But it’s not just the number of storms that has been concerning; it’s their intensity. This week, NASA captured a rare trio of tropical cyclones spiraling in succession just above the equator in the northeastern Pacific. The storms include two current hurricanes, Lowell and Karina, as well as a tropical storm named Marie that is still intensifying as it tracks northwest in parallel to the Pacific coast. According to NASA, the satellite image documents just how unusually powerful the Pacific Ocean’s storms have become this hurricane season. “Of the three, Lowell became the strongest, with winds reaching Category 5 strength for several hours on September 2,” Adam Voiland, a technical writer with the NASA Earth Observatory, explained in a post by the U.S. space agency. “Around the same time, Karina, spinning a few thousand kilometers to the east, achieved category 4 strength, a rare case of category 4 and 5 hurricanes occurring simultaneously in the area.” But meteorologist Andrew Markowitz, a former chair of the American Meteorological Society, was willing to put it a little more dramatically: “The only other occurrence of this in the world was [hurricanes] Irma and Jose in September 2017 in the Atlantic,” Markowitz posted to X. “Wild stuff!” Truly EPIC imagery This rare procession of storms was photographed by NASA’s Deep Space Climate Observatory (DSCOVR) satellite this Tuesday, September 1, via its Earth Polychromatic Imaging Camera (EPIC). DSCOVR—a strategically significant platform co-managed by the U.S. Air Force—orbits about one million miles from Earth in a unique location where the gravitational pull between our planet and the Sun is equal, Lagrange Point 1, allowing it to hover in place over Earth’s sunlit side. Also of note in the image is a curiously long horizontal band of clouds and thunderstorms along the equator, appearing to underline the three tropical cyclones. This line of storm clouds—which looks to be thousands of miles long—sits at the so-called Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), a collision of northeasterly and southeasterly trade winds that helps create tropical cyclones. Fortunately, two of these three storms pose no risks to human populations on land, although the National Weather Service did issue an advisory for Hawaii, where “swells from Lowell are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions during the next several days.” 🌡️ El Niño is firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months. WMO forecasts show ~100% likelihood that it will persist through February 2027. A very strong El Niño ≠ same impacts everywhere. 🆕 WMO El Nino Update: https://t.co/KUPq04jjkT pic.twitter.com/PAx1EZTCOH — World Meteorological Organization (@WMO) September 3, 2026 “Literally off the charts” Broadly speaking, the takeaway from this image is that the energy that’s been packed into the Pacific Ocean from climate-induced heating is in scary new territory right now. Subsurface temperatures in some patches of the Pacific this summer rose more than 14 degrees Fahrenheit (8 degrees Celsius) above normal, according to the United Nations’ World Meteorological Organization (WMO). “If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began,” WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo told a press conference in Geneva this Thursday, according to Reuters. “So literally off the charts.” These high subsurface ocean temperatures also mean that this super-charged El Niño is now forecast to drag on longer itself, raising the dire prospect of more months of extreme heat, flooding, and droughts, alongside these record-setting tropical cyclones, the WMO warned. The UN agency noted that it has taken the unusual step of forecasting that El Niño will persist on into February 2027 with “close to” 100% confidence. “Never before has the UN weather agency issued such an unequivocal forecast for El Niño,” WMO stated in its announcement. Consequently, the heat from the current El Niño is reportedly on track to generate intense Category 5 hurricanes at record-breaking numbers this year, and the rampant recent activity in the Pacific underscores that impact. “We are already seeing the disruption and devastation caused by droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to worsen as El Niño intensifies,” Celeste Saulo said.

item.title: You don’t need to code or spend money to improve KDE—here are 7 ways to help
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.85
Open-source software is wonderful: it's free, diverse, and surprisingly accessible. You might feel that software development is a secret world of privilege and insider knowledge, but OSS has made great strides to overturn this misunderstanding. Whatever your skill set, you can make a difference and improve open-source software like KDE. If you can write, draw, code, speak more than one language, or just use your system, you can help out. Use KDE as much as possible By running the desktop, you're helping out without even realizing it OK, this might sound too good to be true, but just by using KDE, you are helping to improve the overall system: congratulations! First, the built-in Dr Konqi software will automatically offer to send a bug report if a KDE app ever crashes. This contains details of what happened and your current environment, so the devs can debug the problem. You don't have to report bugs, but it just takes a single button press to do, so there's little reason not to. You can also report telemetry data by enabling it in KDE's System Settings app, via the User Feedback module. This sends anonymous information about the apps you run, how long you run them for, and so on. Again, this is entirely optional, but it's vital for the system to improve based on real-world usage. Report any bugs manually A well-crafted bug report is invaluable to the developer team If you encounter a more complex crash, like a bug in an app that doesn't support Dr Konqi, you can report it manually using the KDE Bugzilla issue tracker. This process isn't for the faint-hearted, but you can rest assured that your feedback will help to improve the system for everyone. The bug tracker isn't the only way to report something; you can send ideas, discuss new features, or alert the developers to security vulnerabilities too. Flex your design skills With your help, KDE can look its very best Let's face it: engineers aren't always the best qualified when it comes to creating stunning imagery, or even designing slick interfaces. Linux has long suffered from a perception that it just doesn't look that good, and while this complaint is a bit overplayed, there's an element of truth to it. Fortunately, you can help, either by working on the look of the core product or on a secondary element like a KDE project's web design. Even more fortunately, all the tools you'll need are freely available, from KolourPaint-a quick and simple paint tool-to GIMP, the free alternative to Photoshop that's packed full of features. The KDE team uses familiar tools like Figma for collaboration, and you can contribute icons, cursors, wallpapers, and many other types of artwork. Translate text Help people all around the world KDE software is used worldwide, with around 60–80 different languages supported depending on the component. All those languages need translators to convert in-app text and documentation. If you're suitably qualified, check out the KDE Localization team, which deals with language translation alongside other international issues; everything from icon design to text encoding. Work is organized using mailing lists; there will either be one for the application you're interested in, or you can use the general-purpose kde-i18n-doc Write documentation Explain how things work and help others understand the system If you only know one language, that's fine; there's still plenty of writing to be done! Another task that developers often fail at — or are simply uninterested in — is writing documentation. If you have a flair for prose, consider the many areas in which your words can be a part of KDE. Most end-user documentation is hosted online at the many wikis maintained by the project. Again, the central point of contact — and best place to begin — is a mailing list, kde-doc-english. Spread the word Tell everyone else how amazing a free OS can be Are you an expert in marketing or a social media pro? If so, KDE can use your talents in promotion. Members of the KDE Promo team reach out to existing and potential users to discuss what the desktop does and how it can help them. The promotion effort takes in a variety of activities, from writing blog posts to attending conferences and scouting for new contributors. If you're a people person, this is certainly a great way to get involved. Make code contributions Build the apps, libraries, and core utilities that define KDE Last — but far from least, of course — is the work involved in building KDE, the software itself: programming. You'll start by learning to build KDE and its associated programs, using a freely available toolset. There's more information in the official mailing list, kde-devel, and you can even join a mentoring scheme for one-to-one assistance with an experienced developer. Remember that you can use a developer skill set for more than just hardcore programming, too: bug triaging, software testing, and technical documentation all benefit from knowledge and understanding of the codebase. Contributing can be addictive, even in small quantities I've personally contributed to open-source software, but only in fairly small ways: a bug report here, a minor patch there. But every time I've had code accepted into a project, it's accompanied by a warm, fuzzy feeling that my work has been appreciated and is genuinely going to help other people too. But there are many ways you can contribute to open-source projects, even without coding, and there's plenty more information on contributing to KDE on the project's main Get Involved page.

item.title: How to avoid paying a smart doorbell subscription fee
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.61
Are you hoping to avoid yet another subscription? Rather than opting for a Ring Protect or Nest Aware plan, buy a smart doorbell that gives you options instead. Here’s how to avoid the ongoing fees. Premium subscriptions are optional Accept fewer features Broadly speaking, most smart doorbells come with basic functionality out of the box. You’re able to answer the door on a smartphone or tablet, connect to the camera to view a live feed and get limited notifications of activity. Amazon’s Ring doorbells come with a 30-day trial of Ring Protect, while Google’s Nest doorbell has a 3-hour video history included for free but requires a premium Nest Aware subscription for longer. Some features like Ring’s Person Alerts and Google’s sound detection also depend on these services. If you want your smart doorbell to work more like a security system, you’ll need some way to save your recordings. Though many smart doorbell providers will try to tempt you into a monthly or annual subscription, there are other ways of doing it. If all you want is the basic functionality of being able to remotely answer the doorbell and not missing a package then you can ignore these options altogether. Store captured footage on an SD card You might miss out on some features, but you won't pay for video storage The most convenient way to avoid paying a smart doorbell cloud storage fee is to buy a smart doorbell that stores footage on a memory card instead. This is a cost-effective way to store recordings since flash memory is cheap and you can spend as little or as much on a card that suits your budget. Some of the cheapest doorbells on the market store footage on local memory, like the WYZE Video Doorbell v2 and the eufy Video Doorbell C210. Many of the more expensive ones have this option too. You don’t even need to manage space manually as most doorbells that offer this option will automatically remove the oldest footage and keep recording. In the event that you need access to your footage for some reason, you can simply eject the memory card and put it in a computer to copy the files across. There are a few downsides to this approach, the most obvious one being a lack of redundancy. Since all of your footage will be stored on a single memory card, if something happens to your storage medium the footage will be lost. This includes an intruder tampering with your doorbell. Though most doorbells that offer this option have a locking mechanism in place, these aren't infallible. If the intruder knows that your doorbell is a variety that uses a memory card for storage, they may feel inclined to break in and steal the card. On top of this, you might find yourself in a situation where you need to access recordings remotely. If the only place you have stored your footage is on local memory, you won’t be able to review the footage until you physically gain access to your doorbell. Of course, local memory card backup works great as part of a multifaceted approach to data storage. Get a HomeKit Secure video doorbell Let your HomePod or iPad do the heavy lifting If you happen to be an Apple user with an iCloud+ subscription, HomeKit Secure Video might be the best solution. For this to work, you will need a HomeKit hub such as an Apple TV 4K, a HomePod, or an iPad that remains home and acts as a local server. You'll also need a smart doorbell that is compatible with HomeKit Secure Video such as the Aqara Smart Video Doorbell G4 or the Logitech Circle View Doorbell. These aren’t the cheapest doorbells on the market, but since they can use Apple’s servers for data storage you’ll likely make your money back in the long-run. HomeKit Secure Video can be used to stream video live from your doorbell camera using the Home app on any Apple device connected to your Apple ID. Live feeds are encrypted end-to-end for security purposes. You’ll also get notifications of events detected by your camera, including people calling or packages being delivered. This footage is analyzed locally on your HomeKit hub rather than being sent to a remote server. This privacy-centric approach taken by Apple has been criticized in the past since it isn't as advanced as some of the alternatives that are processed in the cloud. You can use a single camera with a 50GB iCloud+ subscription, or you'll get up to five cameras with a 200GB plan. If you subscribe to the 2 TB plan, you can use as many cameras as you like. Footage stored on Apple’s servers is kept for 10 days and does not count towards your iCloud storage quota. The big benefit to using HomeKit Secure Video instead of solely relying on a memory card is that your footage will be available remotely, so you can view it from anywhere. Store footage on a local recorder Some doorbells are made for local storage Many “proper” home security systems use an NVR—or network video recorder—to store footage locally within the premises. This is overkill for a video doorbell system, though you can certainly find doorbells out there that support the necessary protocols. A better solution is to buy a smart doorbell that comes with a user-friendly solution like the eufy Video Doorbell S220. This doorbell uses eufy’s Homebase system, which acts as a hub for local recordings. There are no ongoing costs since captured footage is stored locally on the Homebase. eufy’s solution is user-upgradeable and works with the company’s other security cameras. Analysis takes place locally on the hub, with all footage encrypted. The fact that the Homebase remains inside your property means that tampering with the doorbell will not jeopardize your footage. You’ll pay a bit more for a bundle that includes a Homebase, but there’s no ongoing fee. Some doorbells include cloud or FTP support Build your own security camera server! If you avoid companies like Ring and Google, you might just find a doorbell that allows you to “roll your own” backup solution. This can require some work on your part, and there are very few models on the market that offer this option at present. Arguably the best right now is the Reolink Video Doorbell PoE or Reolink Video Doorbell Wi-Fi, depending on your needs. These affordable cameras can be had for around $100, use microSD storage, and automatically sync recordings with an FTP server of your choice. You’ll need to follow Reolink’s instructions to get everything working. Alternatively, the Netatmo Smart Video Doorbell offers up to 32GB local storage on a microSD card, with optional Dropbox or FTP upload. The big problem here is that this doorbell has been discontinued and can be hard to find. Use Home Assistant instead Own your own smart home Home Assistant is an open-source smart home platform that allows you to use devices from a range of different smart home ecosystems. In order to use Home Assistant, you’ll need to install it on a device such as a Raspberry Pi or spare computer that remains running on your local network. Since everything takes place locally, Home Assistant will record video captured by your smart doorbell (and similar cameras) to local storage. If you want to capture more footage, add more storage and scale up your Home Assistant server accordingly. The biggest hurdle you’re likely to encounter with the Home Assistant approach is finding a suitable doorbell and setting it up accordingly. There are many threads on the Home Assistant message boards asking for recommendations, with some members going as far as building their own solutions. If you aren’t already using Home Assistant, this approach will require a bit of work. You should search the Home Assistant Integrations database to see what options are available to you. Some manufacturers like Aquara have committed to providing support for Home Assistant through Matter support. On the upside, Home Assistant is completely free to download and install. You’ll lose nothing but an afternoon downloading and testing it out on an old piece of hardware, and you’ll likely discover just how powerful Home Assistant automations can be in the process. In some cases, a cloud subscription is just better and easier If money isn’t a concern and you’re happy to pay for a premium cloud backup and extra bells and whistles, premium subscriptions have their place. HomeKit Secure Video is another great option that doesn’t require too much setup.

item.title: 3 little-known Excel tools worth exploring this weekend (September 4-6)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.40
Excel has plenty of features that can make everyday spreadsheet work easier, but some of the most useful ones are surprisingly easy to overlook. If you have a little time to experiment this weekend, try three of my favorite hidden gems. Custom Lists can teach Excel your own order Make Excel fill and sort the way you actually work Excel already knows that Monday comes after Sunday and February comes after January. But you can also teach it sequences that are specific to how you work. Custom Lists let you create your own order and then use it with Excel's fill handle or sorting tools. For example, a project tracker might use three priorities: High, Medium, and Low. To create this sequence: - Go to File > Options, then open the Advanced menu. - Scroll to the General section and click Edit Custom Lists. - Select NEW LIST. - Enter the items in the order you want them. - Click Add, then OK. Now type the first word in your list into a cell and drag the fill handle down. Instead of repeating that word, Excel continues with the next items in the sequence you created. You can also drag the sequence across a row if you want to create a set of column headings or another repeating structure. You might be thinking this is only useful for niche scenarios, but Custom Lists really earn their keep when you need to sort data according to your own logic. Excel's standard alphabetical sort would put these priorities in the order High → Low → Medium, but that's rarely useful. With a custom list, you can have Excel sort the data according to the order you've defined. Here's how: - Select your table. - Go to Data > Sort. - Select the column you want to sort. - Choose Customized List from the Order menu. - Select the custom list you created, then click OK. Excel sorts the entire table according to that hierarchy. You can also import a longer sequence from an existing worksheet rather than entering each item manually. Once created, the list is saved in Excel's settings, so you can use it again in other workbooks on the same computer. Excel's Camera tool can put live data anywhere Turn a range into a picture that stays up to date Copying cells from one part of a workbook to another is easy enough, but a normal copy can quickly become outdated when the original data changes. Excel's Camera tool creates an image of a cell range that stays linked to the original cells. Change the source data, and the picture updates too. This can be particularly useful when creating a dashboard. Suppose a detailed monthly budget sits on one worksheet, while a separate dashboard needs to display those figures. Instead of copying the cells and maintaining a second version, use Camera to display the original range on the dashboard. First, you'll need to add Camera to your Quick Access Toolbar (QAT): - Click the down arrow on the right-hand side of any tab on the ribbon. If you see Show Quick Access Toolbar, click it to activate your QAT. - Click the QAT down arrow and select More Commands. - Select All Commands in the Choose commands from menu. - Scroll to and select Camera, click Add to add it to your QAT, then click OK. You'll now see Camera in your QAT. Now, select the cells you want to display, click Camera, move to the destination worksheet, and click and drag to place the picture. The result looks like an ordinary image while remaining connected to the source range. If a budget figure or some formatting changes in the original cells, the corresponding figure in the image changes as well. The captured range can also be moved and resized, making it easy to position alongside charts, headings, or other dashboard elements. Camera works best with fixed ranges. If the source is an Excel table that regularly expands, newly added rows may not appear in the captured image. And if you want to capture a chart or another object, select the cells behind it rather than the object itself. Analyze Data can find insights without formulas Let Excel do some of the investigative work When you're working with a large table of records, finding useful patterns can mean building formulas, creating PivotTables, or manually sorting and filtering the data. Analyze Data (previously called Ideas) can give you a useful starting point much faster. If you're using Excel for Microsoft 365 and have an internet connection, you can use this tool to automatically examine a structured dataset for patterns and summaries. To use it, select a single cell inside your data, then click Analyze Data in the Data tab. In some versions of Excel, this button is found in the Home tab. Excel opens a pane containing automatically generated insight cards based on the information it finds. You can also type a question into the box at the top of the pane. For example, because this dataset contains "Genre" and "Rating" columns, you could ask, "What average rating does each genre have?" Excel analyzes the data and produces a result that may include a summary table or visualization. If the result is useful, click the contextual Insert button to add the generated chart, PivotTable, or PivotChart to your worksheet. You can also try one of the suggested questions Excel generates based on your data. Analyze Data works best when the source is properly structured. Make sure your data has a single header row and avoid unnecessary blank rows or columns. Formatting the range as an Excel table with Ctrl+T is also a good idea. There's always more to discover in Excel This weekend is as good as any to explore some of Excel's lesser-known features. Custom Lists can make Excel follow your preferred order, Camera can keep a live view of important cells elsewhere in a workbook, and Analyze Data can quickly uncover patterns in a table. There's so much hidden away in Excel that the discovery never really ends. So, if you still have some time to explore, take a look at some little-known Excel clicks that can further power up your spreadsheet skills.

item.title: Background Windows apps are quietly eating your Wi-Fi — here’s how to stop them
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.25
Do you have a fast internet connection, but your Windows PC often feels slower than it should? Have you already tried switching your DNS providers and other internet speed optimization hacks, but still no luck? Well, I’ve been in the same place you are — and after some digging around, I found that a few background apps and processes were causing the problem. Here’s how to find out if that’s happening on your PC and how to stop it for good. I’ll stick to Windows 11’s native tools for this one. But if you’re open to installing a third-party app, I’ve covered a free and open-source network monitor at the end. It can block specific apps from accessing the internet. Find all the apps that are using your internet You can't fix what you haven't measured Before you can stop background apps from hogging your bandwidth, you first need to know which ones are actually using it. Now, for this discovery process, your first instinct might be to open Task Manager, and yes, it does show network usage per app — but you’re only seeing real-time data. Say an app or process was running overnight and drained 5GB of your data but is currently sitting idle. You’re going to completely miss that if you open Task Manager right now. What you want instead is cumulative usage. For that, head to Settings -> Network & internet -> Advanced network settings -> Data usage. This screen lists every app on your system along with how much data each one has consumed over the last 30 days, sorted from hungriest to lightest. Most of it will make sense — your browser will likely be at the top, followed by things like Steam or OneDrive if you use them. What you’re looking for is an app that you rarely use but is consuming gigabytes of data for no apparent reason. Those are the potential troublemakers. Limit background app permissions Not all apps need to run after you close them Now that you know which apps are the problem, the first fix is to cut off their background activity. To do this, head to Settings > Apps > Installed Apps. Find the specific app, click the three-dot menu next to it, and select “Advanced options” or “Modify” — whichever shows up for that app. Scroll down until you see “Background app permissions” and set it to "Never". This will stop the app from running in the background, which not only saves it from slowing down your PC by consuming your CPU and RAM, but also saves Wi-Fi bandwidth by preventing those routine app updates. Now, I should mention that this method will only work for apps installed through the Microsoft Store and the apps Windows ships by default. If you installed an app the regular way — by downloading an installer EXE from the internet — you won’t be able to “modify” the app’s permissions using this method. You can use Portmaster — a free and open-source network firewall — to block internet access for those apps, which effectively does the same thing. I’ve talked about Portmaster in a later section. Configure delivery optimization for Windows updates You shouldn't stop updates — but you should negotiate with them If you look closely at my data usage screen, you might notice that “System and Windows Update” is at a whopping 93GB. Considering my total consumption for the month was around 205GB, that means Windows itself — not individual apps — was eating nearly half of my monthly data. Now, you obviously need to keep Windows updated, so the goal isn’t to stop updates — but rather to control how and when they download. First, if you’re on a metered connection, go to Settings -> Network & internet, select your Wi-Fi or Ethernet connection, and turn on “Metered connection.” This tells Windows to limit data usage and de-prioritize big feature updates and other optional stuff. Your regular security updates will still come through. As a more aggressive measure, you can also “Pause Updates” for up to five weeks. This gives you the flexibility to prevent updates entirely during that period and then manually resume them when you have access to an unmetered network, like your office Wi-Fi or when you’re at a friend’s place. Just remember to ask for their permission first. That said, even if you have an unlimited internet plan, you might not be worried about saving data, but you should still optimize for saving bandwidth. You don’t want Windows to suddenly pull a multi-gigabyte update in the background while you’re on a video call or gaming online. Granted, Windows does throttle background downloads on its own to some extent, but setting an explicit cap means an update can never flood your connection at the worst possible moment. To do this, head to Settings -> Windows Update -> Advanced options -> Delivery optimization. Then, under Download options, you get two options to cap how much bandwidth updates are allowed to consume — you can limit it to absolute Mbps values or as a percentage of measured bandwidth. I’m personally using the percentage option and don’t give it more than 30%. Use Portmaster to block internet access for any app Get granular control over how your apps are accessing the internet Windows' built-in settings can only take you so far. If you want a more comprehensive overview of what's happening on your network — and actual control over it — I'd strongly recommend installing a dedicated tool, specifically Portmaster. It’s a free and open-source application firewall. Once installed, it shows you every app and service on your computer that's connecting to the internet, along with exactly which servers each one is talking to. Also, apart from simply monitoring your network activity, you can use the app to block an app’s internet access entirely — or even prevent it from connecting to specific servers. This effectively lets you create an offline version of all the apps on your system. Other than that, you can also enable various filter lists that block known trackers and ad networks, which can reduce the overall load on your network and lead to faster load times. Portmaster is not a sponsored recommendation. I use it personally and find it genuinely useful.

item.title: Don't buy a used Raspberry Pi until you understand these 4 "gotchas"
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.32
Memory price hikes have pushed new Raspberry Pi prices up across the board and the secondhand market has started looking more appealing than it has in years. Unfortunately, while used Pis can be good deals, the market is also full of pitfalls that don't exist when you buy new. There are a handful of specific things you should double-check before you hand over your money, ranging from damage to conflated model information. None of them are always deal-breakers, but they're potential problems worth keeping an eye out for. Not all Pi generations are equal Double-check which board you're buying I often see Raspberry Pis listed on Facebook Marketplace just as a "Raspberry Pi," with no further information—I'm left zooming in on poorly lit photos to try and determine which model I'm looking at. They can look fairly similar, especially if you don't spend a lot of time with them. The model and RAM matter enormously. The Pi 1 and 2 are both 32-bit, single-core devices, and the Pi 3b barely keeps up against modern Pis. As a concrete example, the Pi Zero 2, which is the size of a stick of gum, can get very close to the computational performance of a Raspberry Pi 3B, though the Zero 2 has only 512MB of RAM while the Pi 3B has 1GB. The Pi 1 and 2 are notably slower and not worth buying, unless you're just collecting them for fun. Software and OS support for older devices is going by the wayside as they've become outdated. Even if you can find software that'll run on them, the hardware spaces are now "bad" enough that you can't do that much with them anyway. Make sure you get a good look at the board and verify the specific model, RAM amount, and revision number against your needs. Watch for weird pricing fluctuations Scam prices are a bigger problem now Besides increasing the prices of Raspberry Pis to unprecedented heights, the memory crisis has also opened up a new scam avenue: fake price hikes. It is an unfortunate reality today that the price of computers and computer components often jump by $50, $100, or even more literally overnight. Scammers have started taking advantage of that and deliberately hiking prices above even the inflated "true" retail price to make a buck, hoping that the unwary buyer pays without double-checking the pricing. Amazon third-party sellers and Facebook Marketplace resellers seem to have been the worst offenders, and I'd be careful buying any PC component or SBC from one. Raspberry Pi deliberately rolled out lower-memory options to help keep costs manageable. If you do need a Pi, I'd get it from one of the Raspberry Pi Foundation's approved vendors if possible. If you do buy a Pi used, double-check the current market price from one of those vendors, not Amazon. Run it before you buy it GPIO pins, ports, and power circuitry can be subtly damaged Raspberry Pis aren't like GPUs. They live fairly difficult lives as computers go—they get dropped, attached to drones and flown into trees, people carelessly attach power supplies to GPIO pins, or spend 18 months outside in an allegedly-waterproof box. That also means that used Pis often have pretty significant wear and tear. Before you buy a Pi, power it on and make sure it at least starts. Some damage (like a bent or broken GPIO pin) is readily repairable; a cooked memory module is a different class of problem entirely. If you see signs of burn marks or large amounts of flux residue (a sign someone has been soldering, which can damage components), I'd stay clear completely. Check for counterfeits, clones, or stripped boards I've seen too many fakes There aren't too many counterfeit Raspberry Pis out there on the used market, but it is very common to see other SBCs mislabeled as something like a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. It has also been fairly common historically for a seller to use a picture of a Raspberry Pi and then hand you a clone, like an Orange Pi. There is nothing inherently wrong with the clones. Some of them are great, but if you're paying for a Pi, you should get a Pi. Clones also often lack the same software support Pis have, which can be a huge headache. I've also noticed that an increasing number of SBCs are sold on Facebook Marketplace with their RAM removed, presumably so someone can either sell the RAM separately for a premium or use it in a project of some kind. Sometimes this is surreptitiously mentioned in the listing; other times you'll just notice that there is a weird empty spot on the board in a photo. Whatever the seller's motivation and honesty level is, a Pi without RAM is useless—don't buy one. Don't trust a deal that seems too good to be true To buy a Pi safely, always double-check the specific model, double-check the price, and make sure to look for signs that it is physically damaged. If you take those precautions, you can actually find some pretty good deals still. Many people that purchased Pi 5s at release are willing to let their old, used Pi 4 go at a very reasonable price. The Pi 4 is a bit older now, but fully capable of hosting a small media server, a Pi Hole, or running any number of other small homelab jobs. I would generally recommend against buying the Pi 5 1GB or 2GB variants used; they still sell for "reasonable" prices compared to their higher-memory variants, and the trouble that comes with used SBCs is not worth the small savings you might get on a current-gen device.

item.title: 4 more excellent local LLM projects you can run for free on a slow laptop
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.24
An old laptop isn't the kind of device you think of when someone says "local AI," but as long as you pick the right AI, they can be pretty useful. Whatever device you use, it needs 8GB of RAM at a minimum, though 16GB is better. Luckily, even laptops from five years ago frequently had that much memory available. Cherry Studio is a local-first AI studio Don't upload sensitive documents to the cloud If you've ever wanted to use an AI to analyze a bank statement, medical records, or a tax document, but you don't want to upload it to the internet, you should try Cherry Studio instead. Cherry Studio is a free, open-source desktop app that acts as a front end for local AI models running with Ollama. It supports built-in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), so you can provide it with information to work with. You can load in PDFs, documents, spreadsheets, and then talk to an AI running on your local PC about the data. Some small AI models (4–12 billion parameters) will run reasonably well on a CPU, and if you have a GPU, you can run even faster models. It also includes a whole range of built-in tools and MCP, which allows you to connect it to most anything you want. Remember that RAG is only fully private if you use a local model. If you use a cloud embedding service, your documents still leave your PC. Jan is a polished chatbot It is similar to ChatGPT in many ways If you're not a fan of the command line, Jan is a pretty good option. It is a fully open-source desktop app that combines a model downloader, an inference engine, and a chat interface into one package. That means you don't need to work with the terminal to pull models with Ollama or anything like that. It is designed for convenience, and you don't get the granular customization with Jan that you do using llama.cpp directly, but that is a small price to pay for the simplicity. You also need to try and keep your model sizes and expectations in check. 8GB of RAM (or even 16GB) can't match the reasoning capabilities of a frontier, cloud-based model. Still, it can be useful for extracting data or discussing the contents of a folder. Transcribe audio for free with whisper.cpp Fast speech-to-text on a CPU If you ever need to transcribe audio to text, Whisper.cpp is a great option. It is a CPU-optimized variant of OpenAI's whisper models. On even a moderately capable CPU, you can get real-time or close to real-time audio transcription. That makes it suitable for simple voice recognition tasks for a voice assistant. If you have a low-power CPU, Whisper is still great for batch processing audio transcripts that you don't need done in real time. Your only costs are the laptop itself (which is often something you already own) and the electricity, The small or base models are accurate enough for most applications and will happily run in 8GB of RAM. Depending on your workflow, you may also need FFmpeg to handle file conversion first. However, with a little bit of setup, you get automated AI transcription that is completely private. Add a coding autocomplete to VS Code with Continue A small local coder model can do small, simple tasks well If you're a programmer working with an NDA, or just someone that values their privacy, you could try out Continue. Continue is an extension for VS Code that allows you to connect your IDE to a local AI server to provide inline autocomplete. You can also chat with the model about your code in a menu on the side. Typically, when you think of vibe coding you think of large, expensive frontier models, but they're not really necessary for simple things like generating regex and simple lines of code. You can find models in the 1.5B to 4B parameter range that are actually fairly capable. The only significant trade-off is latency. Completion on an older laptop CPU is not instantaneous like it is with a cloud service, and the larger your model, the worse that gets. I'd recommend using the smallest possible model for tab-autocomplete and only using a larger model for the chat panel to get the best performance-to-utility ratio. Sometimes a bit slow is completely fine Local AI on an old laptop when you can keep your projects focused, or you don't need it to run in real time. So long as you're careful about your application, it is an easy win for privacy and cost. If you aren't sure where to start, try Jan. It is very easy to get running and is useful "out of the box." Whisper.cpp is another favorite. It runs on almost anything, including a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5. That makes it suitable for a DIY home voice assistant that is completely private.

item.title: 5 hidden tricks hiding in your PC's headphone jack that beat Bluetooth every time
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.16
For many people, Bluetooth headphones are not and never have been a straight-up replacement for wired—they're just convenient to use on the go. But manufacturers have been trying to kill the 3.5mm jack for years now, stripping it from flagship phone models and even laptops. When this happens, however, you're losing more than just a headphone slot. Because this flexible little port is no one-trick pony. It can actually do quite a lot. And with its mere 5-10ms of latency, it can do those things very fast. Send lossless digital audio out through an optical cable Some 3.5mm jacks are secretly optical ports in disguise On some PCs—more often laptops and certain motherboards—the 3.5mm jack does double duty as a mini-TOSLINK optical output. A quick way to find out if this applies to yours is to darken the room and see if you can spot some red light emitting from around the jack. This is an emitter LED sending audio as pulses of light, sitting right alongside the copper contacts that handle your analog plugs. With this, you can run a clean digital signal straight to a soundbar, AV receiver, or external DAC using a cheap 3.5mm-to-TOSLINK adapter. However, there's no electrical power involved here, so the device you're feeding needs its own power and its own optical input. And, over optical S/PDIF, a PC will usually downmix to 2-channel PCM unless the sound hardware supports Dolby Digital Live or DTS Connect, which encode 5.1 on the fly for the cable. Turn it into an audio input to record from other gear Your output jack can be re-tasked as a line-in A 3.5mm jack is physically the same hardware whether it's pushing sound out or pulling it in, and on a lot of Realtek-based PCs, you can flip its role in software. Open the Realtek Audio Console, find Connector Retasking, and you can tell the driver what you actually plugged in. In plain terms, connector retasking lets the audio driver treat one physical jack as a different kind of connection—so a port that ships as an output can be reassigned as a mic or line-level input, if your codec and board support it. Suddenly you can record a synth, a mixer, or a cassette deck straight into your machine. As with most of the items on this list, however, whether you can do it or not depends on your hardware. Specifically, your codec, board, and driver version. And for laptop owners, it's even more complicated. A single 3.5mm combo jack on a laptop is usually TRRS, which only provides a mono microphone input, not a proper stereo line-in, so it's not suited to recording a stereo source like a synth or turntable at line level. Feed a bigger sound system Like an amp, powered speakers, or a soundbar Here's a good one—you can connect a 3.5mm-to-RCA or 3.5mm-to-3.5mm cable to the aux input on a stereo amp, a set of powered bookshelf speakers, or a soundbar. If you've been suffering through the tinny speakers built into your monitor, I bet you can hack together a better setup this way. There's a right way to do it, though. A PC headphone jack is an amplified output tuned to drive headphones, not a true fixed-level line-out. So when you feed powered speakers or an amp, start with the PC volume low and raise it gradually to avoid a hot, distorted signal. And if your gear offers a choice, remember how the two paths differ: the optical route sends digital audio for the receiver to convert, while the 3.5mm route sends already-converted analog—if your gear has both inputs, optical keeps the conversion (and any PC electrical noise) out of the signal path. Record real instruments by turning your PC into an interface Guitar, bass, or keyboard, straight into the jack Building on that input trick, the jack can become the front door to a home recording setup. With a small iRig-style adapter (or a retasked line-in), you can capture a guitar, bass, or keyboard into a DAW, and some of those adapters even let your PC stand in for a pedalboard as a multi-effects processor. Don't expect too much from this little hack, however. A guitar or bass is a high-impedance instrument signal, so it usually needs an interface or a Hi-Z input to be captured cleanly. Plugging straight into a mic jack often gives a weak, noisy result. Think of this as the cheap way to start rather than a studio replacement; a dedicated USB interface will always be quieter and lower-latency, and you'll still want a decent pair of headphones to monitor what you're capturing. But for laying down an idea at midnight, the jack you already have is more than enough. Split it so two people can listen at once One jack, two (or more) sets of headphones This is one of the most useful but also one of the best-known tricks for headphone jacks. We've had Bluetooth headphones for so long, and yet support for connecting multiple sets to one device has been so, so slow and patchy. With wired headphones, all you need is a three-dollar Y-splitter. It turns a single jack into two, so two people can share a movie on a laptop without huddling over one earbud each—and some splitters fan out to as many as six sockets. However, splitting literally divides the signal, so each pair can end up a little quieter, especially with harder-to-drive headphones. But for casual listening on a plane or a couch, though, you'll probably never notice. Not bad for a port everyone keeps trying to kill Some people will have a PC that can do just about everything on this list, while others will only be able to do one or two, but the point is—the 3.5mm jack can do lots of cool stuff, and manufacturers are wrong to try and sideline it. If you want to try any of these out, just remember to check if your hardware is compatible before buying any adapters.

item.title: I finally found an easy way to make Windows remember exactly where every app window belongs
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.86
Every morning, I open the same apps and then spend the next few minutes dragging, resizing, and rearranging them across my two monitors. By the afternoon, everything has shifted again. I was getting tired of rebuilding the same desktop layouts, so I went looking for a better way. Then I found an easy-to-use PowerToys tool: Workspaces. Getting started with PowerToys Workspaces It's not as complicated as it sounds If you've never used PowerToys before, don't worry. Getting Workspaces up and running takes less than a minute. First, install PowerToys from the Microsoft Store, then: - In your system tray, right-click the PowerToys icon. - Click Settings. - Scroll to Workspaces. - Make sure the toggle is on. The PowerToys interface can vary slightly between versions, so you may see Workspaces in a different location. Now that Workspaces is enabled, you're ready to find the Editor. In my setup, Workspaces appears in the Quick access area. When I click it, I'm taken straight there. If you don't see it there, click Windowing & Layouts > Workspaces, then select Open editor. This is where you'll create and manage your saved app layouts. From here, you can arrange your apps and save the setup for later. PowerToys Workspaces remembers where my apps belong I created separate setups for weekdays and weekends Workspaces lets me save a collection of apps along with the positions of their windows. When I launch that workspace later, PowerToys opens those apps and restores their saved positions. I use my PC differently depending on what I'm doing, so I've created separate Workspaces for my weekday and weekend routines. My Weekday workspace is built around the apps I use for work. I have Word, Excel, and Notepad on my left monitor, with Slack, Asana, and Edge on my right monitor. That's the arrangement I want to see when I sit down to work, so I've saved it as a workspace rather than rebuilding it every morning. My Weekend setup is completely different. I can have Edge open to my golf tracking website on one screen, with Xbox and a weather app on the other. When I want to switch from work mode to my weekend setup, I can launch the corresponding workspace instead of opening each app and arranging everything manually. Yes, there are other ways to achieve something similar. I could use AutoHotkey to create a script that opens certain apps, or build my own Windows shortcuts and scripts to automate parts of the process. The difference is that those methods make me tell Windows what to do. With Workspaces, I can simply arrange my desktop the way I want it and tell PowerToys to remember it. No scripts needed. Don't confuse Workspaces with FancyZones. FancyZones gives you reusable zones for positioning windows, while Workspaces remembers which apps belong in those positions. You don't need FancyZones to use Workspaces, either. Creating a workspace takes only a minute Arrange everything once and save it Creating a workspace is straightforward. Once you've opened the Workspaces Editor, click Create Workspace, open the apps you want, and arrange their windows as you like. You don't need two or more monitors to make the most of this feature; it works just as well with a single screen. Once everything looks right, close anything you don't want included, click Capture, then give the workspace a name. Before you save the workspace, there are two more options worth considering: - Create desktop shortcut: Adds a shortcut to your desktop that you can double-click whenever you want to launch that workspace. This is the quickest way to get back to a saved setup without opening PowerToys. - Move existing windows: Moves apps that are already open into their saved positions when you launch the workspace. This is useful if you already have some of the apps running and don't want Workspaces to open another set of windows. Don't worry if you make a mistake when capturing your workspace. After clicking Capture, you can click Remove next to any app you don't want to include. You can also open an app's drop-down menu to change its saved window position to Maximized, Minimized, or Custom. Custom lets you adjust the left, top, width, and height while the preview updates to show the result. The same menu also includes a Launch as Admin option, which can help if an app needs administrator privileges to launch or be repositioned correctly. Workspaces can launch apps with specific content, too. You can add an app's CLI arguments from its drop-down menu in the Workspace Editor—for example, you could have Excel open a particular workbook or your browser open a specific website. The available arguments vary by app. Some apps may still behave differently from others, so you might need to experiment with their available options to get the behavior you want. I can mess up my layout and restore it My saved workspace becomes a reset button This is probably my favorite part of Workspaces. Once I've launched a workspace, I'm free to mess with it. I can move Excel somewhere else, resize Word, minimize Edge, or close an app altogether, and those changes don't alter the saved workspace. Because I have Move existing windows enabled, I can launch the workspace again, and PowerToys restores my open windows to the positions I originally captured. That effectively gives me a reset button for my desktop. I can change my layout during the day without worrying that I've lost the arrangement I actually want. If I later decide to keep a new arrangement, I can edit the workspace, make my changes, capture the new layout, and save it again. There are just two things to bear in mind once you get going. Workspaces adds a new arrangement to what's already open rather than replacing it. It also remembers the screens connected to your PC, so your layout may change if you regularly connect or disconnect a monitor. I no longer have to rebuild the same desktop For me, the appeal of PowerToys Workspaces is simple: I decide where each app belongs, save the arrangement, and come back to it whenever I need it. And that's part of what I like about PowerToys in general: Workspaces is just one of the many useful additions tucked inside the suite. For example, it lets you extract text from images, pick colors from anywhere on your screen, and batch-rename files. So if you haven't explored the suite before, now's as good a time as ever to get started.

item.title: Excel dashboards kept sending me down a rabbit hole. Gemini got me out
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.75
I'm forever creating dashboards in Excel, and while I get a lot of satisfaction from it, that's part of the problem. I end up going down a rabbit hole, adding more charts, and then wondering whether I left anything out. There's no handbook for creating a dashboard in Excel, as every dataset is different. So I decided to let Gemini do the decision-making for me. I gave Gemini my spreadsheet data and a single instruction I wanted it to decide what mattered I started with two CSV files containing a small library dataset: 40 authors and 180 books. I used CSV files rather than XLSX files because, in my experience, AI chatbots tend to handle datasets better when I strip out all the Excel-specific baggage. The files were linked by the AuthorID column, but I deliberately didn't explain this to Gemini—I wanted it to discover the relationship between them on its own. I kept my actual instruction surprisingly short. Instead of specifying a layout or telling it which charts to use, I simply gave it the data and asked it to analyze what it had been given before deciding what would make the standalone offline app useful. I did make sure it included the ability to add and manage authors and books, export the data, reset it, and keep my changes between sessions. Those were important because I wanted to test whether the finished app could actually replace the sort of ongoing spreadsheet workflow I had in mind, rather than simply produce a nice-looking demo. But that was essentially it. I was interested in seeing whether it could make sensible design decisions from the data itself, rather than simply following a detailed specification I'd written. Why Gemini? I've tested AI for various different projects in the past, and Gemini has often come out on top. For example, I found that Gemini was better than ChatGPT at turning my data into a dashboard in Excel. I've also compared how Gemini and Claude coped with turning a spreadsheet into an offline app, and Gemini's output felt more practical and usable. So I wanted to see whether Gemini could go one step further: take two separate CSVs, understand the relationships between them, and generate a standalone interactive app. Gemini built a dashboard I actually wanted to look at It didn't try to visualize everything The result was much more restrained than some of the dashboards I've built myself—but that's a good thing. Gemini built a clean overview with four summary cards that show key information from the library, including the number of authors and books, the number of pages read, and the average rating. Underneath, it used four straightforward bar charts showing books by genre, reading status, top authors by average rating, and authors by country. What impressed me most was what Gemini didn't do. It could have filled the screen with pie charts, percentages, and other visualizations simply because the data was available. Instead, it made a judgment about how much information belonged on the main screen and left the rest alone. It also gave the app a proper navigation structure. I could move between the overview, Book Explorer, and Author Directory, then drill into individual authors or books when I wanted more detail. Author information, for example, wasn't dumped onto the main dashboard. I had to click through to see an author's details and bibliography. In Excel, I'd have to make those decisions myself, then build the worksheets, navigation, links, filters, and supporting elements to make everything work together. Gemini simply made the choices for me. A good-looking app is useless if the data doesn't work I put Gemini's creation through its paces Once I liked the look of it, I wanted to see whether the app was actually usable. I opened the Book Explorer first, where I could search by title or author, filter by genre and reading status, and sort the results by title, rating, publication year, or page count. These controls worked together, too, so I could, for example, filter the library by a particular genre and reading status and then search within those results. Next, I made some changes to the data in the app to see how it reacted. First, I added an unread book to an existing author. The book count updated to 181 instantly, the new title appeared in the catalog, the author relationship was correct, and the author's bibliography reflected this change. I then added a read book for the same author and gave it a rating of 5. Gemini handled the rating logic correctly: the rating field only became active when I selected Read, while books marked Reading or Want to read could be added with the rating left blank. Next, I added a completely new author and then created a book for that author. The counts in the top-right corner updated, the new book was correctly associated with the new author, and the author's book count and other derived information updated accordingly. When I refreshed the page, my changes remained, and the same was true when I closed and reopened the HTML file. The whole thing also worked offline, which was one of my original requirements. And when I exported both the Books and Authors datasets as CSV files, the new records and their relationships were included. Finally, I reset the app, and everything returned to the original 40 authors and 180 books. Gemini made some surprisingly good decisions But there's one thing to be aware of I've run lots of experiments on making AI tools produce working code, so I wasn't surprised that Gemini could generate a working app from spreadsheet data. But what did surprise me was the quality of the decisions behind the app. The overview wasn't overloaded, the four charts were easy to understand, the summary cards gave me the headline figures, and deeper information was available when I needed it rather than being pushed onto the main screen. That restraint is probably the part I'd find hardest to reproduce if I started building the interface myself. Gemini effectively acted as the person saying, "That's enough." One thing I'd keep in mind, though, is the size of the dataset. In an earlier experiment with a much larger dataset of around 5,000 records, Gemini struggled to embed something of that size into a single standalone HTML app. That wasn't an issue with this 180-book library, but if I were working with a much larger dataset, I'd consider manipulating or reducing the data first rather than expecting Gemini to package everything into one file. Gemini gave me something that felt like a real app I set out to escape my usual Excel dashboard rabbit hole, where I would normally keep adding charts and tweaking the layout until I convinced myself everything was covered. This time, I handed those decisions to Gemini, and the result was an app that felt like it had been designed around my data rather than around Excel.

item.title: 6 ways you can turn an old speaker into a private Amazon Echo replacement
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.67
Most of us have an old bookshelf speaker, soundbar, or Bluetooth speaker lying around somewhere. They still sound good, the problem is that they're not very "smart." If you want to get away from always-on microphones, sending data to Amazon, and a trend towards ever-increasing subscriptions, you can turn an old speaker into an Echo replacement. The open-source world has an entire stack of software that allows you turn almost any speaker into a smart speaker with a bit of work. Some are complex, involved projects; others are practically plug and play. Plug your speaker into a Home Assistant Voice Preview An off-the-shelf box that turns any speaker into a local smart speaker If you want a private, local system without spending hours setting something up and troubleshooting, Nabu Casa's Voice Preview Edition is a reasonable choice if you don't need lightning-fast responses. It is a purpose-built device with a wake-word, two microphones, and an aux port that allows you to plug into a speaker. It is as close to an all-in-one local solution as you're going to find at the moment. You also need a Home Assistant server running on your network to handle the actual conversation. Nabu Casa's Voice Preview Edition costs about $70. Build a "satellite" with a Raspberry Pi A DIYer's wheelhouse: A Pi, microphone, and a speaker If you have a Raspberry Pi sitting around in need of a project, you can build something called a Wyoming satellite. It basically functions as a network-attached microphone and speaker. You say something, then the Wyoming Satellite transfers your command back to a Home Assistant instance for processing. You'll need a Pi, a microphone or microphone HAT, and your old speaker. A Wyoming Satellite doesn't do any on-device processing besides wake-word detection, so even a Pi Zero 2 W will work for this. Make sure you use the Wyoming satellite guides rather than old Rhasspy tutorials. Rhasspy was technically deprecated in 2025 and is slowly becoming outdated. Create your own ESP32 satellite A cheap microcontroller that gives your speaker the ability to hear If you want a project that is more hands-on and technically involved, you can build your own satellite using an ESP32 board. The ESP32-S3 is specifically popular for this use, but there are plenty of others you could make work too. There are specific kits available, like the ESP32-S3-BOX-3, or you can piece the entire thing together. The entire setup is tiny, consumes next to no electricity, and if you're crafty, you can often conceal it inside your speaker.
