Just be sure not to damage any ports or vents you find if you have to modify the body of the speaker itself. The tradeoff is complexity. All the speech processing runs on a Home Assistant server (or something equivalent), which involves some setup. Make sure to use ESPHome during your build, it'll save you time. Repurpose an old Android phone as the brain No Pi needed You can create a local assistant without buying new hardware using a spare Android Phone. Home Assistant has a companion app that allows it to function like a small satellite; you can then pair it with your speaker via Bluetooth or the headphone jack, if your phone has one. Keep in mind that phone batteries don't do well if they're left plugged in 24/7, and that third-party wake word support can be a little touchy. You may have to go with something that responds to a physical tap instead. Run the full local AI setup on a home server You can self-host the entire brain on a local PC The most complete—and capable—replacement for an Echo involves running an entire AI stack on your local hardware. This is the approach that I use. My home server actually runs several AIs together to create a fairly seamless experience. Qwen 3:14b provides the "brain," llama 3.2 turns things I say like "turn down the music" or "That music is too loud" into specific commands," Kokoro synthesizes speech to give my setup a voice, and Parakeet gives the whole setup ears. That allows it to act, in many ways, like a full replacement for Alexa. I can talk to it normally, and it understands my commands; given a question, it can reason about the input I provide and synthesize an answer. It even has a small personality file that biases how it answers, so it isn't generic sounding. The test satellite is built using a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. Eventually, I'll 3D print a few cases and position them in a few different rooms. The only drawback to this approach is that it requires at least one dedicated GPU to work well, which adds to the cost. There are many ways to start Once you have a speaker, there are a million ways to approach turning it into an Amazon Echo replacement. The simplest option is the plug-in option from Nabu Casa—there is very little manual configuration required there. I'd recommend a Raspberry Pi as a satellite next, for a blend of capability and flexibility, and only add in the local AI stack running on a home server later if you have the hardware for it.

item.title: 3 Home Assistant projects to repurpose old hardware this weekend (Sep 4-6)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.38
Tech prices are going through the roof, with the high cost of RAM affecting everything from Raspberry Pis to high-end gaming PCs. The good news is that with Home Assistant, it’s often possible to repurpose old tech so that you don’t need to buy anything new. Turn an old Echo Dot into a local smart speaker Escape the Alexa ecosystem When Alexa first appeared on the scene, it seemed like this might be the way that we would control all of our smart home devices. Shows such as Star Trek: The Next Generation made the idea of talking to our computers feel like the most efficient way to use them. The reality turned out to be disappointing. While Alexa is useful for basic things such as turning on lights or asking simple questions, Amazon’s locked-down ecosystem means that an Echo smart speaker today isn’t much more useful than it was when the first models launched. It’s a shame, because the hardware even in older Echo smart speakers is actually pretty solid, with microphone arrays and beamforming that can pick up voice commands even in noisy environments. Thankfully, if you have an old second-generation Echo Dot, you can break free of the shackles of Alexa and turn it into your own local smart speaker. There are several projects that let you use your Echo Dot as a local voice satellite for Home Assistant so that you can speak to Assist using your Echo without having your commands end up on Amazon’s servers. One project even allows you to run speech recognition and a small LLM directly on the device, so that much of the processing happens on the Echo rather than on your Home Assistant server. Whichever option you choose, you can do a lot more by using an Echo Dot with Home Assistant than you ever could with Alexa. Build a smart home hub from a laptop motherboard The scale model of your home is optional There are plenty of options for running Home Assistant. I ran it for a couple of years on a Raspberry Pi 3B+ without any major issues, and I now run it in Proxmox on a mini PC. There are plenty of other suggestions that are often given, including running Home Assistant on an old laptop. The problem with using an old laptop is that you have to deal with issues such as maintaining battery health, high-power consumption, a mostly redundant screen, and the fact that it looks like an old laptop. One clever Home Assistant user solved this problem by ripping the motherboard out of an old laptop and running Home Assistant on it, using the laptop’s original cooling hardware along with the RAM and storage. A bare motherboard still isn't the most beautiful-looking Home Assistant server, so the user built an entire scale model of their home to house the motherboard and components. The model isn’t just for looks; it includes LEDs in the rooms to mimic the real lighting states, and an ESP32-S3 running ESPHome allows the user to talk to the house and get voice assistant responses. You don’t have to go to the same extreme of building a tiny version of your own home. However, the idea of using the components from the laptop rather than the entire laptop itself is an interesting one and might be something worth considering if you have an old computer lying around. Give a Meta Portal a second life with Home Assistant Put abandoned hardware to good use There are plenty of tech devices that have come and gone without making much of an impact, and the Meta Portal (originally the Facebook Portal) is definitely one of them. Launched in 2018, the Portal was a line of smart displays primarily intended for video calling via Messenger or WhatsApp. By 2022, Meta ended development and sold off the remaining inventory of Portal products. For a long time, these devices were basically e-waste, but in June 2026, Meta added official Android Debug Bridge (ADB) support to the devices, allowing people to bypass many of the limitations of the locked-down Meta software and sideload their own Android apps. The upshot is that it’s now possible to do a lot with a Meta Portal. One community project uses Ava Pro, an Android platform built for Home Assistant, to turn the Meta Portal into a voice-controlled speaker for Music Assistant. Another option is Portal HA Bridge, which turns a Meta Portal into a Home Assistant device exposing screen controls, motion detection, camera streaming and more. As a result, some Home Assistant users are picking up old Portals from secondhand marketplaces. You can still find them for reasonable prices, but you might want to grab one before they become too scarce. Repurposing is one of the best things about Home Assistant I love Home Assistant for so many reasons, but the fact that you can often use it to repurpose old hardware is definitely up there. I’ve given new life to broken iPads, Echo Show devices, and old phones, saving me from having to buy new hardware.

item.title: 3 open-source virtual desktop tools that make Windows’s built-in feature look outdated
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.20
Windows 11 has a robust virtual desktop feature, but it is rather basic. It probably doesn't help that Microsoft only built its own virtual desktop solution long after Linux and macOS had shown us what they could do. The result is that there have been third-party virtual desktop apps for a long time now, across several versions of Windows. With so much time, user feedback, and competition, some of these third-party options are still going to be a better fit than the basic solution that comes with Windows today. There are quite a few options, but this is a good cross-section of what's out there. Desk Switcheroo puts a desktop manager on your taskbar And it has a portable version too! Desk Switcheroo is probably the most comprehensive replacement for the Windows Task View tool on this list. You get a compact widget that can be anchored close to your taskbar, from where you can make the magic happen. The widget shows the current desktop number, a custom label, and you can even set it to show you the current desktop's position within the total desktop count. You can use the arrow buttons or mouse wheel to shift between desktops without opening Task View. If you click the widget, you get a full desktop list, letting you jump to a specific labeled desktop instantly, again without opening Task View. You can also quickly create, delete, rename, and reorder your desktops. You can also assign each desktop a color and wallpaper, temporarily preview another desktop, or display thumbnail previews when hovering over entries. Desktop Switcheroo also adds some useful new tricks to window management. For example, you can pin a window across all your desktops, which is useful if you have to use your calculator app on different desktops without opening multiple iterations of it. A rules engine can automatically send matching windows to specific desktops, while event hooks can run commands when desktop-related events occur. SylphyHornPlus adds the controls Microsoft forgot It hides itself well Downloading or installing SylphyHornPlus can trigger your antivirus. As far as I can tell, this is a false positive and is related to how the app listens for global hotkeys. However, ensure you download the app from its real page, or use the Winget command to install it. SylphyHornPlus is a great choice if you already like the vanilla Windows virtual desktop interface, but want to expand what it can do. Instead of replacing Task View, it adds shortcuts, notifications, gestures, and management tools around the native feature without altering them. With global hotkeys, you can just switch directly to a specific desktop instead of scrolling through them, or using Task View. You can also use the hot keys to move windows to other desktops, create or remove them, and change their order. You can set up a notification that reminds you of which desktop you're on, and can have its position and appearance customized. It's not just the keyboard controls that are better. The app supports mouse wheel and rocker gestures. So you can do a lot of the stuff you want using just the mouse, but without clicking through a bunch of menus. While SylphyHornPlus doesn't have any window setup saving powers that I could see, you can export and save your app settings. So if you reinstall Windows or use more than one machine, you can have your tweaked settings on hand all the time. FancyWM gives every desktop a self-organizing layout What's old is new again FancyWM is only partly open-source. The author has open-sourced core parts of the backend, but the application itself is not open-source as a whole. You can download and use it for free, and make an optional payment to support them. The only difference is that you'll get an occasional pop-up asking you to support the project. FancyWM (Fancy Window Manager) is more than just a virtual desktop tool for Windows. It's a full-fledged window manager that could make your life so much easier. It uses dynamic tiling to make the most of your screen real estate, which automatically makes it great if you have an ultra-wide monitor or if you're using a large 4K display. When you open your apps, FancyWM automatically tiles them in panels, instead of letting them overlap. This is actually something that old versions of Windows did, using window tiling as the default. So it's interesting to see it come back as a productivity hack. It supports horizontal, vertical, and stacked panels, and these can be nested to build more complicated layouts. Windows automatically resize as applications are opened, closed, or moved. One thing that makes FancyWM stand out from other tiling window managers is that there's no trick here with a proprietary hidden workspace. Instead, the app integrated with Windows' native virtual desktop technology. This app is highly keyboard-driven if you want it to be. Using only the keyboard, you can instantly jump to any desktop or send the currently active window to another desktop. Panel arrangements can also be maintained globally or separately for each monitor. This all adds up to a much more powerful and cohesive system than combining Windows Snap Layouts with Task View virtual desktops. While Snap can quickly arrange your open windows into a layout, it doesn't keep managing them. FancyWM adapts your window tiles in real time as you open and close them. So each desktop ends up staying organized no matter what you're doing. There's nothing actually wrong with Windows virtual desktops out of the box, but if you start relying on this feature as part of your workflow, you'll quickly run into limitations that these apps can help solve.

item.title: Samsung turned its old smartwatches into e-waste, and the FOSS community is struggling to keep them alive
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.12
Samsung spent over a decade building a smartwatch platform on Tizen, then walked away from it in under two years. Now open-source developers are racing to keep thousands of orphaned watches functional before batteries outlast the software. Why Tizen smartwatches are becoming e-waste Samsung's shutdown timeline leaves working hardware stranded Samsung previously confirmed that support for its Tizen-powered smartwatches would officially end in September 2025, just a year ago, closing out an era that began with the original Galaxy Watch. The wind-down actually started earlier, with Samsung notifying users it planned to sunset Tizen OS by the end of 2025 and immediately blocking new Tizen watch content from the Galaxy Store. The rollback traces back to September 30, 2024, when the Galaxy Store stopped offering paid content for Tizen devices, and purchases users had already made would stop being available for download, though existing downloads already on a device would remain there. This cutoff affects every Samsung Gear smartwatch and Galaxy-branded Tizen watch, including the Galaxy Watch, Galaxy Watch 3, Galaxy Watch Active, and Galaxy Watch Active 2. Devices released after the Galaxy Watch 3, starting with the Galaxy Watch 4 line, are unaffected because Samsung had already moved them onto Wear OS, the Google-backed platform it now builds its watches around. Not only is Wear OS the superior platform when it comes to ecosystem and adoption, but with Samsung's old watches being the only watches to use Tizen, users would run into trouble even if Samsung hadn't cut off downloads. For watch owners, then, the practical result is a watch that still boots and still tells time, but can no longer install new faces, apps, or updates. It isn't bricked, but it's frozen in place, and a frozen smartwatch with no upgrade path is, functionally, headed for a drawer or a landfill. The hurdles toward a second life Tizen's closed hardware layer resists the usual open-source playbook That doesn't mean that developers aren't trying to make something out of these watches, but it's hard. The most active volunteer effort here is AsteroidOS, an open-source, Linux-based smartwatch platform built on components like OpenEmbedded, opkg, Wayland, Qt5, systemd, BlueZ, and PulseAudio, originally developed by French programmer Florent Revest. The project has had real success reviving watches, but almost all of that success has come on Wear OS hardware, not Tizen hardware, and the reason comes down to plumbing. AsteroidOS typically relies on libhybris to port itself onto Android-based watches, a compatibility layer that lets Linux software talk to Android's proprietary hardware drivers. Samsung's Tizen watches were never built with that Android driver layer in the first place. That gap shows up clearly in AsteroidOS's own documentation. For the Samsung Gear S2 Classic, the project notes that the device's vendor kernel is a very old 3.4 build with no existing abstraction for the Tizen hardware layer, so developers are attempting a mainline Linux kernel port instead of the usual libhybris route. But even sourcing the code to work from is a hurdle: downstream kernel sources for that watch are hosted on a contributor's personal GitHub page because Samsung no longer hosts them itself. Flashing anything onto the hardware brings its own friction, since these watches take firmware either wirelessly through Samsung's NetOdin protocol or over USB through the standard Odin tool, sometimes requiring a cable soldered directly to internal pads. Yikes. The project's official porting tracker is candid about where things stand: the Samsung Gear S2, S2 Classic, and S3 might be supported by AsteroidOS eventually, but they will need more work than other watches on the list. This isn't unique to AsteroidOS or even to Samsung. Across the broader modding community, there's a long-running complaint that manufacturers satisfy the letter of the GPL by publishing kernel source that doesn't actually match what shipped on the device, which leaves developers reverse-engineering drivers instead of building from a clean baseline. Will it be done sometime? Progress is real, but it's measured in years, not months There's genuine momentum behind AsteroidOS, just not necessarily where Tizen owners need it most. The project released version 2.0 nearly eight years after its first stable release, and the new version expanded hardware support meaningfully. It now covers Fossil's Gen 4, Gen 5, and Gen 6 watches, the Huawei Watch and Watch 2, several Ticwatch E and Pro models, the Oppo Watch, and the 2015 Moto 360, alongside partial support for a handful of other models. Most of those, notably, are Wear OS devices where the libhybris approach already works. Still, there are signs the Tizen side is inching forward. The Samsung Gear 2 is now the project's first watch supported through a mainline Linux kernel, meaning it runs without needing libhybris at all, and the Asus ZenWatch 2 has picked up very basic support running on a mainline kernel too. That mainline-kernel approach is exactly the strategy being applied to the Gear S2 and S3, so every improvement made for one Samsung watch has a decent chance of transferring to the others. AsteroidOS remains, by most accounts, the only large-scale effort focused specifically on repurposing existing smartwatch hardware rather than building new devices around open software, which means its pace effectively sets the pace for the whole ecosystem. Keep in mind that none of this happens on a corporate roadmap. It's contributor time, old hardware datasheets, and a lot of trial and error on watches Samsung has already stopped thinking about. A working Tizen build on a Gear S3 is plausible within the next year or two based on current porting activity, but there's no firm date, and watches like the original Gear S2 may simply run out of willing contributors before they run out of battery cycles. An old platform's afterlife depends on volunteers, not Samsung Samsung's Tizen watches aren't dead, just abandoned by their maker. Whether they get a real second life now rests on a small, unpaid community reverse-engineering hardware Samsung never intended anyone outside the company to touch.

item.title: This decade-old laptop next to my router is the most useful device on my network
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.55
When someone new comes over, one of the first questions I get is why in the world I have a random laptop plugged into my router. Depending on how tech-savvy they are, my answer usually ranges from "Oh, it’s just for movies" to "This is my home server, and here's what it does." So, here’s why I actually keep a decade-old laptop running next to my router. My old laptop started life as a humble media server It began as a very modest project I'll admit, I've never been much of a Linux tinkerer kind of person. I always just had a Windows desktop PC and Android phone that I occasionally did cool stuff on, but that's about it. After months of talking to my colleagues at How-To Geek and some deliberation over whether to buy a NAS to start a home media server, I realized that I had everything I needed—I could just build one from an old laptop with a broken screen that I had tucked away years ago. The laptop is nothing special. It's an old Lenovo Miix 2-in-1 with an i5-7200U, 4GB of soldered RAM, and a 128GB NVMe. I knew that I would eventually find a way to repurpose it, and the day finally came when I decided to turn it into a small-scale project, just to see if I'd like it. It was much less intimidating than spending hundreds of dollars on a device that I might not use; I'll tell you that much. So, I bought a cheap USB-C hub with an HDMI output, a few extra USB ports, and a microSD card reader. After successfully installing Ubuntu Server on the laptop, I connected a few USB flash drives I had lying around to expand the measly 128GB internal storage so that I had space for at least a few larger backup files, movies, and shows. I then proceeded to install Jellyfin, spent some time figuring out how to set it up and how to optimize it for my use case, and then loaded up some old media I had lying around. It was a humble beginning, but I finally had a device that I could easily stream content from to all the other devices in my house. Then I fell into the self-hosting rabbit hole One service quickly led to another My homelabbing journey had humble beginnings, but it turned out that I liked my new little Jellyfin machine way more than I expected, so I soon fell into the self-hosting rabbit hole. I started looking for other self-hosted apps I could spin up on my home server. My colleague Patrick suggested I use Docker to manage the apps in their own individual environments, called containers, to keep my system clean and easier to troubleshoot, so that's what I did and rebuilt Jellyfin. I first optimized everything around Jellyfin, adding apps like Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, and Bazarr to manage my library. Then I discovered Immich, and after trying it out for a bit, I realized I could replace Google Photos if I invested in an external hard drive—and I did. I bought a 6TB hard drive to replace those tiny, overheating USB flash drives and loaded all of the personal images I'd accumulated over the years onto the server. Then I added Home Assistant and migrated my entire smart home to it, and the list just continued growing from there. I couldn't believe what this old laptop with a 2-core CPU and just 4GB of RAM could do. All these little services run constantly in the background, without fail. AdGuard Home gave my old laptop a reason to sit by the router My server became an active part of the network Perhaps one of the most important and interesting self-hosted apps I keep running on my laptop is AdGuard Home. It's a network-wide DNS server that filters out unwanted traffic, such as trackers and telemetry. I installed this just to see how it works, but soon discovered that moving DNS handling away from my underpowered router to my laptop was one of the best things I could do for my network. Normally, a router has to do a lot of work: it routes traffic between the internet and your local network, assigns IP addresses, handles DNS forwarding, manages Wi-Fi, switches traffic between devices, and so much more. Just one of these tasks can be a lot to ask from a budget router, and unfortunately, in my case, it seemed like DNS handling sometimes suffered as a result. But after I spun up AdGuard Home, set up a few custom filters, and assigned it as the primary DNS server on my router, the web experience got so much faster on every single device. Instead of waiting a few seconds for a webpage to load while my poor router struggled with the DNS request, everything loaded almost instantly. It makes sense—despite being old, the laptop is much more powerful and has less work to do in general than my router, which allows it to handle DNS requests more easily. It also has vastly more RAM, allowing it to keep DNS responses in its cache for quick access when a page has already been loaded. AdGuard Home gave me more control over my network I can finally see what was happening Performance was far from the only benefit with AdGuard Home. The app allows me to monitor DNS requests across my network, blacklist or whitelist certain domains, and even completely block some devices, like my smart home gadgets, from accessing the outside world. And just like that, the laptop I remember having in my drawer became a very active part of my network. Given how big a benefit moving my DNS off my router was, I'm thinking about adding a second, smaller device to act as a fail-safe in case AdGuard Home on my laptop ever goes down or takes too long to respond because of everything else it's running. It's worth pointing out that other DNS services exist aside from AdGuard Home, such as Pi-hole, which can easily run on a Raspberry Pi, Technitium DNS Server, and Unbound. Ultimately, these apps are awesome if you care about your network, as they give you greater control over how DNS is being handled on your network, while potentially providing some indirect performance benefits. That old laptop turned out to be far more useful than I expected It's hard to believe that my whole setup started with a laptop that most people would probably glance at at a garage sale or flea market, see the broken screen, and pass on even for just $20. After tinkering with it and loading up a collection of self-hosted apps, I transformed it into a Swiss Army knife of a home server that handles everything from my backups and media to my smart home and, most impressively, my DNS.

item.title: This $15 ESP32 board gave my Jellyfin library the marquee it deserves
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.42
I miss the good old days when you had to queue for a movie, lining up outside the theater and passing the Now Showing posters which would get you excited about what you were about to see. I wanted to build something similar for Jellyfin using a cheap ESP32 display. I built a Now Showing display for my TV A Raspberry Pi and the screen of an old iPad I've already built a Now Showing screen for my TV. It uses a Raspberry Pi as the brains, and the display ripped from an old iPad 2 to show the movie posters. The display is fixed inside a photo frame, which looks smarter than I expected. An automation in Home Assistant pulls the poster image from whatever is currently playing in Jellyfin on my TV and displays it in the frame. It means when I'm watching a show or movie, I have the artwork displayed next to the TV. I've added some additional features so that the display will show an image for whatever channel I'm watching on my set-top box. It even displays photos from a shared album when the TV isn't in use. It's become one of my favorite things in my home. I wanted to build something similar for my computer Watching movies on my laptop deserves the same marquee We watch movies from my Jellyfin library on the main TV when we're watching as a family or as a couple. I'll also watch on the TV on the rare occasions when I'm home alone, as watching with surround sound makes the experience more immersive. Sometimes, however, I'm forced to watch movies on my laptop while the kids selfishly hog the TV just because their program is live and isn't available to stream on demand at any time, like that's a valid excuse or something. When I'm watching on my laptop, I miss having the Now Showing poster that's by the TV. I decided to see if I could build something similar for my home office so that I could display movie posters when I watched movies alone in the dark like a sad old man. I didn't have a spare Raspberry Pi or an old iPad 2 that I could cannibalize, so I needed to think of another option. A Cheap Yellow Display was just enough to do the job The limited memory was a real issue The most obvious option I had to hand was a Cheap Yellow Display. This is a $15 ESP32 development board with a built-in color touchscreen. It has on-board Wi-Fi, so I knew I'd be able to get the current movie image onto the device. The biggest concern was that my Cheap Yellow Display has very little memory. Even with a small JPEG image, the ESP32 needs to decompress it to raw pixel data to display it on the screen. A full-screen RGB565 image needs 153,600 bytes of memory at the CYD's resolution, which is more than the free memory available on the CYD after things such as Wi-Fi and the display driver had taken their share. A smaller image would load, but it only took up a portion of the screen and just looked weird. The solution was to download the image at a smaller size and use custom code to scale it up as it was drawn on the screen. The result is a little blocky, but it's good enough for my purposes, and the images display without running out of memory. The final step was to create an automation in Home Assistant that monitors the Jellyfin player on my laptop and reads the ID of the movie that's playing. It uses the ID to generate a link to a small version of the movie poster on my Jellyfin server and then sends the URL to the ESP32 through ESPHome. When the movie changes, the ID changes, and so does the image on the CYD. When the Jellyfin player is stopped, the URL is cleared, and the CYD displays text reading "COMING SOON." My Now Showing display is good enough for now A larger screen would definitely be an improvement Although the screen of the CYD is tiny, and the image isn't displayed in the highest quality, the Now Showing poster actually looks better than I thought it might. It's a similar experience to the setup in the living room, but on a smaller scale. Ideally, I'd like to upgrade to a larger screen with a higher resolution, which would require more memory than my CYD has. Using the same Raspberry Pi and iPad display setup as the living room is probably overkill for my home office, as the display would sit on my desk and be too large in such close proximity. Something a little larger would be the sweet spot. A CYD can be incredibly useful Despite the limited memory, a Cheap Yellow Display can be put to good use in many ways. The touchscreen display means it can do more than just show images or information; it can be used to control your smart home, too.

item.title: I didn’t expect Dell’s entry-level XPS 13 to feel this premium
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.36
I’ll admit, I’m not sure what I was expecting when I first opened up the box for the latest Dell XPS 13 laptop. However, I know for sure I wasn’t expecting to love this tiny laptop as much as I do. At $699, this could be the mid-range Windows laptop to beat in 2026. Dell XPS 13 (2026) - Operating System - Windows 11 Home or Pro - CPU - Up to Intel Core Ultra 7 355, 8 cores, up to 4.7GHz - GPU - Integrated Intel Graphics - RAM - Up to 32GB LPDDR5x, up to 9600 MT/s Dell's latest XPS 13 is its smallest XPS yet. Packing the Core 5 or Core Ultra 7 processors and up to 16GB of LPDDR5x RAM, this ultra-compact laptop is perfect for your day-to-day tasks. - Ultra-compact, premium design - Strong everyday performance - Comfortable typing experience - Great screen - Limited speaker bass - Not designed for higher-performance tasks like gaming or photo/video editing Price and Availability The Dell XPS 13 is available to purchase directly from Dell and Best Buy, coming in three models with pricing starting at $699. There's the version reviewed here with a Core 5, 8GB RAM, 512GB storage, another model with the same Core 5 CPU, 16GB RAM, and 512GB of storage, and then the highest end model with a Core Ultra 7 CPU, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage. Specifications - Brand - Dell - Operating System - Windows 11 Home or Pro - CPU - Up to Intel Core Ultra 7 355, 8 cores, up to 4.7GHz - GPU - Integrated Intel Graphics - RAM - Up to 32GB LPDDR5x, up to 9600 MT/s - Storage - Up to 1TB PCIe NVMe SSD - Battery - 52Wh, 3-cell - Display (Size, Resolution) - 13.4 inches, 2560 × 1600, 30–120Hz - Camera - 1080p at 30fps with infrared Windows Hello camera - Speakers - Four speakers; 8W total peak output - Colors - Sky or Storm - Ports - 2× USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 on Core 5 models; 2× Thunderbolt 4 on Core Ultra models; both support DisplayPort and Power Delivery - Network - Intel Wi-Fi 7 BE213, 2×2 - Dimensions - 11.69 × 7.9 × 0.5 inches (W × D × H) - Weight - Starting at 2.2 pounds (1kg) - Model - XPS 13 DX13260 - Adaptor and Battery - 65W USB-C adapter; 52Wh battery - Card Reader - None - Keyboard - Backlit keyboard with dedicated Copilot key - Display type - Touchscreen LCD, 500 nits, InfinityEdge - Audio - Four speakers and dual-array microphones - Security - Windows Hello facial recognition The Dell XPS 13 is one of the smallest laptops I've ever used Though small in build, it's mighty in features I've used many laptops throughout the years, the Dell XPS line included. While it's been about a decade since I've used an XPS, the XPS 13 absolutely blew me away with its size. Given how many laptops I've used over the years, I've also used my fair share of small laptops. The smallest laptop I've ever used has to be the 11-inch MacBook Air, or the 12-inch MacBook — both of which it's been about a decade since I've used. Many manufacturers have aimed at packing bigger laptops into smaller form factors, but Dell went a different direction with the latest XPS 13. It still has a 13.4-inch screen, but the body is basically designed around the display's panel. There are hardly any bezels on this laptop, and there isn't a wasted inch anywhere that I can find. Dell did an absolutely fantastic job on the design here. While you might expect this small laptop to lack major features, that's actually quite the opposite. Dell managed to pack a 1080p30 webcam in the XPS 13, alongside an IR camera for Windows Hello. Dual microphones are also present for a decent audio setup, and that's just the beginning. On either side of the XPS 13, you'll find a USB-C port. On the entry-level model (which is what I'm reviewing here) both ports are USB 3.2 Gen 2 with DisplayPort support and Power Delivery. On the models with the Core Ultra processors, both ports are Thunderbolt 4 with DisplayPort 2.1 and Power Delivery. The speakers are decent, but the small body definitely doesn't leave a lot of room for big, boomy bass. I don't mind watching a YouTube video on it or playing some background music, but I definitely fire up my Bose QuietComfort headphones whenever I want to actually enjoy listening to something. I was also quite surprised by the keyboard. One of the most surprising things to me is the power button. While it looks like a normal key, it's much more difficult to press, which is actually really nice as it means I won't accidentally click it when reaching for the backspace or delete key. The overall layout of the keyboard is a bit cramped for my personal preference, but it's a small laptop, and Dell did a really good job with the keyboard layout overall. I recently took a trip to Boston for a press event and brought the XPS 13 along with me and it was a joy to write on during the trip. Dell also got the trackpad almost perfect. It's a fairly great trackpad, all things considered, but I really wish it would have been a force touch trackpad. As it is, there's no middle pivot like we used to see in trackpads years ago (and some mid-range laptops still have), which is very nice to see. I had no issues using the trackpad, and I think it's a solid part of this laptop overall. I was surprised to find Wi-Fi 7 in tow here, which actually makes a marked difference in wireless performance if you have a compatible router. My UniFi Dream Router 7 was sitting about 10 feet away from the XPS 13 while I was downloading some games on Steam and Xbox, and the XPS 13 was seeing download speeds of 750 to 800Mb/s, which is nearly maxing out my network’s Gigabit WAN connection. Mid-range specs don't mean mid-range performance I'm amazed at how far mobile processors have come My review unit from Dell for the XPS 13 is the base model, which is actually somewhat surprising. Often, a brand will send out at least the mid-range, or even the top-tier model to give a reviewer the best experience possible. But, Dell made the right choice here, I think, when sending out the entry-level model. I was absolutely surprised by the performance of this laptop. And, since it's the base model, whether you buy the very model I'm using or a better one, you'll see the same or better results as what I got. The Core 5 320 CPU is part of Intel's Series 3 Core processors. It's got six cores, and the laptop has 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM installed. While that might not seem like a lot, it actually is more than enough for most workflows. As seen in the benchmarks, this laptop isn't breaking any records for its performance. However, where I'm surprised is just how usable it is being an entry-level laptop. I still remember years ago, I avoided anything that didn't have at least an i7 in it. Laptop or desktop, an i7 was a must. These days, a Core 3 or Core 5 is actually more than usable. Dell proves that here. While I wouldn't buy the XPS 13 for gaming, it actually handled Forza Horizon 5 better than I expected. Other games, like No Man's Sky and Minecraft, also run halfway decent here — though Minecraft with no mods definitely runs the best out of the three. Overall, the performance didn’t leave me hanging anywhere. I wouldn’t necessarily buy the base model to do heavy photo or video editing, but it definitely has enough juice to handle normal computer tasks, like writing documents, working with spreadsheets, browsing the web, and other normal things. Dell gets the everyday experience right with the XPS 13 Out of all the laptops I've tested, this is the one I consistently reach for The thing that surprised me the most about the XPS 13 is simply how much I enjoyed using the laptop. Often, I’ll use a laptop for a review and then move onto the next system (or back to my primary computer). With the XPS 13, that’s not exactly the case. Of course, I’m still using my more powerful MacBook Pro for my video and photo editing, but the XPS 13 has simply been a joy to use, and I keep reaching for it for simple tasks like browsing the web or writing articles. The overall experience is just superb on the XPS 13, and I don’t say that lightly. If someone asked me to recommend a mid-range, compact Windows laptop for everyday use, the XPS 13 is the first laptop that would come to my mind. Should you buy the Dell XPS 13? I’ve kind of already given away the answer, but yes, I think you should buy the Dell XPS 13, so long as you make sure to temper your expectations some. The higher end models will most surely handle more demanding tasks like video or photo editing better than my entry-level model. However, if you just need a solid laptop to browse Facebook Marketplace, watch YouTube or Netflix, and read How-To Geek, then the XPS 13 is a fantastic choice. At its $699 starting price, I really don’t think there’s another laptop in this price range that offers as premium of an experience as this one does. Dell XPS 13 (2026) - Operating System - Windows 11 Home or Pro - CPU - Up to Intel Core Ultra 7 355, 8 cores, up to 4.7GHz - GPU - Integrated Intel Graphics - RAM - Up to 32GB LPDDR5x, up to 9600 MT/s Dell's latest XPS 13 is its smallest XPS yet. Packing the Core 5 or Core Ultra 7 processors and up to 16GB of LPDDR5x RAM, this ultra-compact laptop is perfect for your day-to-day tasks.

item.title: No tracker tag? Gemini can now store item locations right in Find Hub
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.82
What you need to know - Gemini can now remember where you left important items, even without a tracker. - You can tell Gemini where you stashed an item or snap a quick photo, and it logs the detail directly to Find Hub. - Then, ask Gemini where your item is later, or view all saved locations in Find Hub's new memory tab. Google’s September Android Drop is introducing a handy upgrade to Find Hub that allows Gemini to remember where you left important items, even if those items don’t have a tracker attached. With the latest change, you can tell Gemini where you put an item instead of using a Bluetooth tracker to find it later. For example, you could say, “Hey Google, remember in Find Hub that I put my passport in my bedroom drawer” and optionally attach a photo for additional context. Gemini then saves that information in a dedicated “remembered items” tab in Find Hub so you can easily get back to it again by just asking where it is. This feature plugs a hole in Google’s current tracking setup. While Find Hub is ideal for tagged belongings, there are plenty of things you routinely misplace — such as passports, spare keys, documents, or other small essentials — that aren’t worth attaching a tracker to. This new feature essentially provides a lightweight memory layer for those items. The feature will be rolled out to Android 16 and newer devices in countries where Gemini and Find Hub are supported. Google says it will be available soon. This is just one part of the September Android Drop, which also includes enhancements such as Motion Assist to help alleviate motion sickness and new upgrades to Google Messages. However, for those of us who spend far too much time looking for lost items, this new Gemini feature may be the most impactful update of them all. item.title: Google Health's late August update adds more manual workout logging freedom
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.42
What you need to know - Google Health is rolling out v5.07 to Android and iOS users late this week, bringing a major update to manual workout logging. - Users can now "add or adjust" their metrics much easier, and any changes will appear in their post-workout summaries much quicker. - Other updates this week include trail run and incline data in "Running Distance" totals, a fix for Maps in the Health app, and more. Google Health is rolling out one more update late in August that's just what the doctor ordered for fitness users. The company detailed v5.07 in a community post for the Google Health app this morning (Aug 28). This update is rolling out for Android and iOS users late this week, bringing three important "Activity and Fitness" updates. These improvements concern the Health app's manual workout logging capabilities. Google says users can now "add and adjust more metrics when logging an exercise manually." Any edits made should now appear more quickly in your workout summary. What's more, Google Health now lets users add more metrics and workout information when switching from pool swimming to an open swim exercise. If you're taking things outside, the patch notes state the maps experience has been upgraded. Users should experience faster loading times and "smoother rendering." The patch also solves a bug where some users wouldn't see a map after finishing a run or a long walk. Similarly, the patch this week brings trail runs and incline runs into your "Running Distance" totals. For weight trackers, Google highlights its work in bringing more clarity to trends. Users should be able to notice changes more easily in the weight graph. Lastly, a connection problem between Health Connect and certain Android phones has been fixed. Consistency is key This update falls right in line with Google's Nutrition Logging update. It's that ability for users to add the metrics that matter. The details that matter. Its devices and app do a good job of capturing the majority of what we need, but what about those minute details? What if something needs to change? The program's not going to do that. Placing that ability in the user's hands is always a plus. The consistent Google Health updates continue, even into the final days of August. The last major patch that turned heads was the app's Nutrition Logging patch. This arrived in v5.04, in which Google introduced "custom foods." The purpose was to give users a personal touch behind how they log the meals they've eaten. Users can now "create, edit, and delete" their nutrition logs with more freedom. However, while useful, Google Health added another feature: Quick Logging. The company designed this to be an alternative to the traditional Nutrition Logging approach. Users don't have to search or add the specific name of what they've consumed. Instead, all they're required to add is the meal's calories and macronutrients. Google also added Naps in the Today tab and a Cycle Health update, making it easier for users to track long-term trends. item.title: What's next from Google Translate will upgrade Android in all the right ways
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.22
What you need to know - Google rolls out two major updates for the Translate app to end the week, beginning with multitasking capabilities for Android. - Android users can now continue translating speech in the background, giving them the freedom of opening other apps or locking their device. - For iPhone users, Google says they now have support for real-time translations via earbuds or by holding their phone to their ears. Google wants to end the week with an update for its Translate app across its supported devices. The company says Android users will find capabilities flexible enough for their day-to-day. This morning (Sept 4), Google says its latest features rolling out for Android and iOS will assist users with translating over 70 languages in "near real-time." Users on Android reportedly hold live translation sessions that last "longer than five minutes." Google states the Translate app can now continue translating even while in the background. This lets users hop into other apps and multitask or lock their phone. Google Translate will continue working, ready to reveal its translated content for you when you're ready. This is rolling out for Android users today. Google says it's preparing an update for Apple iOS users, but that is "coming soon." If you have an iOS device, this late-week update brings translation capabilities through a connected earpiece. Android users received it in a previous update. Google Translate will deliver audio translation directly through your earbuds. However, if such a device isn't connected, Google says iOS users can hold their phone to their ear, as if on a call. Like the update for Android, iPhone users can expect this to begin appearing today (Sept 4). The work continues Google Translate isn't among the apps that always get major updates, but the company has been improving it little by little. In a similar vein to Duolingo, the Translate app added "streaks" for users practicing new languages. What's more, this earlier patch expanded the beta for Android's real-time translation support while wearing headphones. Gemini's been brought into the fold heavily for the translation app. It's the AI's speech-to-speech capabilities that get the job done. Earlier this year, Google rolled out a huge Translate app update for iOS users for headphone support. The feature offers a few different modes: Listening, Conversation, and Text-only. "Listening" is for real-time translations. "Conversation" lets you speak in English and lets the person you're talking to hear it in their native tongue. Android Central's Take The usefulness of Google Translate has shot up considerably over the past few updates. They've been strung out, so there's quite a bit of time in between each one. Nevertheless, what Google's brought has been useful. It feels like the days of carrying around a Spanish-to-English dictionary are gone. You can rely on your phone; whether you're learning the language with guided practice or listening to its translations. Just take it with a grain of salt, sometimes. Not every translation is as accurate as I'd like it to be. item.title: Lumus, Quanta reach licensing agreement for next-gen waveguides for AR glasses that may turn the tide
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.19
What you need to know - Lumus is expanding its partnership with Quanta this week, which brings a licensing agreement between the two companies for next-gen waveguides. - Lumus states Quanta will manufacture its next-gen waveguides: the Z-30 2.0, A-Lens 30 (30-degree FOV), and A-Lens 50 (50-degree FOV). - The company was at CES 2026 where it stated it's future for waveguides for AR glasses will be "thinner, lighter, and easier to produce." This morning (Sept 1), Lumus, a developer of waveguides for several big-name brands, announced a major partnership expansion. In a press release, Lumus announced that it has expanded its partnership with Quanta Computing. This expansion sees the two companies reaching a licensing agreement "to manufacture three new geometric waveguides for AR glasses." The post states Lumus is developing three new waveguides: the Z-30 2.0, A-Lens 30 (30-degree FOV), and A-Lens 50 (50-degree FOV). Thanks to the new licensing agreement, Quanta will handle manufacturing. What we can expect from the Z-30 2.0 is a 30-degree FOV "in a thinner, lighter optical engine." Lumus adds that its latest technology increases the display's brightness, alongside direct prescription lens bonding. The two new A-Lens waveguides (30 and 50) are Lumus' "lower-cost" production solutions. The next-gen A-Lens waveguides are reportedly cutting down the weight and thickness by 50%. However, Lumus states it maintained its image quality and efficiency with this upgrade. This is an ongoing trend that Lumus is trying to introduce into this advancing world of AR glasses. Trimming down waveguide weight and thickness is key, but so is image quality, brightness, and cost. Earlier today, Lumus' CEO, Ari Grobman, said, "Our relationship with Quanta has always been built around solving the practical challenges of bringing advanced AR optics into mass production. This agreement allows us to bring our next generation of lower-cost waveguides into manufacturing with a partner that understands both the technology and the production requirements behind it." Here comes the future, and Lumus is leading it As mentioned before, Lumus creates waveguides for several brands, even for Meta and its Ray-Ban Display Glasses. Earlier this year, Meta announced that it was doubling the production of its Ray-Ban glasses to meet demand. This was something Lumus echoed in its press release this morning. The demand for smart glasses continues to rise, but there's room for improvement. Its work to reduce the weight and thickness of its waveguides for AR glasses is one such upgrade. Additionally, the lower-production-cost A-Lenses are designed to help bring more products to consumers. We'll have to see how things pan out going forward. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android On a related note, Lumus was at CES 2026. This major tech event is where the company first stated what its plans were for the future of AR glasses. Lumus said, "That's the future for us—making these waveguides thinner, lighter, and easier to produce." Its announcement today further echoes that sentiment. item.title: Google adds shared Keep notes and custom themes to Messages
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.81
What you need to know - Google Messages gets two standout updates, including Custom Chat themes and Google Keep integration as part of the September Android Drop. - You can tap the plus button to add a Keep note, letting everyone view, edit, and contribute without leaving the conversation. - Personalize individual chats using curated wallpaper collections (like Animals, Landscapes, or Space) or your own gallery photos. Google's September Android Drop is here, and while there’s a lot to go over, two features for Google Messages are stealing the spotlight: custom chat themes and seamless Google Keep integration. Beginning today, you will be able to bring a Keep note directly into a Google Messages conversation by tapping the plus button. This lets everyone in the chat view, edit, and add to shared notes, whether you're building a grocery list or planning a vacation. The idea appears to be to turn your Messages conversations into the place where plans are actually made. This might be particularly handy for group chats, where information can get lost in the flood of messages. Google is also rolling out Chat theme, which lets you set different backgrounds and color treatments for individual conversations. Google has curated collections of wallpapers to choose from — including Animals, Landscapes, Space, and more — or you can upload your own photo from your gallery. Google recommends everything from a latte theme for a coffee buddy to a beach photo for a vacation group chat. Messages automatically matches the chat bubble colors. This is much more than the simple “Change colors” option we saw back in 2024. It’s rolling out now in Google Messages. Remember, these customizations are just for you, so that beach photo you set for the vacation chat isn’t going to show up on anyone else’s phone. Google actually announced these custom backgrounds and themes a few days ago, in a post to the Google Messages Community, so the September Android Drop is another confirmation that the feature is coming. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Expect to see both features become more prominent as Google pushes the September Android Drop to supported devices. item.title: Rakuten Kobo's major in-store e-reader expansion at Best Buy makes it so easy to shop
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.68
What you need to know - Rakuten Kobo is bringing its e-readers to stores for the first time, and it's doing so with 500 Best Buy shops across the U.S. - Consumers can shop the Kobo Clara Colour, Clara BW, Libra Colour, Kobo Stylus 2, and Kobo Remote. - Online availability for these Rakuten Kobo products remains on kobo.com, Staples, Target, and more. If you've ever wanted to physically shop Rakuten Kobo products, you're getting your wish. Today (Aug 27), Rakuten unveiled its newest partnership with a major retailer across the U.S. A press release states Rakuten Kobo e-reader products are heading to 500 Best Buy stores across the U.S. This will be the first time that consumers can shop in stores for Rakuten Kobo products. Previously, as the company highlights in its post, consumers could only shop online for these e-readers. To complement the retailer expansion, Rakuten Kobo's CEO, Michael Tamblyn, said, "Many readers want to be able to pick up a device, see the screen, and feel it in their hands before they commit. With Kobo eReaders now available at Best Buy, more American customers can do just that." Coming to Best Buy stores will be the Rakuten Kobo Clara Colour and Kobo Clara BW. Both devices are "compact and waterproof." What's more, consumers can shop the expansive Kobo Libra Colour. Rounding out Rakuten Kobo's retail expansion are the Kobo Stylus 2 and the Kobo Remote accessories. While it's nice to actually see and envision how these tablets would look in your hands in a cozy chair, Rakuten Kobo says there's more to experience. After purchasing, the post states each e-reader provides access to the Kobo Store and Kobo Plus. The former lets you shop for new books to read, while the latter is a subscription service. Kobo Plus offers a selection of packages with "support for a wide range of eBook formats, and an industry-leading experience for borrowing eBooks directly from local public libraries with Libby and OverDrive." More e-readers hit Best Buy I think I'll always enjoy reading a physical book the most, but e-readers have continued to grab my attention. The idea of buying a book and not having to wait for it to ship or get delivered is nice. I can hop right in, cozy up in a comfortable place, and enjoy myself. Rakuten Kobo understands that sometimes, you need to see (and feel) the device you're interested in. It helps takes the guesswork out an important purchase. We covered Rakuten Kobo's launch of the Libra Colour and Clara Colour. These tablets feature E Ink's Kaledio 3 module screens with stronger processing and improved battery capacities. The Libra Colour, which is what consumers can find in-store at Best Buy, features a 7-inch display, 32GB of storage, and full support for the Kobo Stylus 2. Another highlight of the Libra Colour is its ergonomic design. Rakuten Kobo worked on its form factor with comfort in mind for longer reading sessions. If you enjoy reading a physical book, the Libra Colour might give you those same vibes—it's just digital. item.title: Google raises prices on the TV Streamer and Nest cameras effective today
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.43
What you need to know - The Google TV Streamer has jumped from $100 to $150 at the Google Store and Best Buy. - Retailers including Amazon may still have older stock at the original price, but supplies could disappear quickly. - The Nest lineup also gets across-the-board markups, with all five Nest cameras and doorbells seeing price increases of $20 to $50. If you've been holding off on picking up Google’s smart home hardware, your hesitation just got a lot more expensive. The tech giant has quietly increased prices across its streaming and security hardware lineup. The Google TV Streamer arrived in 2024 for $100, replacing Chromecast as Google’s flagship streaming box. It was also pretty easy to find below that price, with holiday discounts knocking a few bucks off. Now, Google has quietly bumped up the device’s price by $50 to $150, as spotted by 9to5Google. The new price is already appearing at Google Store and Best Buy, though some retailers are still selling remaining stock for $100. For example, not all listings have been refreshed by Amazon yet. If you are fast enough, you may be able to pick up older stock at launch prices before it is cycled out. Google mentions increased component costs, with the Streamer’s 4GB of RAM and 32GB of storage making memory costs a likely factor behind the increase. Other recent Google hardware has already been under the same broader cost pressures. The Nest lineup is taking a hit, too. Google has increased the price of all five of its currently available cameras and doorbells by $20 to $50. The battery-powered Nest Cam is now $200, up from $180, while the second-generation wired Nest Cam Outdoor jumps from $150 to $200. The third-generation wired Nest Cam Indoor rises to $130 from $100. Both the wired and battery Nest Doorbells now cost $200, up from $180. Interestingly, the Nest Cam with Floodlight bundle is still priced at $280, and the Nest Hub, thermostats, and the new Google Home Speaker remain unchanged for now. item.title: Qualcomm's Adreno 'Neural Fusion' GPU will lean on AI to upgrade phone gaming
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.93
What you need to know - Qualcomm continues to tease its next Snapdragon debut with the Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. - The company says this chip utilizes AI-drive rendering tech, placing stronger resolution and frame generation directly into the graphics pipeline. - What's more, the GPU adds the Adreno HPM, which helps move larger chunks of data for rendering at a time, effectively saving more battery power. - Snapdragon Summit 2026 takes place from September 22-24 Qualcomm's Snapdragon Summit is coming up later this month, and the company is teasing its graphical improvements. Qualcomm sent a press release this morning (Sept 2) detailing the Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. If you thought this wouldn't involve AI, think again. Qualcomm says Neural Fusion is an "AI-driven rendering technology that combines neural processing, AI super resolution, and frame generation into a unified graphics pipeline." For context, Qualcomm says it's looking to deliver what consumers want from mobile gaming: console-like graphics, strong frame rates, and better battery life. This is important because Qualcomm states its Adreno Neural Fusion GPU nails all three of these desires, and consistently, too. The post credits this GPU power to the chip's new Adreno Matrix Cores. This reportedly brings its AI rendering engine into the graphics pipeline, giving developers the exact tools they need to bump up the graphics for your phone. Lower latency is another positive in this change. Helping that lower latency is the Adreno HPM (High Performance Memory), which feeds more data to the GPU for rendering, thanks to a "dedicated optimized cache of 18MB." Many of these changes help Qualcomm hit that last point: better gaming battery life. With the Neural Fusion GPU capable of moving more data at a time, it's effectively moving a lot less, which doesn't eat up your battery. Then, you have its AI models playing more closely to the graphical unit. Qualcomm will undoubtedly show off the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips in greater detail during its Summit from September 22-24. What we've been waiting on? Qualcomm's teasers will likely continue until its Summit in a few weeks. The latest major teaser we got spurred excitement. Qualcomm highlighted "Dual 8 Elites" on approach for 2026. Our eyes are looking at that long-rumored Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 "Pro." Qualcomm hasn't said anything yet, so do with that information what you will (it is rumored, after all). What the company has said is that its Dual 8 Elites will bring "better connectivity, camera functionality, and graphics for games." Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android What's interesting about those "Pro" rumors is that not everyone's phone could see it. While yes, these Snapdragon chips are reserved for flagships, the Pro could only seek out Ultra devices—the Galaxy S27 Ultra would fit that bill. We still have a while until Snapdragon Summit 2026 in Maui, Hawaii. Android Central's Take I believe it was Android Authority's coverage that likens what Qualcomm's doing with the Neural Fusion to Nvidia's DLSS 5. If you're a gamer or you've kept up with gaming in general, this hasn't sat well with people. DLSS 5 "enhances" your graphics through AI, but from the examples out there, people aren't convinced the original artists' intent remains. I hope Qualcomm's AI doesn't do that. And if it does, can I turn it off? I'm all for incredible gaming performance on phones, but not if the game doesn't look as intended. item.title: This is how Xiaomi's 'smart privacy display' could work on its next-gen phones
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.76
What you need to know - Leaks on social media suggest that Xiaomi is working on a "smart privacy display" feature, similar to Samsung's Galaxy S26 Ultra. - This feature would stop prying eyes from viewing your screen from angles; however, it could also alert the user about another person's gaze. - An automatic function, dubbed "page privacy display" in the leak, states Xiaomi's version would automatically protect your payments, texts, logins, and more. Following Samsung's Privacy Display for the Galaxy S26 Ultra, rumors said Xiaomi was looking to do the same. A glimpse at how this could work surfaced on social media, claiming Xiaomi is going the "smart" privacy display route. To end the week, Polish tipster Kacper posted what's been alleged as Xiaomi's upcoming "smart privacy display" on X (via GSMArena). This page is likely tucked into the software's settings page with the following description: "screen visibility is reduced. Your device will alert you when another person's gaze is detected." The "reduced" visibility concerns others peeking at your screen from the side. However, Xiaomi is preparing a little more. The tipster claims Xiaomi is working on a group or "scenario" feature for its smart privacy display. With this, users can group multiple apps or notifications under the privacy display's protection. If users don't go this route, the tipster suggests Xiaomi will automatically turn on its protections for "specific sensitive pages." A screenshot highlights "page privacy display." This would turn the feature on in a case-by-case situation. If you're texting, digitally paying, or logging into an account, the privacy display would activate. It appears that users would need to enable this feature. Taking inspiration Rumors that Xiaomi might pursue a privacy display like Samsung's started in February. Funnily enough, these rumors surfaced just before Galaxy Unpacked, where the Galaxy S26 Ultra and co. were revealed. A tipster alleged a privacy display similar to Samsung's was being "tested domestically." Xiaomi and Honor were two major companies that might've started chasing this new tech. A few months later, in May, Xiaomi's interest came to the forefront. It was stated that HyperOS 4.0, Xiaomi's software skin for Android 17, could introduce its privacy display. This could be revealed in October, which might also coincide with its next phone series: the Xiaomi 18, as GSMArena also notes. These phones (18 Pro, 18 Pro Max) are expected to continue that magic back display that was clearly popular for the company. Android Central's Take Early rumors said Xiaomi was going to make its version "like" Samsung's, and the rumors now clearly show the angle it's trying to take. Imagine using your phone and seeing a notification that someone is trying to peek at your screen. It's already weird as it is, but if Xiaomi's version goes off without a hitch, it could help. I'm eager to see how this works. What I really need is Xiaomi's live demo, which probably won't happen until October, unless we get teasers beforehand. item.title: The rumored folding iPhone Ultra looks sick, but Android foldables offer something more: choice
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.28
Rumor has it that Apple will announce the iPhone Ultra at its upcoming September 9 event, making it the first iPhone to sport an "ultra" moniker. We're not expecting it to push the boundaries of battery technology or camera prowess, but it is slated to do one big thing that no other iPhone has (intentionally) done: fold in half. This is going to drive a huge boost in sales for foldable phones, a category that has consistently grown since the first models arrived in 2019, but hasn't seen a particularly massive tentpole release like this one yet. Of course, as with anything Apple makes, you'll only get what Apple gives you, and rumor has it that Apple is announcing only one size and shape this time around. But Android foldables, which have been around for eight years now, have had time to develop and branch out. Android offers a substantial choice of manufacturers, shapes, sizes, and capabilities that Apple simply can't offer. If foldable phones are looking like your next big purchase, here are many reasons you should choose an Android-powered one. What is a folding phone and how do they work? Folding phones usually come with two displays: an inner display and an outer display. The inner display is made of special ultrathin glass that can bend (unlike normal glass) and is reinforced with a preinstalled screen protector. The phone's frame is split into two halves connected by a specialized hinge, allowing you to open and close the phone. The foldable inner display is a special type of flexible OLED panel that's built to bend, too. A specialized hinge holds everything together, keeping dust and water out of the phone. It's a true marvel of engineering, and some foldables are even extremely durable, as proven by my Honor Magic V6 torture test. Both the inner and outer displays work the same way a regular smartphone touchscreen does. You can open apps on either of them, allowing you to choose the size of the "canvas" you want to view them on. What types of folding phones exist (and why would someone want one)? The leaked image of the iPhone Ultra above shows what's known as a book-style foldable. When a book-style phone is closed, its size and shape are similar to those of a standard smartphone, so all your favorite apps look and feel nearly identical to those on your existing smartphone. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Opening a book-style phone doubles its size, turning it into a small tablet that lets you get more done without switching to a laptop or other computer. I work on the go quite a bit, and a folding phone makes it easy to get most of my work done efficiently. I rarely watch videos on my phone, but when I do, the extra-large inner display is a real treat. Because of the large size, multitasking is one of the best features of a book-style foldable. You can run two or three apps side by side on these phones, and even put apps in floating windows, like on a laptop OS. Plus, the taskbar on the inner display makes it feel even more like a multitasking beast, similar to a laptop OS (like Windows or macOS). Book-style foldables come in many sizes and shapes, though most are slightly taller and narrower than your average smartphone when closed. Google began its foldable journey with a shorter, wider model, but made the next three entries a bit taller. Meanwhile, Samsung just introduced its first shorter, wider model (the Galaxy Z Fold 8), and Apple's iPhone Ultra is rumored to use this same size and shape. Shorter, wider models are best for video content and feel a lot like holding a small TV when unfolded. Apple's iPhone Ultra is said to come in just one shape and size, while Android foldables offer tons of different sizes, shapes, and form factors. You can even get tri-fold foldables! While book-style foldables get the bulk of the attention, flip-style foldables were better sellers for a few years. Phones like the Motorola Razr 2026 series look like a slightly taller normal smartphone when opened, then fold into a perfectly pocketable half-sized phone when closed. These phones solve the issue of overly large phones while still giving you the flexibility to use a small screen for things like notifications and messaging, then a larger screen when you need it. We generally recommend Motorola's Razr flip phones over Samsung's Z Flip line because Motorola's outer screen is more capable, and the company's designs are far more interesting. Flip phones are also wonderful for photos and videos thanks to their shape. It's easy to bend a flip phone at a 90-degree angle and use it as a "tripod" to take group photos. You can also use this same shape and hold it sideways to take video like a classic camcorder. Do folding phones have any downsides? Folding phones offer unique form factors and ways to interact with your favorite apps, but not everything is a win-win. When shopping for a book-style folding phone, the first thing you'll probably notice is the price. Yeah, there's quite a bit of sticker shock here, and that's mainly because this is a two-in-one device. Think of it as buying a phone and a tablet at the same time, and you'll understand. Flip-style phones are typically priced the same as traditional flagship phones but tend to have one fewer rear camera. Even Motorola's Razr Ultra line doesn't have a third camera on the back, despite the higher price. Both flip and book-style foldables are often a bit less powerful than top-tier traditional flagship smartphones. The problem is that there's not as much space in these phones for cooling, since they have to be thinner than a traditional phone to avoid feeling like a brick when closed. Lastly, durability. Folding phones got a bad rap pretty early on when the original Galaxy Z Fold's inner display would spontaneously break, but those problems have generally been solved. There's always a chance the folding glass could break, but these phones have undergone so many years of evolution and hardening that such a failure is almost unheard of. Stores like uBreakiFix readily have parts to repair them, and phone companies offer warranties and other insurance programs that help cover any potential issues. As someone who has reviewed dozens and dozens of folding phones over the past seven years, I've never seen a phone break in person. My wife has also been using flip phones for the past four years, and the only time one of hers broke was after being dropped with the phone unfolded. Considering how many traditional smartphones break every day from drops, there's no reason to suggest that these phones are any less durable with regular use. Nick started with DOS and NES and uses those fond memories of floppy disks and cartridges to fuel his opinions on modern tech. Whether it's VR, smart home gadgets, or something else that beeps and boops, he's been writing about it since 2011. item.title: Google Messages just became a lot more fun with new chat themes, but it could learn a thing or two from Apple Messages
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.18
Google has been steadily improving its Messages app over the years, especially since the advent of RCS. We've been seeing some fun features arriving in the app, such as Voice Moods and Selfie GIFs. However, until now, customizing your chat look has been limited to just changing the color of your chat bubbles, and even that was pretty limited. Now, Google has introduced new chat themes, which can fully transform your conversations. It lets you pick from a selection of photos (or you can upload your own) as a background and even changes the color of chat bubbles to match. It's actually a pretty fantastic upgrade to the Google Messages experience that makes it feel much more fun, although I do think it went a step further. I'll walk you through changing your chat theme in Google Messages and explain why I want a little more. How to change your chat theme in Google Messages 1. Open a message. Tap the three dots in the top right corner of your chat. 2. In the overflow menu, tap Chat theme. 3. Select from among the provided themes or tap Choose a photo to upload an image from your gallery. 4. Select a photo from within a theme or within your gallery. Tap Next. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android 5. Choose a color combination in the Colors row or stick with the automatic selection. You can preview your theme and colors in the image above. 6. Tap Apply to save your theme to the chat. Enjoy your new chat theme! Chat themes are fun, but... Chat themes are something I've been wanting in Google Messages for some time. On the one hand, I like the relative simplicity of the app, but on the other hand, it can feel quite monotonous with the simple black or white background. Changing chat bubble colors were a nice way to break up some of that monotony, but they were limited to just nine color options and none of them were particularly good. Chat themes is a great step forward, and in some ways, makes Google Messages feel as fun as Backgrounds on Apple Messages. However, there are a few things I think Google could have implemented to make this a much more full-featured experience. It feels like a missed opportunity that Google didn't implement Nano Banana in any way whatsoever. Gemini is already integrated into Google Messages, letting you chat with the AI or remix images shared in a chat. I would have loved to see an option to generate a background on-device with Nano, similar to how iPhones let you describe or edit preloaded backgrounds with Apple Intelligence. I also think Google could take chat themes a step further by having them sync across devices. Right now, when using Chat themes, you'll notice at the top of the page that "only you will see these changes." That means once you apply a theme, it will show up for you but not for the recipient. On the one hand, I get it, because your friend may pick a theme that you find annoying, inappropriate, or just don't like. However, even Apple Messages syncs backgrounds for both users across iPhones, and some apps like Instagram and Facebook Messenger also sync chat backgrounds (though with a limited selection), which has led to some fun surprises and "fights" over which one to keep. As one friend puts it, it would be fun swapping a background "and seeing how long it takes someone to notice." Perhaps Google can add a toggle that lets the person changing it sync their background choice across devices, while letting the recipient either keep it or select their own without syncing it back. Finally, I've noticed a weird bug that freezes the Google Messages app when I tap a theme but don't apply it, then exit back to the chat. Fully exiting the Google Messages app will bring things back to normal. My colleague, Nick Sutrich, has also noticed this, though it doesn't seem to occur for everyone; a friend hasn't experienced this behavior. I do notice, however, that when he swipes back, he's met with a dialog asking if he wants to leave the page without saving the changes. That only appears for me when I opt to reset the background to default and try to exit without saving. It's a relatively small bug that Google can hopefully fix soon.
