item.title: Making the AI-powered case for legacy modernization
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 3.52
Sponsored In partnership withInfosys For years, legacy technology has been a problem companies knew they needed to solve, but one they often struggled to tackle. The cost, complexity, and risk of replacing business-critical systems could make modernization feel like a disruption to manage instead of an opportunity to pursue. But with the rise in customer expectations and the changes AI brought to the economics of software development, that calculation is changing. Bupa’s modernization of its My Bupa mobile application offers a case study in what becomes possible when a legacy migration is treated as a business transformation rather than a technology rewrite. Bupa CIO of health insurance Asifa Sherazi describes the risks of waiting for legacy systems to become an emergency: “The end-of-life technology is a risk that compounds quietly, and then arrives all at once.” For Bupa, moving its application from Xamarin to native Swift and Kotlin improved the app rating from 3.7 to 4.7, while the user-perceived crash rate fell by nearly 24 percentage points on Android and eight points on iOS. “What they’ll notice is that when they need us, often at a stressful moment, it just simply works,” Sherazi says. Sanjeev Tripathi, senior vice president and region head of BFSI, healthcare, and public sector for Australia, New Zealand, and Southeast Asia at Infosys, contends that AI is helping change the equation. “The emergence of AI is fundamentally shifting the economics of modernization,” he says, reducing the effort, risk, and time traditionally associated with these programs. At Bupa, combining AI-assisted reverse engineering with forward engineering helped deliver the transformation in approximately 60% less time than would have been possible in the pre-AI era. Sherazi and Tripathi also highlight the human dimension of modernization: preserving institutional knowledge, giving teams capacity to adapt, and creating an environment where employees can surface problems early. Looking ahead, both experts see modernized platforms as foundations for more personalized, predictive and AI-driven experiences. The payoff of modernization may be less about replacing aging technology and more about building the flexibility needed for whatever comes next. “Modern platforms will become the base for far more intelligent AI-driven ecosystems, where AI is not just an add-on, but it is built into everything from design to operations. That's how the modern platforms will evolve, and the customer experiences will become far more personalized and predictive,” says Tripathi. For Sherazi, that shift is already changing the questions organizations can ask: “It used to be, can our platform support that? Now, it’s: is that the right thing to do for our customers?” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys. Full Transcript: Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I'm Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. Our topic today is legacy modernization. Companies across industries continue to struggle to bring AI modernization to legacy technology stacks, increasing the risk of losing vendor support, degraded customer experience, and limited capacity for innovation. Two words for you: future-ready foundation. My guests are Asifa Sherazi, who is CIO of health insurance at Bupa, and Sanjeev Tripathi, who is senior vice president, region head of BFSI, healthcare, and public sector for Australia, New Zealand, and Southeast Asia at Infosys. This podcast is produced in association with Infosys. Welcome, Asifa and Sanjeev. Asifa Sherazi: Thank you, Megan. Delighted to be here. Sanjeev Tripathi: Thanks, Megan. Wonderful to be here. And good talking to you again, Asifa. Megan: Thank you both so much for being here. Asifa, if I could start with you just to set the context for our conversation. There are seven million healthcare customers across the Asia-Pacific. Could you tell us a bit more about Bupa and the challenges it's faced in its modernization plan? Asifa: Yes, absolutely. Let me start with something about Bupa that shapes everything we do. We are a global healthcare organization. Think hospitals, clinics, dental, age care, digital health, alongside our insurance business. We reinvest back into the organization, so into our services, our capability, our teams, and our outcomes that we deliver for our customers. In Asia-Pacific, we serve around, as you said, seven million customers across health insurance and health services, individuals, families, corporate clients, patients. Our purpose, helping people live longer, healthier, happier lives is more than just a statement. It actually shapes our strategy, guides our investment decisions, and influences the choices our teams make every day. Now, for most of our health insurance members, the day-to-day digital relationship with Bupa begins through My Bupa, our self-service platform. It's the front door for managing cover, updating policy details, submitting claims, checking entitlements. Alongside of it, Blua plays a complimentary role. Where My Bupa helps members manage their cover, Blua helps them manage their health, digital healthcare services, clinical support, preventative health. And together, they let us move beyond transactional interactions towards more personalized, proactive care. Here was our challenge. Our mobile app, My Bupa, was built on Xamarin, and Microsoft support for it ended sometime in 2024. We had extended support in place, so our customers remained protected throughout, but we were clear-eyed that this was a bridge, not a destination. The runway was finite, and it was shortening for us. We made the decision to modernize from a position of stability proactively for the long-term safety and experiences of our customer rather than waiting until circumstances forced our hand, because the platform carrying our most important customer relationship was in effect standing still while the world around it was moving. Megan: Right. So you decided to act really proactively in that sense. And so, Asifa, what are some of the risks then of sticking with end-of-life technologies, and how will moving away from legacy technologies help you improve the customer experience? Asifa: Yeah. Look, the end-of-life technology is a risk that compounds quietly, and then arrives all at once. We saw it in three ways. The first is security and compliance. Once a technology is out of vendor support, the flow of security updates and fixes changes fundamentally. In our case, we put extended support in place as a bridge so our customers stayed protected. But extended support buys you time, it doesn't buy you a future. In healthcare, we hold some of the most sensitive information a person will ever share with an organization. That isn't data to us, it's trust. And trust is extraordinarily expensive to rebuild. We weren't prepared to run that risk on a shortening runway. The second is losing control of your own roadmap. How I'd explain that is iOS and Android don't stand still. Every operating system release, every change to app store requirements becomes something that you react to rather than plan for. As each one slows you down a little further, over time, that opens a widening gap between what customers expect and what you can actually give them. We're all customers. We don't benchmark a health insurer against other health insurers. We benchmark against whatever app we used last. And the third way was, and this is one we'd flag for peers, is the shrinking talent pool. Xamarin is legacy technology, and the engineering expertise available for it is limited. You end up with a critical customer platform supported by a narrowing group of specialists. That's a workforce risk wearing a technology costume. We partnered with Infosys and we migrated the entire application estate from Xamarin to fully native Swift and Kotlin, and the customer outcomes are why we're comfortable talking about this today. Our app rating moved from 3.7 to 4.7. Some of the stats that I'd love to share are that the user-perceived crash rate fell by nearly 24 percentage points on Android and eight points on iOS. The Android login success per visit doubled back up to 77%, and that's one the team that is most proud of, because a login failure isn't a technical event. It's a person who wanted to check their cover and they couldn't. The team achieved 100% feature parity in a single release, and 90% of our active customer base moved to a new version, and they've, I think, downloaded nearly 1.8 million unique downloads. From our customers' perspective, customers will never think about any of this as a technology change, and they shouldn't have to either. What they'll notice is that when they need us, often at a stressful moment, it just simply works, and that's the outcome we were really after. Megan: Those are some really striking results and statistics that you've shared there on the success of the migration. I mean, Sanjeev, could you talk a bit about why modernizing legacy technologies is so critical at this time, and how Infosys has approached that transformation journey with Bupa? Sanjeev: Sure, Megan. To be honest, legacy modernization initiatives are not new, and there has always been a strong desire to drive modernization across the entire technology landscape. And Asifa covered all the points that I was going to cover about the risks that have been there. But I'll reiterate, the reality is the industry has been held back by the cost complexity, and also the risks that have been associated with any legacy modernization initiative that has been undertaken historically. As Asifa mentioned, customer expectations of what was acceptable five, 10 years back are simply not acceptable anymore. The customers today expect a seamless, intuitive, responsive interaction across every channel. And Asifa also covered the growing challenges around security, resilience, talent availability, and so on. Finding talent on legacy technology is extremely, extremely difficult, and that introduces risk in every organization and in every legacy platform, most of which are actually business-critical platforms as well. Security vulnerabilities are getting increasingly difficult to manage, and as I mentioned, finding deep expertise in older technologies is very, very difficult now. So what has changed? What has changed is that we now have new tools that are available to us to address these challenges. The emergence of AI is fundamentally shifting the economics of modernization, and it's doing that by helping organizations to reduce the effort, risk, and also the time that is traditionally taken for programs like these, and that is why we believe that the time is now for legacy modernization. In fact, in Infosys, we have six strategic value pools that we have identified in our AI-first value framework, which is publicly available, and legacy modernization is one of these six value pools. And in the market, we are seeing very strong interest across our client base, and they recognize that the opportunity to unlock both technical and business value is now. With Bupa in particular, we approached the journey as a business transformation rather than simply a technology rewrite, and our approach had two key phases. One is reverse engineering, and then forward engineering. Let me just quickly cover what these two are. Reverse engineering, what we did is we extracted and we understood the rules, the processes, and the logic within the legacy environment, and that's a standard approach we took, we take in any legacy modernization program. What that does is it allows us to preserve the critical business functionality, but at the same time, it avoids the risks that often come with large-scale migration programs. The second aspect is forward engineering, where we re-architected the solution to enable a reimagined customer experience. The objective is not just a feature-by-feature migration or ensuring feature parity, which is important, but it is even more important that since we're investing this kind of money to create a modern platform that is scalable, maintainable, and is also capable for future innovation, and that's what Asifa mentioned about you need to be in control of your own roadmap. You have to build a platform which is capable of supporting future innovation as well. We essentially ensured nothing was lost in translation, and we significantly improved the platform stability and long-term maintainability. And some of the metrics that Asifa mentioned reflects the meaningful improvement in customer experience as well. Finally, just one more point before I close this question is the time to market. I spoke about the time is now, and because we've got the power of the tools that are available now. What AI allowed us is to accelerate the transformation dramatically. What would have traditionally been a long and complex modernization, was delivered in approximately 60% less time than what would have happened in pre-AI era, and that is the real story. Megan: So AI in this context is a real enabler in terms of the economics and the speed and all of those things you're talking about. If I could come back to you, Asifa, as much as modernization is a technology challenge, there is the human component as well, and I wondered if you could talk about how you prepared employees for these new technologies, and what challenges and solutions you faced on that front as well? Asifa: The human side of it is what I'm really passionate about. Technology was only half the challenge. The real work was helping people move from what they knew to what was possible. Modernization isn't just about replacing systems, it's about giving teams the confidence, the capability, the clarity to embrace a different future, and that's what determines whether change actually succeeds. From that experience, there were three human challenges that stood out for us. The first one was scarcity of expertise on both sides of the transition, and like we said before, Xamarin is a legacy app. We were moving away from a legacy technology, supported by a rapidly shrinking specialist talent pool, and modernizing onto two native platforms. Documentation of that existing environment was limited. Much of the operational knowledge sat in individual experience and in the code base itself, and that created a real dependency on a small number of people. And for the team, it was a confronting reality and a powerful reminder that modernization isn't just about technology imperative, it's actually a resilience one. What changed the dynamic was using AI to do the archeology. As Sanjeev mentioned, Infosys applied AI-assisted reverse engineering to harvest the legacy Xamarin code and extract the flows, the rules, the business logic, and generate native-ready user stories and acceptance criteria from it. The team did a lot of work. They mapped hundreds, I think nearly 1,500 regression scenarios to native epics, and that way, parity critical journeys were preserved by design rather than by memory. The human effect was just as important. Knowledge stopped living with a handful of individuals and became shared across the team, and our people could spend less energy holding institutional memory and more on designing and improving. So that was the first challenge. The second challenge, Megan, was capacity and not willingness. Our business analysts were fully committed to ongoing feature delivery. And this is a live customer-facing app, and you cannot pause improving the customer experience while you rebuild underneath it. AI-driven discovery and documentation removed almost an estimated of 400 hours of manual BA effort, and that's not a headcount story, that's actually people not being asked to do two full-time jobs at once. The third challenge that stood out was pace. Our original internal estimate was around 18 months, and thanks to Sanjeev and the team, almost like a one-team approach of how do we tackle this, the team delivered it in seven, and that's exhilarating. t's also demanding, and both things need saying out loud. We mobilized cross-functional squads across engineering, architecture, testing, release, because managing parallel environments while protecting BAU commitments is such an emotional load as well as a logistical one. We leaned in hard alongside the team, being present rather than reporting from a distance, regular check-ins, genuinely listening to concerns, unblocking things quickly so people weren't sitting waiting on a decision. And Megan, one thing I'll say is when you're compressing 18 months to seven, the most useful thing leadership can do is remove the friction in front of someone else and get out of their way. But the thing that made the biggest difference was surprisingly simple, actually. We built a visual depiction of the transformation journey, and we updated it every month so the team could actually see how far they've come. Because when you deepen migration of this scale, it's really easy to only see what's left to be done, and being able to look back at the ground that's already been covered gave people real intent and real momentum. And genuinely, it was exhilarating to watch. Watching the team's pride became their fuel. Megan: I love that idea of it being exhilarating, but exhausting. I think that's a great description. Asifa: Yeah. And the leadership lesson for all of us was just simpler than any of it. Programs like this have hard weeks, there's going to be incidents, delay, difficult conversations. And Sanjeev, you and I have had those conversations many times. The job of leadership in those moments is to absorb the ambiguity rather than transmit anxiety, because if people feel safe telling you bad news early, there's almost nothing you can't fix. I say this plainly because it's the truest thing about the whole program. I am so incredibly proud of this team, because what they achieved in seven months, while continuing to serve customers every single day without disruption, was genuinely remarkable. But what I'm really proud of isn't the speed and it isn't the engineering, it's that the team never lost sight of who it was for, so every decision that we were making, and they came back, it just came back to the person at the other end of the app. Megan: It sounds like you did an incredible job focusing on that people element just as much as the technology, which is so important. And Sanjeev, we've heard some of the incredible results Bupa has had with this, but more broadly, I suppose, looking across modernization use cases, where do you find that companies see the most ROI, and what advice do you have for leaders who need to focus on transformation at that legacy level? Sanjeev: Thanks, Megan. That's a very important and actually a very good question, because what we see is modernization ROI is sometimes viewed too narrowly through just a technology lens, and as Asifa mentioned, it is broader than just technology. Legacy modernization has aspects associated with business implications as well, so I'll just cover that very quickly. There are two dimensions, as I mentioned. One is technical ROI or technology-related ROI, and second is business ROI. On the technical side, and as you heard from Asifa as well, the biggest benefits come from faster time to market, platform stability and resilience, of course, and a lot of times, in fact, almost in all the cases, lower operating costs, and that is one of the aspects associated with some of the legacy modernization programs. Besides this, access to broader, more readily available talent pool, and security management, and ensuring that the platforms are secure and free from, as much as possible, free from vulnerabilities in the current environment. At the same time, making it easier to innovate, releases become faster so that the feature delivery into the market becomes faster, and also able to respond to any new technology innovation that comes into play. But this is only on the technology side. On the business side, however, the returns are often reflected in customer outcomes, and what we typically see are improvements in measures such as net promoter score, and in this case, for example, application ratings that you see on the app store. Both of which are actually very strong indicators of customer satisfaction and digital experience quality. I think it is important for us to cover, look at the ROI from both technology, but more importantly, from a business perspective. The second part of your question was about what would be my advice to leaders, and I think Asifa covered it very well, where she mentioned that the one-team approach, the providing safe environment to the team to be able to say what is going well, but also what is not going well, and keeping your eye on the end outcome. I think those are very important things. But I would also like to add that don't treat modernization as a technology initiative. It is a unique opportunity for us to rethink the business platform itself, and rather than pursuing a like-to-like migration, use the investment that you're making to improve customer experience, simplify processes, and re-architect for capabilities such as real-time personalization and data-driven decision-making. The greatest returns come when technology transformation is directly linked to business outcomes. And finally, and this is something that I have seen from personal experience multiple times, is you have to think from first principles. AI does not replace good engineering practices. It enables organizations to execute those practices faster, and it enables it faster, but also more consistently and at greater scale. The foundations of good architecture, sound engineering, and clear business objectives will continue to remain important, and in fact, their importance is going to increase as we progress. That, I think, is what I would say anybody embarking on a legacy modernization program should be focused on. Megan: I love the idea that this is not just about migration. This a chance, as you say, to reimagine what you can deliver and what's possible. Fantastic. Let's close with a forward look. Asifa, what innovation are you looking forward to that wouldn't have been possible before this, and what do you see on the horizon? Asifa: There's definitely lots of things on the horizon. But what excites us most isn't specific technology, it's that the question in our conversations has changed. It used to be, can our platform support that? Now, it’s is that the right thing to do for our customers? And that's a profound shift. There's three things, Megan, that genuinely weren't possible before, and we've touched on this a little bit, and Sanjeev's touched on it as well. This first is speed as a permanent capability. Since launch, Android and iOS, the team has shipped multiple rapid-fire releases, including our migration to a new payment gateway. Builds are now completing four times faster, codes are reaching to testers in about an hour, and we've reduced our code base by 30%, and our application footprint's reduced 18% as well. A simpler estate isn't an aesthetic preference anymore, it's what makes the next change cheap, and we've bought ourselves optionality to do that. The second is quality at that speed, which is the part we've been most skeptical about five years ago. AI-driven triage and predictive defect analysis, we ran it across nearly 1,400 cases to focus on testing on the highest risk journeys, which meant we went live with zero security defects and zero high severity defects, and Sanjeev mentioned that just before. The old trade-off between moving fast and moving safely is being renegotiated right in front of us, so that's the second point. The third one is AI-driven accessibility testing, which the teams treated as a critical rather than an optional opportunity. In healthcare, people who most need to reach us are very often the people whom our poorly designed interface is a genuine barrier, and so being able to test that systematically at scale was a real advance for us as well. And Megan, you mentioned on the horizon. It'll be remiss of me not to take the name of agentic AI. The shift from AI that supports a task to AI that completes an outcome end-to-end with proper governance, human oversight at the key decision points. What this program showed us is that the constraint is no longer the models. It's whether your platforms, data, processes are modern enough to let AI act safely, which is precisely why this work mattered now. Sanjeev alluded to it as well about that underlying architecture. Responsible AI as a source of advantage, not a compliance exercise, I would say. In health, if people don't trust how you're using their information, nothing else you build matters. We didn't modernize to have modern technology. We modernized to earn the right to do the next thing, and to do it in weeks rather than years. Megan: Absolutely. And now you have those foundations in place, like you say, all of these opportunities open up. Fantastic. And Sanjeev, just finally, as companies complete these migrations, what kinds of innovations and benefits are you seeing, and what do you expect in the next five years? Sanjeev: Sure. Again, good question, Megan. The reason is there is no uniformity on how these migrations are being done even today. As I mentioned earlier, so where there is simple lift and shift of existing code base onto a new platform, a like-to-like replacement, the benefits generally tend to be limited. Where we apply first principles, thinking about re-imagining, re-architecting, and refactoring the system to establish foundations for a far more flexible system, where rules are not boxed into the architecture, but are managed in a way that changes can be incorporated faster, personalization can be achieved in real time, and time to market improves multifold. That's where we are really seeing far more benefits coming through. And to take the example of Bupa, it is a pretty clear step change, both in terms of customer experience and how fast teams can actually deliver now. I think the app ratings have gone up significantly. The customer experience has improved. Even simple things, such as login success rate, has improved quite significantly. And on the engineering side, we are now building and releasing features roughly about four times faster, and we are also seeing the migration of nearly 100% of the customers onto the new platform. Now, if I look ahead over the next, you mentioned about next five years, I don't know about five years, four years, but over the next few years at least, I think it is going to get very interesting, because modern platforms will become the base for far more intelligent AI-driven ecosystems, where AI is not just an add-on, but it is built into everything from design to operations. That's how the modern platforms will evolve, and the customer experiences will become far more personalized and predictive. And even the way we build software will shift, with AI playing a much bigger role in the development process itself. Megan: Fantastic. Really exciting changes on the horizon then. Thank you both so much. That was Asifa Sherazi, who is the CIO of health insurance at Bupa, and Sanjeev Tripathi, senior vice president, region head of BFSI, healthcare, and public Sector for Australia, New Zealand, and Southeast Asia at Infosys, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England. That's it for this episode of Business Lab. I'm your host, Megan Tatum. I'm a contributing editor at Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. We were founded in 1899 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and you can find us in print, on the web, and at events each year around the world. For more information about us and the show, please check out our website at technologyreview.com. This show is available wherever you get your podcasts. And if you enjoyed this episode, we hope you'll take a moment to rate and review us. Business Lab is a production of MIT Technology Review, and this episode was produced by Giro Studios. Thank you so much for listening. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight. item.title: GPT-6 Astra Is Here: What You Need to Know About ChatGPT's New Model
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 7.08
OpenAI is rolling out GPT-6 Astra, the latest model to come to ChatGPT, following a self-imposed delay to help ensure its security features are used responsibly. OpenAI calls Astra the “world’s most intelligent and aligned model," claiming it's state-of-the-art for browsing, computer use, cybersecurity, software engineering, science, and professional work. AI companies tend to hype up every model release, however, so we'll have to see how it performs in practice. GPT-6 Astra is rolling out to organizations in OpenAI's Daybreak program, with a release coming for paid subscribers on Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans in the next few days. OpenAI has not yet clarified whether free users will be able to access GPT-6 Astra, but if it follows its previous rollouts, free access with limits may come at a later date. The rollout got off to a "messy" start, CEO Sam Altman says. Those who couldn't access it will get "one banked reset for every day you don't have access to Astra on your paid ChatGPT plan, starting today," OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux tweeted last night. "Team is moving mountains to give access as fast as we can." The Astra model outperforms OpenAI's previous releases, with benchmarks showing it beats competitors such as Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 and Google’s latest Gemini 3.8 Flash across a range of intensive tests. GPT-6 came out on top in benchmarking results for ARC-AGI-3, which tests the ability to solve unfamiliar problems; FrontierMath Tier 4 (v2), for mathematical problems; Terminal Bench 4.0, for coding; and Agent's Last Exam, for agentic features. OpenAI says the tool is better for agentic work than previous models, with what it calls “substantial improvements in understanding user intent and model behavior,” allowing you to delegate tasks more effectively and be confident the model won’t misunderstand you. It also claims agents will have improved decision-making when a prompt doesn’t clearly explain a task, meaning you're less likely to receive incorrect information. GPT-6 is also said to be faster than ever for browser and computer work. OpenAI confirmed previously announced plans to limit the cybersecurity features within GPT-6 Astra, citing concerns that its advancements could be used by bad actors to launch sophisticated attacks. “Astra will refuse to comply with more advanced cybersecurity tasks such as creating proof-of-concept exploits for vulnerabilities," it says. Instead, it’s letting its select Daybreak business partners begin experimenting with the full tool, allowing each to use Astra to identify flaws in their own systems before patching them. This comes after in-development models, unrelated to Astra, were found to have broken containment and hacked another AI platform, Hugging Face, last month. OpenAI slowed the development and rollout of future models to strengthen security measures after the incident. In a press briefing attended by The Guardian, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said he believes this is the start of the artificial general intelligence (AGI) era, a term used to describe the moment when AI can surpass human intelligence across cognitive tasks. “If we fast forward a couple of years, and we look back and say, when was it really that AGI was created, I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model," he said. “I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era," he added. Altman, however, recently told the Sources podcast that “At best, [AGI is] a very poorly defined term. I was going to say it’s like an irrelevant marketing term.” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang appears to agree. “For many tasks, we could say that we have already achieved AGI. I think all of those milestones...are kind of senseless at this point,” Huang said in an earnings call last week. Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Did You Know Your Roku Has Secret Screens With Hidden Features? Here's How to Unlock Them
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.37
How well do you know your Roku? You might use your Roku TV or streaming device daily, but I bet you didn't know that it has hidden screens that let you access features you might not find otherwise. Roku's secret screens won't be useful to everyone, but they can be helpful if you need to scan for local channels, check your Roku's speed, or test your own applications. Here are some of the most helpful secret screens your Roku has been hiding. Get Local Channels on a Roku TV If you have a Roku TV, such as one made by Hisense or TCL, you can face a lot of frustration if you bought a digital antenna to watch local channels, attached it, but can't find the setting to access it. Pick up your Roku remote, press Home > Home > Home > Home > Up > Right > Down > Up > Left > Right. You'll then see TV Secret Screen. Select Tuner Screen > Begin Tuner Scan, and it will add your local broadcast channels. Reset and Update If your Roku is acting up, resetting it can often restore it to working order. You can do a factory reset the normal way by pressing Home > Settings > System Advanced System Settings > Factory Reset and then following the onscreen instructions. Or you could use the secret menu by pressing Home > Home > Home > Home > Home> Fast Forward > Fast Forward > Fast Forward > Rewind > Rewind. This will get you a menu that has options for a Factory Reset, USB test, Cycle Channel Store Server, Cycle Software Update Server, and Update Software. See All Your Channels For a list of all the channels that you have downloaded to your Roku, as well as which version and build you have, press Home > Home > Home > Up > Up > Left > Right > Left > Right > Left. This will display the list, and then you can click on each one for the option to uninstall it. Check Your Speed If you’re wondering why your streaming seems slow, you can check your Roku’s speed. Press Home > Home > Home > Home > Home > Up > Down > Up > Down > Up. You’ll get access to Resets, Logging, and an AP Speed Test. Access Developer Settings If you're a developer and you want to test a new app on your Roku TV, you'll need to get into the Developer Settings. To do this, you'll press Home > Home > Home > Up > Up > Right > Left > Right > Left > Right. This will bring you to a screen where you can enable the Developer Application Installer to get started. item.title: Is Your Kid Addicted to Their Phone? How to Set Limits with Apple's Screen Time
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.11
Are your kids glued to their iPhones or iPads? To better control how and when they use their devices, you can turn to Apple's Screen Time, which tracks how much time they spend on their devices and which apps they use the most. To help them kick the habit, you can set time limits for specific apps and restrict or disable certain features. You can set up Screen Time directly on your child’s iPhone or iPad or choose their account from your own device. You can also share and sync the same settings across multiple devices if your child uses more than one. Apple’s iPadOS 27, currently in public beta, adds new options for managing a child’s device usage. The interface itself has been redesigned to offer more finely tuned and flexible parental controls for web browsing, messaging, social media, and more. But even without iOS 27, you can still manage all the major features of Screen Time. If you’re ready to tackle your child's tech addiction, here’s how to get started. Set Up Screen Time for Your Child To set up Screen Time on your child’s device, go to Settings > Screen Time. You’ll then see a list of categories to set up individually. You can also set it up on your own phone under Settings > Screen Time if you select the child’s account name in the Family section. If you’re working directly on your child’s device, tap App & Website Activity > Turn on App & Website Activity. The next screen shows you the average number of hours that your child has been using the phone each day. To drill down further, tap See All App & Website Activity. You’ll then see the activity by week and category. Swipe down to view the most used apps. Set Up App Limits Return to the previous screen and tap Downtime. You can now set limits on the days and hours that your child can access various apps and features. Tap Turn On Downtime Until Tomorrow to turn it on immediately. Otherwise, turn on the Scheduled switch and set up the specific hours to create time limits for all days. You can also select Customize Days to schedule different times for each day of the week. Return to the previous screen and select App Limits > Add Limit. Tap All Apps & Categories to block everything. If you want to block only certain categories, select them individually. When finished, tap Next. On the next screen, choose the daily duration to set the number of hours during which the apps and categories you selected are blocked. Tap Customize Days to set a different number of hours for certain days. Tap the checkmark to finish. At the main screen, select Always Allowed. Here, you can choose which contacts your child can communicate with during downtime. Tap Contacts > Specific Contacts, and choose the allowed contacts. Next, you’re able to choose which apps your child can use even during downtime. In the top section, tap the minus (-) icon next to an app and then tap Remove to block it. In the section below, tap the plus (+) icon next to an app to allow your child to use it. At the main screen, tap Screen Distance. This option tries to reduce the risk of eye strain and myopia if your child stares at the screen too long or too close. Tap Continue and then tap Turn On Screen Distance. If your child gets too close to the screen, an alert should appear. Set Up Communication Limits From the main screen, tap Communication Limits to set restrictions on certain types of communication. Select During Screen Time to change with whom your child can communicate. By default, there are no limitations. To dial this back, select Contacts Only or Contacts & Groups with At Least One Contact so that they can communicate only with people in their contacts list. Select During Downtime to set what is allowed during Downtime hours. By default, all contacts are allowed. To limit this to certain people, select Specific Contacts. Any contacts you already allowed will appear. Tap Add Contacts to add more people. From the Screen Time page, select Communication Safety and enable the feature, which aims to prevent your child from seeing nude, gory, or violent images and videos. To learn more about this feature, tap View Child Safety Resources. You're also given the option to enable Improve Communication Safety, which will share data with Apple to help improve the feature for everyone. Additional Content and Privacy Restrictions In addition to limits on app usage and communications, you can also set restrictions on content, purchases, and privacy. On the main screen, select Content & Privacy Restrictions, then enable the switch. In the top section, you'll be able to review the following categories: - iTunes & App Store Purchases: Choose whether to allow or not allow your child to install or delete apps or make in-app purchases. You can also require a password for these actions. - Allowed Apps & Features: Turn off any apps and features you don’t want your child to use during Downtime. These include Mail, Safari, FaceTime, Wallet, AirDrop, the iTunes Store, News, and many others. - App Store, Media, Web, & Games: Here, you’re able to prevent your child from seeing explicit content in the Music, Podcasts, News, and Fitness apps. You can also choose which movies, TV shows, books, apps, and other content to allow based on ratings and other criteria. - Siri: Choose which of Siri’s skills and capabilities your child can access, such as writing assistance, math assistance, and image creation. - Accessibility: You can determine whether your child can use Apple's Visual Intelligence feature to ask their device about images on the screen or in their surroundings. Under the Privacy and Allow Changes to sections, you'll be able to select individual device features and choose whether you wish to allow them or not. This includes Location Services, Photos, location sharing, advertising, Face ID, and more. Lock Screen Time Settings You’ve now finished configuring all the Screen Time settings. To prevent your child from changing things, go back to the main Screen Time page and tap Lock Screen Time Settings. Enter a four-digit passcode that only you should know. If you ever forget the passcode and need to reset it, enter the email address or phone number and the password you use for your Apple account and tap OK. At the main screen, turn on Share Across Devices to propagate the Screen Time settings for your child across their other Apple devices. Screen Time will now monitor how much time your child spends with individual apps, features, and settings on their phone. If you set up Downtime on the device, a message will pop up when five minutes are left before your child is blocked from using the selected apps on their phone. After the time is up, you can add more time by entering the Screen Time passcode and requesting access to additional time. About Our Expert I've been working for PCMag since early 2016 writing tutorials, how-to pieces, and other articles on consumer technology. Beyond PCMag, I've written news stories and tutorials for a variety of other websites and publications, including CNET, ZDNet, TechRepublic, Macworld, PC World, Time, US News & World Report, and AARP Magazine. I spent seven years writing breaking news for CNET as one of the site’s East Coast reporters. I've also written two books for Wiley & Sons—Windows 8: Five Minutes at a Time and Teach Yourself Visually LinkedIn. I've used Windows, Office, and other Microsoft products for years so I'm well versed in that world. I also know the Mac quite well. I'm always working with iOS, iPadOS, watchOS, and Android on my various mobile devices. And these days, I write a lot about AI, so that's become another key area for me. My wife always jokes about all the tech products we have around the house, but I manage to put them to good use for my articles. I like Lenovo computers, so I own a couple of Lenovo desktops and several laptops. I have three MacBooks and a Mac mini. For my mobile life and work, I use an iPhone 16 Pro, iPad Pro, and iPad mini as well as an Apple Watch. But since I write about Android, I own several Android phones and tablets. Like any tech person, I have a cabinet full of cables, wires, and assorted mysterious gadgets. And when it's time to take a break from writing, I have an old Xbox 360 and Nintendo Wii, both of which I use for exercise and fitness games.

item.title: Tesla's No-Steering-Wheel Cybercab Hits Austin Streets
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.94
Tesla on Thursday announced it is adding Cybercabs to its robotaxi fleet in Austin, Texas. First teased back in 2024, Tesla’s Cybercab is a fully autonomous electric vehicle that requires no driver intervention. In the absence of a steering wheel and pedals, the AV uses “camera vision and sensors to intelligently and safely navigate city streets, highways, complicated intersections, and parking lots,” Tesla says on a support page. It appears select customers in Austin can now choose between a Cybercab and Model Y when booking a ride via the Robotaxi app. Availability, however, may be limited as only 45 of Tesla’s 314 robotaxis operational in Texas are Cybercabs, The New York Times reports. Tesla says Cybercabs can be used for errands, commutes, and other purposes. Once the car arrives, its butterfly doors will automatically open as you approach it. You’ll also find options to enter the car, start a ride, or open its trunk, spacious enough for luggage, wheelchairs, golf clubs, and scooters, on the Robotaxi mobile app. Inside the car, you’ll find two bench-style seats at wheelchair height for easy entry and exit. At the center, you’ll see a giant 22-inch touch screen with access to entertainment and connectivity features, including music and gaming apps. From the mobile app, you can also adjust climate and media settings, and save them to your profile for future trips. Soon, these cars will also be equipped with V5 Starlink hardware for satellite connectivity. Initially, Tesla expected to sell the Cybercab to private owners and rideshare companies for about $30,000, but the sale of a car without pedals and a steering wheel has yet to receive regulatory clearance. You can still fill out an interest form on Tesla’s website, though. For now, Cybercab remains limited to Tesla’s robotaxi service in Austin. The company also offers robotaxi rides in Model Y vehicles in Dallas, Houston, and Miami. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Starlink: Bigger Boats Can Use Personal Maritime Plan, Too
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.89
SpaceX has tweaked its new Starlink plan for boat owners to cover slightly larger vessels. The new Personal Maritime plan can now support vessels 60 feet or less in length, up from 40 feet, as noted by a Facebook user who spotted the revision to a service plan agreement document on Starlink.com. “Use on larger craft or yachts (e.g., watercraft exceeding 60 ft. in length overall) is prohibited,” the document now says. Last week, SpaceX rolled out the Personal Maritime plan, following complaints about changes to its satellite internet service that risked pricing out digital nomads at sea. The plan is designed for small boat owners who sail internationally and rely on Starlink from country to country. When Starlink first introduced the plan, the boating community was quick to point out that it didn't cover boats longer than 40 feet. The restriction also created confusion. Some users reported successfully signing up for Personal Maritime, even though their vessel was technically longer than 40 feet, but others say they were denied. The Personal Maritime plan isn’t advertised on Starlink.com. Instead, eligible boat owners are invited to sign up via an email from Starlink. They have to submit documentation, including the vessel’s registration certificate. Other boat owners have to file a customer support ticket to switch. “The Personal Maritime plan is available exclusively for personal, small watercraft use,” the company’s service agreement adds. It costs $185 per month, a $10 increase from Roam Unlimited. But as part of the new plan, SpaceX has also hiked up the rate for Ocean Mode to $6 per GB, up from $2 per GB. Ocean Mode offers Starlink access beyond 12 nautical miles from the coast and in international waters. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. item.title: Why Hasn't Amazon Launched Its Leo Satellite Internet Service Yet?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.88
Amazon's Starlink competitor, Leo, was supposed to launch in mid-2026, but it’s now September, and so far, the satellite internet service has been quiet. What’s up? The company tells PCMag it’s still waiting for all the satellites to reach their assigned operating orbits, so Leo will have enough network capacity and coverage when it officially launches. In July, Amazon hit a crucial milestone when it sent another 29 Leo satellites into space, bringing the total deployed in Earth’s orbit to 396. That's enough to kick off "initial service," Chris Weber, VP for Amazon Leo, said at the time. But even after entering space, some of the satellites still need to reach an altitude of around 600 kilometers, where they’ll orbit and beam high-speed internet data to users on the ground. Tracking from astronomer Jonathan McDowell shows that only 299 of the Leo satellites have reached operational orbit. Another 78 appear to be descending or ascending into position. Meanwhile, a separate group of 14 satellites seems to be relocating and remains close to the operational orbits. (The rest have been or are in the process of being retired.) McDowell estimates most of the functioning satellites will reach the operational orbits by November, but some will take longer. “Their protocols may just involve a lot of preliminary testing," he told PCMag in an email. "And Starlinks often take several months to orbit raise, too.” Amazon didn't comment on when Leo will begin service or when more satellites will exactly launch. The last one took place two months ago. But the company noted that United Launch Alliance is preparing to launch a batch of satellites using its heavy-lift Vulcan Centaur rocket. Amazon has also shipped another batch to French Guiana for a seperate mission using Arianespace. For now, the Leo constellation is relatively small compared with Starlink, which operates about 10,000 satellites in orbit. Satellite industry analyst Carlos Placido also expects Leo to offer service only in certain areas or latitudes once it launches, citing the limited density of its satellite constellation. The first-gen Leo constellation is supposed to span 3,232 satellites, and even then, it won’t cover the polar regions. A second-gen network is in the works to add even more capacity and coverage. As it waits for its satellites to reach the right orbits, Amazon says it continues to expand network testing with employees and select enterprise customers in a closed beta. The company plans on sharing more news soon. Pricing hasn't been announced, but Amazon has suggested it’ll be competitive with Starlink, which already has over 13 million customers worldwide. item.title: LA Schools Join NYC in Blocking Student Access to Generative AI
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.82
From coast to coast, AI is getting a failing grade this academic year. Days after New York City announced a one-year moratorium on AI tools for students through 8th grade, the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) said students will be barred from using AI tools on district-provided devices this academic year. While NYC’s ban leaves some room for high school students to explore the tech with vetted programs, LAUSD seems to have shut off access completely. Students will be able to see Google’s AI summaries on top of search results, but they won’t be able to interact with the AI tool any further, The New York Times reports. The move comes as part of the district’s broader effort to reduce student screen time. Earlier this year, LAUSD banned digital devices for young kids and enforced strict screen limits for others. Some board members were reportedly surprised when the decision was announced at Wednesday’s committee meeting. The ban is temporary, and the committee will make recommendations on AI policy at the end of the school year, an LAUSD spokesperson tells Bloomberg. At both LA and NYC public schools, teachers will be allowed to use AI tools. And students can use AI chatbots on personal devices, so it remains to be seen how effective this will be. The bans arrive amid concerns that a growing number of students are using AI for homework and bypassing the learning process. AI tools are also notorious for providing inaccurate information and entertaining inappropriate conversations. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: AMD Creates a Threadripper Desktop PC for AI Models
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.78
At IFA in Berlin this week, AMD introduced a new powerhouse desktop PC line, Threadripper Halo Station, designed to run AI models locally. "This is the most powerful workstation in the world," says AMD SVP and General Manager Jack Huynh. "Designed and engineered for a complete new era of computing, capable of running AI models that are a trillion parameters." The product is meant for businesses and software developers who prefer running AI in their office rather than in the cloud. The liquid-cooled desktop PC features a 96-core Threadripper Pro 9995WX CPU and two enterprise-grade MI350P GPUs. Buyers can even expand it to four GPUs. “This is about as close as you can get to a personal supercomputer,” Huynh adds. Pricing and launch date were not announced. But the product will likely be extremely expensive, given that it can feature up to 2TB of system memory and up to 576GB of high-bandwidth HBM3E memory if equipped with four GPUs. Threadripper Halo Station appears poised to compete with Nvidia’s DGX Station tower PCs, which support AI models spanning up to 1 trillion parameters, for at least $100,000. Project Zenith Coming to Ryzen AI Halo PCs AMD’s other notable announcement is Microsoft’s Project Zenith, a special flavor of Windows 11 designed for software developers and coders, which we first saw at Build. Zenith will arrive on AMD’s Ryzen AI Halo PCs, which launched in July as mini PCs for $3,999. Micro Center has been selling units with Windows 11 Pro or Linux. Project Zenith stands out for offering a suite of preinstalled developer tools and focusing on a “distraction-free Windows experience.” Microsoft also created the OS for devices with 64GB or more of unified memory, enabling them to run large AI models locally. We don't have pricing or a launch date, but Microsoft says, "Project Zenith is just the beginning," while hinting that it's working with a range of PC makers on more developer-friendly systems. item.title: Don't Want to Pay for Whoop? Screenless Luna Band Costs $149, No Subscription
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.67
Screenless fitness trackers are the new battleground in wearable tech, with recent releases like Garmin’s Cirqa Smart Band and Google’s Fitbit Air arriving to compete with the market leader, Whoop. Now, there's an alternative, and it's cheaper than most of those rivals. The Luna Band comes from smart ring maker Luna. The screenless fitness tracker minimizes distractions while giving you a full picture of your health, tracking activity, sleep, skin temperature, SpO2 (blood oxygen), women's health, Vo2 Max, heart rate variability, and more. The device has a rectangular design and no display, and is attached to your wrist with a nylon strap with a metal frame. Your color options are Aloe Green, Desert Beige, or Onyx Black. Some other sources report the availability of a blue version, but it’s yet to appear on Luna’s website. The device is also water-resistant up to 5 ATM (about 164 feet deep). As it's not powering a screen, Luna’s tracker can offer up to 10 days of battery life from a single charge, which it says takes around 60 minutes. That works through a proprietary charger, which is included in the box. Unlike the Whoop 5.0, the Luna Band doesn’t require a monthly subscription to access features. It’s a flat fee of $149 to buy the tracker, though some of its software doesn't appear to be as advanced as its rivals'. The Luna Band was first unveiled at CES 2026, then entered a limited preorder period, which meant some customers got their hands on the fitness tracker in late July. Now, Luna is ready for a full launch, including immediate availability across the US. You can buy the Luna Band from its official website, with shipping beginning today, Sept. 4. The Aloe Green version will ship on Sept. 7, Luna says. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Steam, UV Lights, and Record-Setting Suction: The Most Cutting-Edge Robot Vacuums at IFA 2026
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.60
For years, IFA was a playground for wild, flashy robot vacuum and mop experiments—think elevating chassis and stair-climbing attachments. But at IFA 2026, the category is finally growing up. Instead of headline-grabbing gimmicks, this year's standout bots double down on what actually matters: raw cleaning power and practical mopping upgrades. They might look less radical, but these real-world improvements make this year's lineup the most exciting generation of robot vacuums we've seen yet. Below, we’ve rounded up our favorite robot vacuums from the show floor, along with pricing and release dates where available. iRobot Roomba Max 875 The iRobot Roomba Max 875 has a simple skirt that lowers from the chassis onto the carpet as it cleans. This skirt creates a temporary seal to help focus airflow on extra-stubborn dirt. The feature is called SealForce, and it's a practical change that could make a huge difference in the most important quality of a robot vacuum: cleaning power. Upright and cordless vacuums have long used seals to aid suction, but robot vacuums haven’t; instead, prioritizing mobility, efficiency, and battery life. A movable skirt could strike a balance between the category's needs and more closely match manual machines in fine-particle pickup. Aside from SealForce, the Roomba Max 875 cleans with an impressive 35,000 Pascals of suction and 20 liters per second of airflow. Its self-cleaning roller mop scrubs with 18 newtons of downward pressure while spinning at 300 rotations per minute. A nozzle in front of the roller sprays steam to loosen stains. The mop even retracts into the chassis, which extends a cover over it to eliminate contact with carpets. The base empties the dustbin and washes and dries the mop. The Roomba Max 875 marks a return to innovation for iRobot, and I can't wait to test it. It’s available now for $1,199. Roborock Qrevo Edge 3 Pro and Saros 20 Flow Complete Roborock’s new vacuums take a more direct approach to increased cleaning power. They don’t have any kind of special trick; they just have a staggering amount of suction. Both the Qrevo Edge 3 Pro and the Saros 20 Flow Complete have a record-setting 36,000Pa of suction power. Both can also elevate over taller thresholds than ever before, thanks to AdaptiLift Chassis 3.0, which can lift as high as 3.5 inches. I’m more excited about the Saros 20 Flow Complete, which doesn’t yet have a price or a firm release date in the US, but it will finally bring a self-cleaning roller mop to Roborock’s lineup of vacuums. The mop will exert 15N of downward pressure while spinning at 240RPM, and similar mops have performed exceptionally well in testing. The Qrevo Edge 3 Pro is available now for $1,499.99 and is the company’s shortest model to date, at just 3.13 inches tall. It does have a navigation tower jutting from the top, but that tower can retract when the bot needs to squeeze under furniture and clean hard-to-reach areas. Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV The Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV vacuums with 30,000Pa of suction and mops using a self-cleaning roller mop that washes itself with 158-degree Fahrenheit water. Aside from its suction power and design, the R3 increases its cleaning potency with vision and smarts. It has the same green laser to detect invisible dust as the existing Dyson Spot+Scrub AI, and adds a UV light to detect invisible stains. Specifically, UV light can reveal dried substances like alcohol, milk, and even urine that can be hard to spot once dry. Shark has a similar UV light on its latest flagship model, the PowerDetect UV. In addition to the R3, the R2 Nurovi is a Costco exclusive that has spinning triangular mop pads to better clean corners. The R1 Nurovi is a vacuum-only bot with an angled side sweeper to precisely move dust from along walls and corners and into the path of the vacuum. The R3 is slated to go on sale in the US on Sept. 15 for $1,199. The $699 R2 and the $549 R1 will also come to the US market. Ecovacs Deebot X12S The Ecovacs Deebot X12S has a chamber designed specifically for dust mites. It pushes down into the carpet instead of riding along the top. Aside from the dust-mite chamber, the X12S has a privacy shield that can cover the navigation camera's lens. It also has a self-cleaning roller mop, a base station that washes and dries the mop, and a quick-charge feature that recharges the vacuum during pit stops. It’s available now for $1,299.99. Eufy Omni E35 The Eufy Omni E35 also targets dust mites with a potent 35,000Pa of suction and received certification from the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America for its success in removing dust mites and cat allergens from carpets and hard floors. The roller mop cleans itself as it works and uses water hot enough to eliminate over 99% of bacteria. It also has a Heavy Stain mode that soaks the area during mopping to loosen stuck dirt. The mop itself applies 16N of downward pressure, and the base washes and dries it after the run. The Omni 35 is now available for preorder at $1,299.99. Narwal Freo 20 Edge Narwal’s flagship Flow series extends the side of the mop cylinder that touches the ground, so more is in contact with the floor at once. The company introduced two new models with this tech at IFA, called the FlowWash Mopping System. Available starting September 7, the $799.99 Freo 20 Edge has 31,000Pa of suction for vacuuming, and the base station empties the dustbin and washes and dries the mop after each run. It also has a slim 3.7-inch height to fit under furniture, and can extend the mop to the side to clean along walls and in corners. Dreame Aqua20 Pro Ultra Roller X Complete Dreame’s latest robot vacuum-and-mop hybrid features a roller mop and steam tech similar to the Roomba Max 875. Only, it heats the steam to a piping-hot 356 degrees Fahrenheit before spraying it onto stains through four vents and cleaning it up with a mop that applies 18N of downward pressure and spins at 300RPM. The mop also extends far to the side to scrape away dirt along walls, and its navigation system can recognize 320 different types of obstacles. A North America release date hasn't yet been announced. I’ve been reporting on tech professionally for nearly a decade and have been obsessing about it for much longer than that. Prior to joining PCMag, I made educational videos for an electronics store called Abt Electronics in Illinois, and before that, I spent eight years covering the smart home market for CNET. I foster many flavors of nerdom in my personal life. I’m an avid board gamer and video gamer. I love fantasy football, which I view as a combination of role-playing games and sports. Plus, I can talk to you about craft beer for hours and am on a personal quest to have a flight of beer at each microbrewery in my home city of Chicago.

item.title: Will Former CEO Tim Cook Speak at Apple's Huge Fall Event? PCMag Readers Are Split
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.44
At Apple's big fall event, scheduled for Sept. 9, the tech giant is expected to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro, plus its long-awaited foldable, and a next-gen Apple Watch. In addition, this will be the first Apple event with John Ternus as CEO, adding an extra layer of intrigue. In anticipation of the "Surprise and Shine" event, we recently ran the third and final round of our Big Guessing Game, in which we asked you to weigh in on what you expected to go down on Sept. 9. (The prize is a new Apple Watch.) Read on to see what our readers predict. Will Tim Cook Speak (or Even Appear) at the Big Event? After 15 years as CEO of Apple, Tim Cook handed the reins over to Ternus on Sept. 1. Cook is not out of the picture, however: He is now the executive chair of Apple's board of directors and is expected to maintain the company's relations with the White House. But will Cook speak, or even appear for that matter, at Wednesday's event? Our readers are split. We asked what you anticipated Cook's level of involvement at "Surprise and Shine" would be. Interestingly, 27% of readers think he'll be a no-show, while 16% believe he'll be there but not speak. However, just over half (57%) say Cook will both appear and speak. What Can We Expect From the New iPhones and Apple Watches? Phones have been getting more expensive lately due to tariffs and the RAM crisis, and Apple has demonstrated it is not immune to raising prices on its products. We asked our readers what the new iPhone Pro model's starting price would be closest to, and they are fairly evenly split among the four options: 27% guess the lowest price we mentioned ($1,200), and 21% think it will be the highest amount ($1,500). Meanwhile, 26% say $1,300, and the same percentage say $1,400. Apple's entire 2025 iPhone lineup uses traditional graphite-based lithium-ion batteries, but might some of the brand's new phones feature silicon-carbon batteries, which can pack far more energy-carrying ions into the same space? After all, Samsung recently adopted silicon-carbon technology for the batteries in the Galaxy Z 8 series. According to one-quarter of our readers, none of Apple's new phones will feature silicon-carbon batteries, though the same percentage says such batteries will be included in three or more of them. About 32% foresee silicon-carbon batteries in exactly two new Apple phones, while 18% think they will be in just one. Speaking of batteries, we also asked about the advertised battery life for the new base Apple Watch. Eighteen percent think the device will have the same 24-hour battery life as the Apple Watch 11. A whopping 77% think it will be more, while just 5% think the charge will dip below a full day. Will Any New AirPods Announced at Apple's Event Have Cameras? Finally, we asked our readers if any new AirPods announced at Apple’s 2026 fall event will have cameras. Last month, Apple accidentally leaked its upcoming camera-equipped AirPods in a video in macOS 26.7. However, according to anonymous sources subsequently cited by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, Apple won’t release a new version of its earbuds until 2027. If Gurman's report is accurate, the 27% of our readers who say no new AirPods will be released this year are correct. Meanwhile, 35% think there will be new AirPods with cameras announced on Wednesday, and 38% say that there will be AirPods announced, just without cameras. Curious to see how accurate our readers' predictions are? Apple's fall event will be livestreamed from the Steve Jobs Theater in Cupertino beginning at 10 a.m. PT on Sept. 9. And, of course, visit us here at PCMag, where we'll be bringing you all the Apple news as it happens. About Our Expert I'm the Executive Editor, Features & Special Projects at PCMag.com. I oversee both traditional features and the wide variety of editorial packages we run, including the Readers' Choice/Business Choice awards and holiday gift guides. I am an adjunct assistant professor at Columbia Journalism School. Prior to PCMag, I was on staff at BuzzFeed News, Input, BreakerMag, and Blender. In addition, I have written for The New Yorker, The New York Times Magazine, The Washington Post, Wired, WSJ. Magazine, and Rolling Stone, and am the author of Everybody Loves Our Town: An Oral History of Grunge, a Time magazine book of the year. Check out my personal website for examples of my work.

item.title: iRobot Built a Transformer Vacuum That Deploys a Mini-Me to Clean Under Your Couch
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.21
BERLIN—iRobot is delivering true innovation at IFA with a concept robot vacuum that blew my mind. Called the Roomba Duo, it's really two robots in one, with some pretty amazing functionality. During a demo, I watched it roll over and suck up a pile of spaghetti on the floor like it was nothing, then wash the carpet where the pasta had been. That's not all. It then used a mechanical arm to deploy a smaller robot that had been tucked into a compartment on top of the main unit. The mechanical arm works similarly to the company's retractable mopping system from earlier models like the Roomba Combo 10 Max. Except instead of a mop, it lowers a whole other robot to the floor: the Roomba Plus 575 Combo, introduced earlier this year. It was an amazing feat of engineering to see in action, one that has to involve some serious counterbalancing. I then watched the nimble Roomba Plus 575 Combo traverse a 1.3-inch threshold without missing a beat. "The benefit of this is you've got the main unit for larger spaces and heavy-duty messes, while the companion unit does all of the smaller, tighter spaces," a Roomba spokeswoman told me. "And they work together with our app." For instance, you could send the smaller unit to clean under the sofa while the main unit cleans a food mess on the kitchen floor. The Roomba Duo is just a concept at this point, and iRobot has no plans to bring it to market any time soon. "It's just to show where we could see the category going, but not at the moment," the spokeswoman said. Even though Duo won't be hitting living rooms, it's still a cool peek into where smart homes are headed. By taking on two of the biggest headaches in cleaning—tackling huge, heavy-duty messes and squeezing under low furniture—iRobot is showing us how we'll all keep our houses clean ten years down the road. About Our Expert I'm PCMag's managing editor for consumer electronics, overseeing an experienced team of analysts covering smart home, home entertainment, wearables, fitness and health tech, and various other product categories. I have been with PCMag for more than 10 years, and in that time have written more than 6,000 articles and reviews for the site. I previously served as an analyst focused on smart home and wearable devices, and before that I was a reporter covering consumer tech news. I'm also a yoga instructor, and have been actively teaching group and private classes for nearly a decade. Prior to joining PCMag, I was a reporter for SC Magazine, focusing on hackers and computer security. I earned a BS in journalism from West Virginia University, and started my career writing for newspapers in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and West Virginia.

item.title: Apple Wants to Wrap Your Room in Sound with New HomePods, Says Leak
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.20
Apple has been part of the smart speaker market since it shipped the original HomePod in 2018. But though users did have the option to hook up two HomePods to play their music in stereo, surround sound (where audio is divided up between four different speakers across a room) has never been on the table as an option. Even if users did happen to own four HomePods and were willing to set it up manually. Now, things could be set to change. According to a trusted Apple leaker, posting on the MacRumors forum, lines of code in the latest audioOS 27 beta reference "tuning files" that interact with speakers in front-left, front-right, rear-left, and rear-right positions. According to pdxfu, in the four-speaker placement, the front speakers will use left- and right-specific audio processing, while the rear HomePods will utilize omnidirectional processing "designed to fill the space behind and around the listener." The code also hinted at a new device on the way. According to the leaker, some of the code references a device that doesn't appear to match any of the currently available HomePods, including the original, 2nd-gen, or HomePod mini. Pdfu says it's impossible to say if this is a reference to a 3rd-gen HomePod or a HomePod mini sequel. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman has reported that a HomePod mini successor with new Siri Ai support is expected soon, adding that the hardware has reportedly been ready for months and is expected to launch this fall alongside iOS 27. A new Party Mode could also be on the table. Party Mode, when enabled, will use an audio-rendering mode called diffuse. This means the sound will be spread into "a wider, more ambient mix," which will "fill a room more evenly instead of creating a perfect listening spot in front of the speakers." Apple Insider notes that as the code references new hardware, it's likely we'll have to wait for Apple to release new devices to see these features in action, and Apple still doesn't have anything officially announced yet. About Our Expert I’m a reporter covering weekend news. Before joining PCMag in 2024, I picked up bylines in BBC News, The Guardian, The Times of London, The Daily Beast, Vice, Slate, Fast Company, The Evening Standard, The i, TechRadar, and Decrypt Media. I’ve been a PC gamer since you had to install games from multiple CD-ROMs by hand. As a reporter, I’m passionate about the intersection of tech and human lives. I’ve covered everything from crypto scandals to the art world, as well as conspiracy theories, UK politics, and Russia and foreign affairs.

item.title: Apple's Sept. 9 'Surprise and Shine' Event: What to Expect, Including iPhone 18, iPhone Ultra, Watch Series 12, and More
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.49
Apple’s Sept. 9 “Surprise and Shine” event isn’t exactly aptly named. Details about the company’s upcoming products have been leaking for months, and I doubt there will be a single jaw left hanging by the time John Ternus—its new CEO—leaves the stage. But if there’s one rumored product poised to steal the spotlight, it’s the iPhone Ultra, Apple’s first-ever foldable. Cupertino is also tipped to unveil the new iPhone 18 Pro series, updated Apple Watches, improved AirPods, and more. With plenty of new hardware on the way, here’s a deep dive into everything Apple is expected to show on stage during the Sept. 9 event. How to Watch Apple's Sept. 9 Event The Surprise and Shine event will take place on Sept. 9 at Apple’s headquarters in Cupertino. It will kick off at 10 a.m. PT / 11 a.m. MT / 12 p.m. CT / 1 p.m. ET. If you didn't get an in-person invite, you can still watch it across a number of different platforms, including the Apple TV app, the Apple Events page, and the company's YouTube channel. Before the show starts, tune in for live coverage from PCMag's Executive Producer, Iyaz Akhtar, and CNET Editor at Large, Bridget Carey, starting at 9:30 a.m. PT / 12:30 p.m. ET. Unfolding the 'iPhone Ultra' First, here's what you shouldn't expect at Apple's Surprise and Shine event. While you may be hoping for a refreshed entry-level iPhone 18 reveal, and perhaps a new-generation iPhone Air, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, Apple won't be announcing these products on Sept. 9. Instead, the company is shifting the spotlight toward the iPhone Ultra, Apple's long-rumored foldable. It's expected to have a short-and-wide form factor similar to the Galaxy Z Fold 8, but it won't feature Apple's best-in-class camera system because it will lack a telephoto lens. However, knowledgeable sources claim that it will have a rival-beating, nearly creaseless display, as well as impressive durability, thanks to an advanced Liquid Metal hinge. iPhone Pros Only Although we supposedly won't see the base models, Apple is broadly expected to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. According to The Information, the Pro models will feature an under-display Face ID sensor, relocating the selfie camera to the top-left of the screen. The Pro models will also reportedly include a “mechanical aperture,” allowing users to control how much light enters the lens. Finally, Apple may move the devices’ memory chips closer to the core processor, potentially helping the iPhones process AI requests more quickly while keeping their reliance on cloud servers to a minimum. The phones will also come in a new batch of colors that don't include traditional black or white. More Wrist Computers Gurman claims that Apple’s modest upgrade trend for its smartwatch line will continue with the Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Both will reportedly get a major performance boost, along with a handful of new health and fitness-related updates. One of those features is an updated heart-rate sensor that continuously tracks your heart rate throughout the day rather than only detecting intense activity. Plus, the company is reportedly considering a ceramic case option, as well as new colors and bands. Fresh Budget Buds The new AirPods 5, an upgrade to Apple's entry-level earbuds, are also expected to make their debut at the Sept. 9 event. Gurman didn't say much about the rumored AirPods 5, but in an X post, he revealed that they'll continue to come in two flavors: one will feature active noise cancellation, while the other will not. There have been whispers about new camera-equipped AirPods coming down the pipeline, but Gurman says that's more of a 2027 conversation. Then There Are the 'Maybes' Of course, there are always products that are much more of a wild card. Gurman says Apple’s new TV set-top box and an updated HomePod mini are expected to launch this fall, but he isn’t sure whether either will show up at the Sept. 9 Surprise and Shine event. The new smart home hub, which will reportedly feature facial recognition to identify users, is even more uncertain: Apple could preview it during the event, but Gurman says its actual launch could come anytime between October and early next year. We won't know for sure about these rumored products until we hear about them directly from Apple. Stay tuned for PCMag’s coverage of the Surprise and Shine event, as we’ll be on the ground bringing you all the latest announcements, hands-on impressions, and analysis straight from Apple Park. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s Senior Writer for Mobile on the Consumer Electronics team, diving into the latest phones, tablets, Bluetooth speakers, audio devices, and other portable gear. I’ve been covering consumer technology for six years. Before joining PCMag, I contributed my tech expertise to Laptop Magazine, Mashable, Tom’s Guide, Esquire, Good Housekeeping, and more.

item.title: Big Time Storage Savings: Labor Day Weekend SSD Deals From Samsung, SanDisk, and More
item.description:

Ever notice that the storage space that comes with your computer or laptop just isn't enough? Thankfully, there are plenty of SSDs that'll give you extra space for all your pictures and projects.
